t.ispani@41.9,41.8:
Most of Georgia's Black Sea coast is subtropical, with tea plantations, citrus groves and lush forests, and on the plain near Kobuleti, between the sea and the hills, lies one of the strangest landscapes in the Caucasus. The Ispani mires are raised peat bogs, domes of sphagnum moss that have grown over thousands of years, fed only by rain, and they are among the few such bogs in the subtropics. They are part of the UNESCO World Heritage Site of the Colchic Rainforests and Wetlands, inscribed in 2021.

The Colchis lowland, the land of the Golden Fleece in Greek mythology, is one of the wettest places in Europe, with heavy rain throughout the year, and its forests and wetlands are relics of the vegetation that covered much of Europe before the Ice Ages. The Ispani bogs are protected in the Kobuleti protected areas, and boardwalks allow visitors to walk out over the moss without damaging it. The bogs are home to rare plants, including carnivorous sundews, and to birds that use the coast as a migration route.

Riding in Georgia is an experience. The main road along the coast, between Batumi and Kobuleti, is busy, with fast and sometimes erratic driving, so stay alert. Overtaking on blind bends is common, and cows wander onto the roads. Inland, the roads climb into the hills of Adjara, with tea plantations and forests, and the road up the Adjaristsqali valley towards the mountains is spectacular, with winding sections, old stone bridges and villages. The climate is humid, with rain at any time of year, and summers are hot and sticky.

Kobuleti, five kilometres away, is a resort town with fuel, shops and restaurants, and Batumi, the main city of Adjara, is about thirty kilometres south, with all services and a lively seafront. Georgian food is a delight: khachapuri, cheese bread, with the Adjarian version shaped like a boat and topped with an egg and butter, and khinkali, dumplings filled with meat and broth. Georgian hospitality is legendary. Walking on the boardwalk over the Ispani bog, with the moss stretching away and the mountains behind, is a peaceful and unusual experience.
t.segment cerro de cojitambo@-2.8,-78.8:
Cojitambo is a rocky hill that rises abruptly above the valley of Azogues, in the province of Cañar, in the southern Andes of Ecuador. Its summit and slopes hold the remains of a Cañari and Inca settlement, with walls, terraces and stairways, and the Inca road ran past it, a segment of the Qhapaq Ñan listed by UNESCO. The Cañari were the people of this region before the Inca conquest, and they resisted fiercely, later siding with the Spanish against their Inca overlords. Today the hill is also a popular spot for rock climbing, with routes on its cliffs.

Azogues, a town of about thirty-five thousand, lies a few kilometres away, with a large church on a hill, the sanctuary of the Virgen de la Nube, and a market. The region is known for weaving toquilla straw hats, known around the world as Panama hats, although they are made in Ecuador. Cuenca, a short ride south, is one of the most beautiful colonial cities in South America, with a historic centre listed by UNESCO, and Ingapirca, the largest Inca site in Ecuador, lies to the north, with a temple of the sun.

The riding in the southern Andes is superb. The Pan-American Highway runs through the valleys, with curves, climbs and views over the mountains, and the minor roads to villages and sites wind through hills and fields. The tarmac is decent on the whole on main roads, more variable on minor ones, with landslides possible in the rainy season. Altitude is over two thousand five hundred metres, and the weather can change quickly, with sun, rain and fog in the same day. Watch for trucks, buses and dogs.

Azogues has pumps, a supermarket and a few places to eat, and Cuenca has everything. Food in the region includes mote pillo, hominy with eggs, cuy, roasted guinea pig, and hornado, roast pork, as well as fresh fruit juices. Climb to the top of Cojitambo on foot, a short but steep walk, and look out over the valley; the Cañari and the Inca chose this spot for its view, and on a clear day, the panorama over the Andes is stunning.
t.segment el tambo honorato vasquez@-2.5,-:
High in the southern Andes of Ecuador, in the province of Cañar, a stretch of Inca road runs between the small towns of El Tambo and Honorato Vásquez, part of the Qhapaq Ñan World Heritage Site. The name El Tambo itself comes from the Inca word for a waystation, where travellers could rest and find supplies. This route was part of the great road that ran north from Cusco to Quito, and in this area it passed close to Ingapirca, the largest Inca site in Ecuador.

Ingapirca, a few kilometres away, is a remarkable place. The Cañari people, who lived here before the Inca conquest, had a ceremonial centre on the site, and the Inca built a temple of the sun on top, with fine stonework typical of Cusco. The elliptical structure, the remains of storehouses and living quarters, and the surrounding landscape make it one of the most impressive sites in the country.

The landscape around El Tambo is high and green, with fields of potatoes, maize and beans, pastures with cattle and sheep, and eucalyptus groves. The altitude is around 3,000 metres, so the air is thin and cool, and the weather can change quickly from sun to rain and fog. The people are mostly Cañari, with distinctive dress, including white felt hats.

Riding in this region is spectacular. The Pan-American Highway runs through the area, with curves and climbs, and the roads to Ingapirca and the surrounding villages are narrower and steeper. Traffic includes buses, trucks and animals, and the road surface can be poor in places, with potholes and landslides in the rainy season. Fog is common, especially in the afternoon, so ride early.

Cañar, five kilometres away, has fuel and simple places to eat, and Azogues and Cuenca further south have proper workshops and hotels. Sunday markets in the Cañar towns are a riot of colour, with roast pork, hominy and, for the brave, cuy, roast guinea pig, the festive dish of the Andes.
t.segment paredones paredones@-2.7,-79.4:
West of Cuenca the Andes fall away towards the Pacific in one of the most dramatic descents on the continent, from the cold lakes and páramo of the Cajas massif to the hot banana plantations of the coastal plain. Paredones, a small Inca site in the Molleturo area on this western flank, takes its name from the stone walls, paredones, that survive among the grass: remains of buildings, enclosures and a stretch of the Qhapaq Ñan that crossed these mountains between the highlands and the coast. It is part of the Andean road system inscribed as a World Heritage Site in 2014.

The site sits high, often in cloud, and on a clear day the views over the lakes and ridges are wide. The Inca chose such places for waystations and control points along the road, and this route connected the highland centre of Tomebamba, today's Cuenca, with the coast.

The road that brings you here is the reason to come. From Cuenca, the E582 climbs into the Cajas National Park, a landscape of hundreds of glacial lakes, rocky ridges and polylepis woods, crossing the continental divide at well over 4,000 metres. Then it plunges westwards, down through cloud forest and tropical valleys to Naranjal and Puerto Inca on the coastal plain, losing almost all of that height in a few hours. The tarmac is generally good but the curves are endless, fog can reduce visibility to a few metres, and trucks crawl up and race down. Temperature can swing from near freezing to thirty degrees in a single descent, so dress in layers you can peel.

Wildlife in the Cajas includes Andean condors, llamas reintroduced to the park, foxes and an extraordinary range of hummingbirds and orchids in the cloud forest below. In the lakes, trout introduced long ago are now a local staple, served fried in roadside restaurants along the road.

Naranjal, twenty-two kilometres away and far below, has fuel and services, and Cuenca, a lovely colonial city and World Heritage Site in its own right, has everything. Fill up before crossing the Cajas, as there are no stations on the high section, and keep an eye on your fuel gauge on the long climb, which drinks more than you expect at altitude.
t.segment llaviuco llaviuco@-2.8,-79.1:
The Incas built a road across the Andes that stretched for thousands of kilometres, linking Quito, Cusco and far beyond, and parts of it still survive in Ecuador. Llaviuco is a short surviving segment, listed by UNESCO as part of the Qhapaq Ñan, the great Andean road system. It lies inside Cajas National Park, in a landscape of high moorland, small lakes and cloud forest, above Cuenca. The stones of the old road are set in the ground by hand, and walking them gives a direct sense of how this empire moved people, messengers and llamas through the mountains.

The setting is magnificent. Cajas is a world of páramo, a treeless highland of tussock grass, cushion plants and hundreds of lakes left by glaciers, and the air is thin, cold and often wet. Llaviuco itself is a lake with a patch of Polylepis forest, a twisted, red-barked tree that grows higher than almost any other in the world. Cuenca, the nearby city, is one of the most elegant in South America, with colonial churches, cobbled streets, a river lined with trees and the Inca site of Pumapungo beneath its modern streets. The famous Panama hat, which is actually Ecuadorian, is woven in this region.

The ride up from Cuenca is a good one. The road to Cajas climbs steadily through farmland and then moorland, with bends, long views and changing weather, and crosses a high pass above four thousand metres. The air gets cold quickly, and fog and rain can cut visibility to a few metres, so carry warm and waterproof gear and ride slowly. Altitude can bring headaches and breathlessness to those who arrive suddenly. The dry months, from June to September, are the best, though the weather in the páramo can turn at any time.

Cuenca, about eighteen kilometres away, has everything: fuel stations, restaurants, hotels and markets. Try a bowl of locro, a potato and cheese soup, and a cup of hot canelazo, a cinnamon and sugar-cane spirit drink, at a roadside stall. Entry rules and fees for the park change, so check at the visitor centre, and bring layers, sun cream and patience.
t.segment botija paqui botija paqui@-2.7,-:
Naranjal is the opposite of the high Andes. Down on the coastal plain of southern Ecuador, the air is hot and humid, the land is green and flat, and the farms grow bananas, cacao and, increasingly, shrimp in ponds along the estuaries. Yet the same Inca road system that crosses the mountains near Cuenca came down to this coast, and the segment at Botija Paqui is a stretch of it that UNESCO lists among the Qhapaq Ñan sites. The road was both a highway and a statement, linking distant provinces to the empire's heart.

The valley that leads down here from the Andes gives a feel for the sudden changes of climate in Ecuador. In a few hours you can descend from cold, windy páramo through cloud forest to tropical lowland, passing banana plantations and cacao groves, with colours and smells changing at every turn. Naranjal itself is a farming town, and cacao beans from this region are exported for chocolate. The lowland rivers carry mud and rain from the mountains, and floods occur in the wet season.

Riding down from the mountains is a joy, with long descents, tight bends and views that open dramatically as you leave the cloud. Surfaces on the main road are generally good, though landslides can close sections after heavy rain and trucks loaded with bananas grind up the hills. On the plain, the road is straight, hot and busy, with heavy traffic, motorbike taxis and market stalls. The best time to ride is the dry season from June to November, and the wet season from January to April can be difficult.

Naranjal has fuel stations, shops and restaurants, and you should fill up before heading into remote country. Eat a plate of encebollado, a fish and yuca soup with onions that Ecuadorians swear cures hangovers, or fried plantain with fresh cheese. Take water and sun protection, and ask locally before walking on any stretch of the old road, since access can be through private land and the surface may be overgrown.
t.imnati@42.1,41.8:
Imnati sits on the Kolkheti lowland, the flat, wet corner of western Georgia where the Rioni river reaches the Black Sea. The land here is marsh, reed bed and alder forest, laced with canals and small lakes, and it is one of the most important wetlands in the region, with a coastal national park that UNESCO recognised in 2021 for its Colchic rainforests and wetlands. Poti, ten kilometres away, is a port town of nearly fifty thousand people, with a harbour full of cranes and a quiet old centre.

The old Greeks called this place Colchis. In the myth, Jason and the Argonauts sailed here to steal the Golden Fleece from King Aeetes, and the Rioni, then called the Phasis, was the river they ascended. The story may preserve a memory of real gold-washing in Georgian streams, where fleeces were once used to catch gold dust. Today the area is the heartland of Samegrelo, or Mingrelia, whose people have their own language and a strong local pride, and whose food is among the best in Georgia.

For a rider the plain is flat and demanding in an unexpected way. The roads are straight, but the surface can be broken, with potholes, standing water after rain and no warning of a sudden hole. Cows, pigs and dogs wander across the tarmac, and drivers overtake with optimism. Keep your speed down and your eyes up. The main highway to Tbilisi runs inland, and the coast road is quiet. Spring and autumn are mild, summer is hot and humid with mosquitoes, and winter brings rain and mist.

Poti has fuel stations and supermarkets, while Urek'i, a seaside resort twelve kilometres away, is known for its dark magnetic sand. Khobi is another small town nearby. For lunch, ask for a Megrelian khachapuri, a round bread with cheese baked inside and more melted cheese on top, or elarji, a cornmeal and cheese dish that stretches into long strands. Hazelnuts, tea and tangerines grow in the area, and the smell of woodsmoke is everywhere in the evening.
t.quito@-0.2,-78.5:
Quito sits almost on the equator and almost two miles up, and the two facts together explain a lot. At about 2,850 metres the air is thin, the sun is fierce, and the days are mild whatever the calendar says, so the city lives in a permanent early spring. It stretches for kilometres along a narrow Andean valley, with Pichincha volcano rising on the western side and, on clear mornings, the snow cone of Cotopaxi and other peaks visible to the south and east.

This is the starting point for the Avenue of the Volcanoes, the name the German explorer Alexander von Humboldt gave to the double line of peaks that runs south along the Ecuadorian highlands, and a good ride begins here. Leaving the city takes patience, since traffic is heavy and the avenues are crowded with buses. Once you are on the Panamericana heading south, the road climbs and falls through green valleys and past farms and flower greenhouses, as Ecuador is one of the world's major rose exporters.

Practical points count at this altitude. Engines lose power in thin air, and carburetted bikes can feel flat, while fuel-injected ones cope better. Weather changes fast, with sun and a cold downpour within an hour, so pack proper waterproofs and a warm layer, since the nights are cold. Quito has fuel stations and workshops across the city, and you should fill up before heading into the mountains, as stations thin out in the high country. Take care with the sun, which at this latitude and altitude burns quickly, and leave valuables out of sight when parking.

Food in Quito is hearty, with locro de papa, a thick potato and cheese soup, and empanadas de viento, fried pastries with cheese and sugar. Try the fruit juices, many of them from fruits unknown elsewhere, such as naranjilla and tree tomato. The Mitad del Mundo monument, about 25 km north of the centre, marks the equator, though the real line is a few hundred metres away. The city's altitude can cause headaches in the first days, so drink water, go slowly and keep the first ride modest.
t.segment palcanan grande palcanan chico@-:
High in the Andes of Chimborazo province, south of Alausí, a narrow path of fitted stone winds across the páramo, the cold grassland that covers the Ecuadorian highlands above about 3,500 metres. It is part of the Qhapaq Ñan, the Inca road system, and this stretch belongs to the route that links the Inca site of Ingapirca with the highlands to the north. Before the Spanish arrived, the Inca built paved paths, stairways and waystations across this country, and parts of them are still in use, walked by herders and, in recent decades, by trekkers following the well-known route from Achupallas to Ingapirca.

The setting is wild. The land is a mix of grass, bogs and glacial lakes, with low cloud sweeping over the ridges, and the weather is cold, windy and changeable, even in the dry months. The air smells of wet earth and grass. You may see llamas, which are kept by local communities, and with luck an Andean condor or a spectacled bear in the wilder areas of Sangay National Park, which lies to the north-east. Birdlife includes hummingbirds, which survive at this altitude.

Most of this segment is for walkers rather than for motorbikes, and the riding in the area is about getting close. Alausí, a town of about 14,000 people 14 km away, is the base for fuel, food and a bed, and it has a station for the railway that runs down the famous Nariz del Diablo, the Devil's Nose, a switchback track cut into the cliff face. Roads in the area are often steep and winding, with sections of cobble, gravel and mud in the wet season. Be ready for fog and heavy rain in the afternoon, and carry warm layers, as the temperature drops fast at altitude.

The best months for the highlands are generally June to September, though weather is never certain. Remember that the altitude is considerable, and tiredness and headaches can come quickly. Local communities, often indigenous Puruhá and Cañari people, live and farm here, so ask before wandering onto fields and treat the stones with respect. A bowl of hot soup and a cup of canelazo, a warm cinnamon and cane spirit drink, in a village is the usual reward after a day at 3,500 metres or more.
t.city of quito@-0.2,-78.5:
The old town of Quito was one of the first places to be listed by UNESCO, in 1978, alongside Kraków, and it is easy to see why. The historic centre is the largest and best preserved in Latin America, a tight grid of steep streets, colonial squares and church domes laid across the slopes below the Panecillo hill. The Spanish founded the city in 1534 on top of an Inca settlement, and over the next two centuries it became a centre of religious art, the so-called Quito School, in which indigenous and European traditions mixed in painting and sculpture.

The best-known building is the Church of La Compañía, the Jesuit church, whose interior is covered in gold leaf from floor to ceiling, so thickly that it can feel overwhelming. Nearby, the huge San Francisco church and convent stand beside a broad plaza, and the Plaza Grande, the main square, holds the cathedral and the presidential palace. Above the old town the Panecillo hill carries a winged statue of the Virgin, and the view across the red-tiled roofs to the volcanoes is the thing to take in on a clear morning.

Riding in the old town is not recommended. The streets are narrow and steep, paved in cobble, with one-way systems, heavy bus traffic and strict restrictions in the historic centre. Park the bike at a secure garage or hotel on the edge and explore on foot, with a careful eye on your belongings, as petty theft happens in crowded areas. Sundays are calmer, with some streets closed to cars. The thin air makes the steep climbs tiring, so take them slowly.

Food stops are easy. Markets and small restaurants serve a hearty lunch of soup, rice and meat for a few dollars, and the historic cafés around the plazas serve strong coffee and sweet pastries. Ecuador uses the US dollar, so cash is simple to handle. For fuel, there are stations on the main avenues surrounding the old town. When the bells ring from the churches at noon and the light turns warm on the white walls, it is easy to see why people fall for this place.
t.riobamba@-1.7,-78.7:
At roughly 2,750 metres above sea level, Riobamba is a high-altitude city that wears its height lightly. It sits in a wide basin in the central Andes of Ecuador, surrounded by volcanoes, and on clear mornings Chimborazo, the tallest mountain in the country at about 6,263 metres, stands in the distance with its snowy summit catching the first light. Because the Earth bulges at the equator, Chimborazo's summit is the farthest point on the planet's surface from its centre, which makes it a tempting claim for the title of the world's highest mountain.

The city has a calm grandeur. Its streets are wide and laid out on a grid, the result of a rebuild after the earthquake of 1797 destroyed the original town. Ecuador's first constitution was drawn up here in 1830, so Riobamba likes to call itself the cradle of the nation. Markets fill the town on Saturdays, with farmers and weavers from the villages bringing produce, wool and animals in from the highlands, and the colours of the Indigenous skirts and hats are a pleasure to see.

Riding in the Ecuadorian Andes is a lesson in altitude. The road north to Ambato and Quito runs along the Avenue of the Volcanoes, and the road west towards Chimborazo climbs quickly above the treeline into a barren high plateau called the paramo, where vicunas graze and the wind is cold. The air is thin, so engines lose power and riders can feel headaches or breathlessness, so go easy on the climbs and drink plenty of water. Tarmac is generally good on main roads, but cattle and dogs can wander out, and fog and rain arrive without warning.

Riobamba is large enough to have everything you need, with fuel, workshops, hotels and restaurants all easy to find. Try hornado, roast pork served with potatoes, and the local ice cream made from fruit juice and ice, known as helado de paila. Early mornings give the clearest mountain views, so plan to be out before the clouds settle.
t.kintrishi mtirala@41.7,42.0:
Adjara is the strangest corner of Georgia, a damp subtropical strip between the Black Sea and the Lesser Caucasus where tea and tangerines grow within sight of snow. Mtirala and Kintrishi are two neighbouring protected areas inland from Kobuleti and Chakvi, and they hold what is left of the Colchic forest, a relict of the lush woodland that covered this coast before the ice ages. Rainfall is among the highest in the country, and the hills are a tangle of beech, chestnut, alder, rhododendron and box, with ferns, lianas and moss on every branch. Mtirala means something like the weeping or the crying one in Georgian, a reference to the constant drizzle and mist, and you can see why.

The Kintrishi river cuts a gorge through the hills, and along it stand small humpbacked stone bridges from the medieval and later periods, built in the days when mule trains carried goods between the coast and the mountains. They are among the best things in the park, and some of them are still crossed by hikers and shepherds. The villages up the valley are among the poorer in Adjara, built of wood and stone with orchards and cattle, and the people are friendly to a stranger who stops for a chat.

Riding is demanding, and a motorbike is not the easiest way in. The road from Chakvi or Kobuleti climbs into the hills past Akhaldaba and Tsikhisdziri, with good tarmac at the start and rougher, patched surface higher up, and the last stretch to the visitor areas is often gravel or mud. Rain makes everything greasy, and landslides are possible after storms. Cows wander on the road, and blind bends are common. Go in late spring, or in September and October when the air is clearer, and expect cloud whatever the season.

The nearest big town is Chakvi, where tea was first planted commercially in Georgia, and the coast road has fuel in Kobuleti and Batumi, the latter a glitzy port city of towers and casinos a short ride south. Fill your tank on the coast, because the hill villages have little. Buy some tea, honey and cheese, and try a hot khachapuri, the boat-shaped Adjarian cheese bread with a runny egg on top. Bring a rain jacket and a change of socks, and be ready for leeches in wet seasons if you wander off the track.
t.latacunga@-0.9,-78.6:
Latacunga lies at about 2,750 metres in the high Andean valley that the explorer Alexander von Humboldt called the Avenue of the Volcanoes, and the name is hardly an exaggeration. On a clear morning the snowy cone of Cotopaxi, nearly 5,900 metres high, hangs above the plain to the east, with Iliniza and other peaks to the west. The town has a slightly worn, dignified look, with many buildings made from pale volcanic stone and plazas shaded by old trees.

Volcanoes have shaped the place in more ways than the scenery. Cotopaxi's eruptions have damaged Latacunga several times, and the town was rebuilt using the volcanic stone, which is why it looks the way it does. Local culture mixes Indigenous traditions with Spanish colonial heritage. The Mama Negra festival in the autumn is a riot of music, costumes and processions, and it brings the whole community into the streets. The Saturday market in nearby Saquisilí is famous for its colour and its trade in everything from livestock to herbs.

From Latacunga the riding is excellent. The Pan-American Highway runs north and south in the valley, with views of volcanoes at every turn. Westward, the Quilotoa loop climbs into the highlands past villages and to a spectacular crater lake. At altitude, the air is thin and cold, so expect your bike to feel slightly flat and nights to be chilly. Rain and cloud often hide the peaks in the afternoon, so go early.

Latacunga is a sizeable town and has fuel stations on the main road, plenty of cafes, markets and guesthouses. Pujilí, nine kilometres to the west, is smaller but has fuel and a lively Sunday market. Try chugchucaras, a rich dish of fried pork, corn and plantain that Latacunga is known for, and bring warm layers and sun protection, since the sun is strong at altitude.
t.tbilisi@41.7,44.8:
Tbilisi spreads along the Mtkvari river in a bowl of dry hills, and its first impression is of balconies. Old houses lean over narrow streets with carved wooden verandas, sulphur bathhouses sit under domes of brick in the Abanotubani district, and on the ridge above, the ruined Narikala fortress watches the city. The name Tbilisi comes from a Georgian word for warm, and the story says that a hunting king found hot springs here and decided to found a city.

This is where the Georgian Military Highway begins, the old road north to Russia across the central Caucasus. Russia built it in the nineteenth century after taking over Georgia, to move troops and supplies, and it follows an even older caravan route through the Darial gorge. Writers and travellers, from Pushkin to Lermontov to Dumas, have described the journey, and the road still has a romantic reputation. Soon after leaving the city you pass Mtskheta, Georgia's ancient capital, where the sixth-century Jvari monastery stands on a hilltop above the junction of two rivers.

From Tbilisi the road goes north along the Aragvi, past the Zhinvali reservoir and up through Gudauri, a ski resort, to the Jvari Pass at about 2,400 metres, before dropping to Stepantsminda beneath Mount Kazbek. Surfaces are mostly good, though lorry traffic is heavy, and tunnels and avalanche galleries add to the adventure. Snow can close the high section from late autumn to spring. Summer is the best season, with clear air, wildflowers and blue skies.

Tbilisi has everything a rider needs. Fuel stations are everywhere, and there are bike mechanics, shops and plenty of lodging. The city traffic is lively and drivers are creative, so be alert, especially on roundabouts. Food is a delight: khachapuri, the cheese-filled bread, and khinkali, spiced dumplings you eat with your hands, are on every menu, along with the local amber wine made in clay vessels. A day to wander the old town is a good investment before heading north.
t.vladikavkaz@43.0,44.7:
Vladikavkaz means rule the Caucasus, which tells you what the Russians thought of it when they built a fortress here in 1784. It stands on the Terek river where the mountains meet the plain, capital of North Ossetia, and from the broad avenues you can see the snow-covered chain of the central Caucasus on a clear day. It is a calm, orderly city with a colonial look, with tree-lined streets, a long riverside promenade and a scattering of old merchant houses.

This is the northern end of the Georgian Military Highway. The road was created to give Russia a safe route through the mountains to its new Georgian possessions, and Vladikavkaz was the gateway, where convoys gathered before heading into the gorges. The Ossetians who live in this region are an Iranian-speaking people with their own proud culture, with traditions of feasting, toasts and stone tower villages. Ossetian pies, with cheese, potato or beef fillings, are a regional speciality, and are usually ordered in threes, with a toast to the Almighty over the first.

The ride south follows the Terek into the Darial gorge, a spectacular narrow defile with vertical cliffs, and then climbs to the border near Upper Lars. The scenery is tremendous, with castle-like ruins on crags, but the road is busy with trucks and often troubled by landslides and avalanches, particularly in spring. Border crossing rules for foreigners have changed several times in recent years, so check the current position before planning to cross. Even without crossing, the valley road is worth a day.

Vladikavkaz and the nearby town of Nogir have fuel and basic services, and the city has hotels, cafes and bike-friendly guesthouses. Before heading into the gorge, fill up, since stations are fewer. Summer is the best season, with warm days and clear mountains, while winter brings snow and closures. Pack warm layers and be ready for sudden weather in the gorge, and carry your documents at all times, since checkpoints are common.
t.alausi@-2.2,-78.8:
Alausí is a hillside town in the Ecuadorian Andes with a railway platform at its heart, and the railway is the reason most people have heard of it. The town perches at about 2,300 metres in the province of Chimborazo, and a few blocks from the main square the Nariz del Diablo, the Devil's Nose, drops away. This is a sheer rock spur that the railway engineers of the early twentieth century could cross only by a system of zigzag switchbacks, in which the train descends by running forward onto one track, reversing down the next, and so on. It was part of the line between Guayaquil and Quito, an immense undertaking, and a symbol of national unity. Today a tourist train runs from Alausí down the switchbacks and back.

The town itself is small and slightly steep, with a church, a pleasant main square and a long street of shops leading downhill. A large statue of Saint Peter stands on a hill above the town, looking over the valley. People here are mostly farmers, and on market days the plaza fills with produce from the surrounding slopes.

The road to Alausí is part of the Panamerican Highway, which runs along the central valley of Ecuador, between the two ranges of the Andes, and is known as the Avenue of the Volcanoes. Coming from the north, the road passes the city of Riobamba, under the snow-capped Chimborazo, which at 6,263 metres is the highest mountain in Ecuador, and because of the Earth's bulge at the equator, its summit is the point farthest from the planet's centre. The riding is good, with long curves through open highland, farm fields and small villages, but altitude brings chill and fog, and landslides can close the road in the rainy season. Take warm clothing, because even at the equator these heights are cold.

Fuel is available in the town and in larger places on the highway, and a few simple restaurants serve soup, grilled meat and potatoes. The dry months, from June to September, are the best for clear mountain views. Leave time to see the railway, and consider an early train, when the valley is full of morning mist.
t.archaeological site of zvartnots with ru:
Zvartnots is a ruin with a great deal of ghost left in it. The name means roughly the temple of the celestial angels, and it was built in the seventh century by the Armenian Catholicos Nerses III, who wanted a church of astonishing size and shape: a round, three-storey building rising from a cross-shaped plan, with a high central dome and a ring of columns. For a few centuries it dominated this plain between the Hrazdan river and the old capital of Vagharshapat. Then it collapsed, probably in an earthquake some time before the tenth century, and the stones lay forgotten under a mound until archaeologists dug them out in the early twentieth century.

What survives is a platform of pale volcanic tuff, the bases of the columns and a scatter of carved capitals, some with eagles and bunches of grapes in beautifully cut stone. Fragments are laid out in the grass, and a small museum next to the site explains what the whole thing looked like. It is a place for slow looking and one of those spots where the imagination has to do part of the work. On a clear day Mount Ararat fills the southern horizon, snow-capped and enormous, and the whole composition of ruin, mountain and sky explains why the site is UNESCO-listed.

The ride is short and urban rather than adventurous. From Yerevan you take a busy highway west, with heavy traffic and drivers who treat lane markings as a suggestion, and the road runs flat across a plain of orchards and apricot trees. Nothing here is technical. The riding value is in the approach and the light: early morning when the sun slants over the ruins, and late afternoon when the tuff glows pink. The airport of Yerevan lies a few minutes away, so planes pass low overhead now and then.

Vagharshapat, three kilometres on, is the spiritual capital of the Armenian Church, home of the cathedral of Etchmiadzin, and a more sensible place for fuel, food and rest than the village next to the site. Summer is hot and dry, spring is lovely, and autumn gives you clear air and the harvest of grapes and apricots. Taking a coffee before visiting the church complexes is wise, because the queues build up by midday.
t.guayaquil@-2.2,-79.9:
Guayaquil is the biggest city in Ecuador, a hot, noisy and energetic port on the Guayas river, a few degrees south of the equator, and the place where a rider's journey up the coast begins. It is a commercial city, and proud of it. In the nineteenth century, cocoa made fortunes here, and the grand houses and the old customs building along the river recall that boom. The waterfront walk, the Malecón, runs for more than two kilometres along the river with gardens, fountains and a lighthouse, and on a warm evening it is full of families.

The city has a few oddities worth knowing. In a small square near the cathedral, wild iguanas lounge in the trees and on the benches, apparently unbothered by the crowd, and the guides will tell you to look up. The old district of Las Peñas, a steep hillside of painted wooden houses, climbs to a hilltop chapel by four hundred and forty-four steps, and the view from the top over the river and the city is excellent. The food is a pleasure, with ceviche served with popcorn, encebollado, a fish soup that is the traditional hangover cure, and fried plantains.

The ride that starts here is the Ruta del Spondylus, which follows the Pacific coast northwest through fishing villages and beaches. The route is named after the spiny oyster, Spondylus, whose red-orange shell was prized by the peoples of the Andes as a sacred offering and traded for hundreds of kilometres. The road runs through dry scrub on the Santa Elena peninsula, then through greener country toward Manabí, with surf towns, mangroves and long empty beaches. Surfaces are mostly good, with sections of roadworks and occasional potholes.

Leaving Guayaquil is the hardest part, since traffic is heavy, with buses, trucks and motorcycles filling every lane, and the heat and humidity are strong. Set off early, before the roads fill up. Fuel is cheap and plentiful, with stations on every main road, though quality and supply vary in small places, so fill up before leaving the larger towns. Rain is heavy between January and April, and the dry season runs from May to December. The coast gets a morning mist, called garúa, in the cooler months, and the sea is cooler than you might expect.
t.chimborazo reserve@-1.5,-78.8:
Chimborazo is a dormant volcano 6,263 metres high, the highest mountain in Ecuador, and it holds a remarkable record. Because the earth bulges at the equator, the summit is the point on the planet's surface farthest from its centre, further out than Everest, a fact that sounds like a quiz answer but feels real when you stand in the thin air at four thousand metres and look up at the glaciers. The mountain is also revered by the Andean peoples who live around it, as a powerful presence, and the scientist Alexander von Humboldt tried to climb it in 1802 and reached about 5,800 metres, the highest anyone had been at that time.

The reserve around it is a stretch of high moorland, called páramo, a windswept landscape of tussock grass, lichen and sand, and it is home to vicuñas, the wild relatives of the llama, which were reintroduced in the 1980s and now graze in small herds beside the road. The air is thin, dry and cold, with strong sun and sudden showers. A paved road reaches over four thousand metres, and refuges higher up, which climbers use as a base, can be reached by gravel track. Nearby towns include Guaranda, a hill town of twenty-two thousand to the west, and Guano, famous for its woollen carpets, to the east, and the cities of Ambato and Riobamba are on the main road and have fuel and services.

The riding to the reserve is an experience. The road climbs from the valleys through fields and eucalyptus plantations to the open páramo, with big sweeping bends, long views, and little traffic except for the occasional bus, truck or llama herder. Bikes lose power in thin air, so be prepared for slower acceleration, and altitude sickness is a real danger, causing headaches, nausea and fatigue; ascend gradually, drink water and take it easy. The weather swings: you may have sun in the morning and hail at noon, with fog hiding the summit, which is often clouded in.

There is an entry procedure at the reserve gate, and the best views come early, when the sky is clear. Carry warm clothes, gloves and a windproof layer, because it can be near freezing even on an equatorial day. Fill the tank at Ambato or Riobamba, since there is nothing near the mountain, and eat a hot meal of soup and potatoes in a village on the way down.
t.cotopaxi@-0.7,-78.4:
Cotopaxi is the volcano every Ecuadorian child can draw: a near-perfect cone of 5,897 metres, capped with glacier, rising out of high grassland an hour or so south of Quito. It is one of the highest active volcanoes in the world, and it last erupted in 2015, sending ash over the surrounding villages and closing the national park for months. The park has since reopened, though access can be restricted whenever the mountain gets restless, so ask locally before you commit to the day.

Machachi is where you fill the tank and eat.

The riding is part of the pleasure. From the Panamericana, a paved road leads up into the park through plantations of pine and then onto the páramo, a cold, windswept tableland of tussock grass, lupins and low scrub, where wild horses graze and Andean foxes and, if you are lucky, a condor cross the sky. The surface is paved at first and turns to cobbles or gravel nearer the lake of Limpiopungo, a shallow lagoon at about 3,800 metres, ringed with reeds and birds. A rough road continues up toward the car park at roughly 4,600 metres, below the refuge, if conditions allow.

Altitude is the thing to respect. Engines lose power in thin air and so do riders, and a headache, nausea or breathlessness is common if you rush up from Quito, which already sits at 2,800 metres. Stay hydrated, move slowly and turn back if you feel unwell. Weather is moody: the summit often hides in cloud, with the clearest hours in the early morning, and rain, hail and cold can arrive any time. The dry months, roughly June to September, give the best chance of a view of the cone, and it is worth asking about entry rules at the gate.
t.cotopaxi area@-0.7,-78.4:
Cotopaxi is one of the highest active volcanoes in the world, a glittering cone of snow and ice rising to about 5,900 metres in the middle of Ecuador's Andes. The German explorer Alexander von Humboldt, who passed through in 1802, coined the name Avenue of the Volcanoes for the double row of peaks that frame the Panamericana highway, and he was moved by Cotopaxi's perfect shape. Its name is often said to mean neck of the moon in Quechua, though the origin is uncertain. The volcano has erupted many times, including in 2015, when it woke after decades of silence and sent steam and ash into the air, so authorities monitor it closely and access can change.

Riding this part of the Avenue means being at altitude, and the first rule is to go slowly. The Panamericana is a well-surfaced road, though busy with trucks and buses, and from Machachi, a pleasant farming town at the foot of the Illinizas, it runs south toward Latacunga across a high valley at about three thousand metres. The air is thin, so bikes lose power, and riders may feel breathless and headachy until they adapt. Weather is dramatic: clear mornings often give way to cloud, and the volcano hides itself for days. Dry months, June to September, are best, and the wetter season brings fog and rain.

Inside Cotopaxi National Park the landscape is high páramo, a wet tussock grassland at around 3,800 metres and above, with Lake Limpiopungo, a shallow lagoon where Andean gulls and ducks gather, set against the cone. Wild horses graze nearby, and lucky visitors see Andean condors, which circle over the cliffs, along with foxes and, if you are very lucky, the spectacled bear. Park roads are mostly gravel and can be rough, and the cold wind is intense, so dress in layers.

For practical matters, the nearest fuel stations are in Machachi, about twenty-four kilometres away, and in Latacunga, a town of about fifty thousand, farther south. Fill up in one or the other, and carry water and snacks. Thursday is market day in Saquisilí, a small town not far away, and it is one of the most colourful markets in the Andes, with Indigenous traders arriving in felt hats and bright shawls. Sample hot canelazo, a cinnamon and sugar cane spirit drink, on a cold evening.
t.batumi@41.6,41.6:
Batumi is Georgia's seaside city, and it feels a little like three cities layered together. The old Black Sea port still has its cobbled streets and nineteenth-century buildings, the boulevard runs for miles along a pebbly beach, and behind it all rise the glassy towers of a recent building boom, some of them rather outlandish. Behind the city the Lesser Caucasus climbs steeply into green hills, and that backdrop is what makes the town interesting for riders.

The ride out is the draw. Within half an hour you can be among tea terraces, citrus groves and steep wooded valleys where the road narrows to a single lane and the villages come with chickens, cows and the occasional unexpected pothole. Adjara is one of the wettest parts of the Black Sea coast, with warm, humid air and heavy rain through much of the year, so the vegetation is thick and lush and the road surfaces can be greasy. Summer is hot and sticky, and early autumn is a good compromise.

Batumi has a botanical garden, laid out in the late nineteenth century on a headland north of the city, and a seaside promenade that locals use from morning to night. Food is the real reason to hang around. Adjarian khachapuri, the boat-shaped bread with cheese, egg and butter in the middle, is the local signature, and you will find it everywhere from simple counters to smart restaurants. Wash it down with the local lemonade or a glass of Georgian wine.

Practical matters are straightforward. Batumi is a city of well over a hundred thousand people, with fuel stations all around it, plenty of cafes, and hotels of every price. Out in the hills, villages are small and stations are fewer, so start with a full tank. Drivers here have their own style, with overtaking on blind bends a common sight, and cows are another hazard on the quieter roads, so keep your speed under control and your eyes up.

It is a lively place to start and finish, and after a long day on mountain lanes, the sea air and a seat by the water are a welcome reward.
t.monasteries of haghpat and sanahin@41.1,:
Haghpat and Sanahin sit on the opposite edges of a deep canyon in northern Armenia, and between them they hold some of the finest medieval religious architecture in the Caucasus. The two monasteries, founded in the tenth century and expanded over the next three hundred years, stand on terraces above the Debed river, near the town of Alaverdi. They are built of dark basalt and pale tuff, with steep roofs, carved crosses and cool, dim interiors, and they are on the UNESCO World Heritage list.

Both were centres of learning. Sanahin, in particular, had a famous school and a scriptorium where monks copied and illuminated manuscripts, and the library, with its niches for books, can still be seen. The old stone crosses, the khachkars, stand everywhere in the grass, carved with lace-like patterns of vines and crosses, each one different from the next. Sanahin is also the birthplace of the Mikoyan brothers, one a Soviet statesman, the other a designer of MiG fighter jets, which seems an odd destiny for a village of monks.

The riding is dramatic. The road from the Georgian border follows the Debed canyon, with steep forested slopes on both sides and the river rushing below. The surface is mostly good, but there are patches of broken tarmac and potholes, and heavy lorries use the route, so take care on blind bends. The villages of the valley, with their Soviet-era buildings and copper-smelting plant, have a rough edge. A cable car lifts passengers from Alaverdi to Sanahin, a short ride that was restored in recent years.

Fuel is available in Alaverdi, a town of around 13,000 people, a few kilometres from the monasteries, and it is wise to fill up there, as nothing is sold near the sites. A small café serves coffee and local food. Visit in the morning, when the light picks out the carvings and the tour groups have not yet arrived, and take a warm layer, as the stone interiors are cold even in summer.
t.monastery of haghpat@41.1,44.7:
Haghpat is a monastery on a ledge, and the ledge is steep. The road from Alaverdi climbs through a series of tight bends, up from the Debed canyon to a village of stone houses and orchards on the plateau, where the monastery stands behind a low wall, its dark domes and gabled roofs catching the light. It was founded in the late tenth century, under the patronage of the Kiurikid royal family, and its main church, dedicated to the Holy Cross, was finished in the early 990s.

What strikes you first is the way the buildings cluster. The main church, the chapels, the refectory, the bell tower and a library are packed into a small space, each leaning on its neighbour, with narrow passages between them. Inside, the church is dim and cool, with a vault of dark stone and a few bright frescoes surviving. In the courtyard, carved crosses stand in the grass among the graves of monks and nobles, and the bell tower, a three-storey structure of pale stone, rises beside them. A famous khachkar of the thirteenth century, with a pattern of astonishing delicacy, is among the finest in Armenia.

Visitors come on foot or by car from the village, and the lane is narrow, with limited parking, so do not expect to get a coach in. For a motorcycle, the climb is a pleasure, with a view of the valley opening up at each turn, but watch for gravel and cows. Fuel is available in Alaverdi, about three kilometres below, and the village at the top has a small shop and a few homes selling honey and dried fruit.

Come early, or come late. In the middle of the day the buses arrive, and the courtyard fills with voices. At the edge of the day the place is quiet, with the sun slanting through the arches and the swifts wheeling over the roofs. It is a place that reminds you how much patient craftsmanship went into the buildings of this small, mountainous country.
t.sanahin bridge@41.1,44.7:
The bridge at Sanahin is older than most of the countries in Europe. A single high arch of dark stone, it spans the Debed river just below the town of Alaverdi, a work of the twelfth century that has outlasted wars, floods and Soviet roadbuilding. It was built for the caravans that used the valley as a route between Tiflis and the Armenian highlands, and it is still sturdy enough to walk across, with a rough cobbled surface and a steep rise in the middle.

The setting is a lesson in contrasts. The canyon walls rise steeply on both sides, covered in oak and beech, and the river runs green and fast beneath the arch. Close by stands a railway line, a Soviet-era factory, and the old copper smelter that gave Alaverdi its industrial character, and the whole scene has a strangely poetic ruggedness, with the ancient bridge in the middle of it all.

Alaverdi, about a kilometre away, has some 13,000 people and the services you would expect: shops, cafés, a market and petrol stations, so this is the place to refuel. The road along the canyon is the main route between the Georgian border and Yerevan, and it is busy with lorries, which struggle on the gradients and fill the air with diesel. Pull in carefully if you stop at the bridge, and keep an eye on the river bank, which can be slippery.

Weather in the canyon is mild in spring and autumn, but summers are hot and winters cold, with snow on the surrounding hills. Mist often fills the valley early in the morning, and when it lifts, the stones of the bridge are wet and dark. It is a good place for a short stop, a photograph and a quiet moment, before the road leads on to the monasteries above.
t.fallingwater@39.9,-79.5:
Frank Lloyd Wright built the house over the stream, not beside it. Fallingwater stands in the Laurel Highlands of southwestern Pennsylvania, at Mill Run, where Bear Run tumbles over a series of rock ledges in a hemlock and rhododendron forest. Edgar Kaufmann, a Pittsburgh department store owner, hired Wright in 1935 to design a weekend house, and expected a view of the waterfall. Wright put the house right on top of it, with concrete terraces cantilevered over the rock, and it was finished in 1937.

The architecture is the thing, but the setting is half of it. The house uses local sandstone laid in rough courses so the walls seem to grow out of the hillside, and the horizontal terraces repeat the stone ledges beneath. The sound of falling water is constant, and indoors the stream runs under the living room through a hatch in the floor. It is among the most admired houses of the twentieth century and is listed, with other Wright works, as a UNESCO World Heritage Site. Tours are timed and limited, so book ahead in busy months, and know that photography inside is restricted.

The riding is a pleasure. The roads around Mill Run and Ohiopyle wander through hardwood forest, along the Youghiogheny River, with gentle curves, short climbs, and surfaces that vary from smooth to patchy. In autumn the colours are spectacular, and in summer the shade is welcome. Kentuck Knob, another Wright house, sits a few kilometres away on a hill, and is open for tours as well. The whitewater at Ohiopyle draws rafters and kayakers in season.

For fuel and food, there is little right at the house. Connellsville, about sixteen kilometres away, is the nearest town of more than five thousand, and Uniontown is a bit farther. Mill Run and Ohiopyle have small cafes and a few places to eat. Weather changes fast in the hills, and wet leaves in autumn can be slick, so go easy on the corners. Allow time for a walk below the house, where you can stand and see it all at once.
t.arkhangelsk@64.5,40.5:
Arkhangelsk is the city Russia built when it had no other door to the sea. Ivan the Terrible ordered a port on the Northern Dvina in 1584, close to where the river splits into a maze of channels and islands before entering the White Sea, and for more than a century it was the country's only seaport open to European merchants. English and Dutch ships came here for furs, timber and tar. Peter the Great visited, built ships, and then founded St Petersburg and took the trade away, but the city kept its character as a northern timber and shipbuilding town.

You feel the water everywhere. The Dvina is wide, slow and brown, and the city stretches along it for kilometres, with wooden houses, Soviet blocks and cranes sharing the bank. The Pomors, the Russian settlers of this coast, lived by fishing and sealing and sailed far into the Arctic, and their culture still colours the local food, which leans to fish, cloudberries and rye. The great scientist Mikhail Lomonosov was born in a village a short way upriver, and his statue stands in the city. Malye Korely, an open-air museum of wooden churches, windmills and farmhouses, sits on the edge of town and is a good place to see what the north once looked like.

The riding out of town is long, flat and forested. Roads to the White Sea coast and toward Onega run through spruce and birch, with bogs on either side, and the surface can alternate between decent asphalt and broken patches, especially after the thaw. Distances are large, and so are the gaps between services. In June the white nights mean you can ride very late, and mosquitoes make stops short. In winter, the whole region freezes hard and daylight shrinks to a few hours.

Arkhangelsk has more than three hundred thousand people, so fuel, food and repairs are all easy, and Isakogorka on the edge of town adds more. Fill the tank before heading out, since smaller villages may have little. Foreign riders should check what is currently possible before planning a trip.
t.mestia@43.0,42.7:
Mestia is the capital of Upper Svaneti, a high, remote region of northwest Georgia, tucked in a valley of the Greater Caucasus, with the glaciers of Ushba, a twin-peaked mountain of over 4,700 metres, rising above the rooftops on a clear day. Mestia lies at roughly 1,500 metres, and the village is crowded with square stone towers that rise four or five storeys. These Svan towers, built mainly in the Middle Ages, were defensive homes for families who lived in a land of feuds and avalanches, and the whole of Upper Svaneti is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

Getting here is half of the experience. The road from Zugdidi follows the River Enguri up past the huge Enguri arch dam, one of the tallest in the world, then climbs into a narrow gorge and winds on through forests and small villages. The tarmac has improved in recent years, but expect potholes, landslide patches, roaming cows and pigs, and the occasional blind corner with a truck coming the other way. Winter brings heavy snow, and spring can bring mud and rockfall, so summer and early autumn are the best times to ride.

The Svans have their own language, completely different from Georgian, and their own food. Try kubdari, a bread filled with spiced meat, and the Svan salt, a mix of salt and spices that goes on almost everything. Guesthouses in family homes are the usual way to stay, with plenty of hospitality and homemade cheese and wine. The museum in the town holds icons, manuscripts and crosses from remote mountain churches, and is worth an hour.

Fuel is available in Mestia, though it pays to arrive with a reasonably full tank and not to rely on supplies in smaller villages further up the valley. The road continues east toward Ushguli, one of the highest continuously inhabited villages in Europe, but that stretch is rough, rocky and often muddy, and is best attempted on a bike with decent ground clearance and tyres. The border with Russia is close, and the mountains of the main range form a spectacular, remote wall to the north.
t.ananuri@42.2,44.7:
Ananuri is the first place on the Georgian Military Highway where history interrupts the scenery. The fortress stands on a bluff above the Aragvi river, which here is dammed into the bright turquoise Zhinvali reservoir, and its pale stone towers and walls make a striking picture against the water and the mountains behind. It was the seat of the Dukes of Aragvi, built in the seventeenth century, and its walls enclose two churches, one of which has carved crosses and vines around its doors that are worth a close look.

The fortress was a place of fighting as well as faith. In 1739, a rival noble family attacked and burned it, killing the duke and his household, and it later became a stronghold against invaders from the north. The castle guarded the route that runs from Tbilisi through the Caucasus to Russia, which has been one of the most important roads in the region for centuries, and walking among the walls you feel how many travellers have passed this way. Stalls near the gate sell local honey, churchkhela and souvenirs.

The riding on this section is great. The road from Tbilisi follows the Aragvi valley north, climbing steadily through hills of oak and beech and then into the mountains, with wide, open bends and a surface that varies from smooth to rough, with potholes and patches where the road has been repaired. Lorries, minibuses and cattle share the road, and the drivers can be unpredictable, so stay alert and expect a lot of overtaking. The reservoir is at its most colourful in summer, and spring brings green slopes and snowy summits.

Fuel needs a little planning. Zhinvali, a small settlement beside the reservoir, has basic services, but the larger towns are further away, so fill up in Tbilisi or in a bigger town before you set out, and check the tank again at the next major stop, as the road to Gudauri is long and there are only a few stations. Bring warm clothing, as the weather changes fast in the mountains, and carry water, since the climb can be hot in summer. Give yourself time to walk around the fortress, because it deserves more than a quick photograph.
t.gudauri@42.5,44.5:
Gudauri is a ski resort first and a village by accident, strung along the road a little below the Jvari Pass in the High Caucasus, at roughly two thousand metres. In winter it is full of Georgians, Russians and Gulf visitors with skis, and the lifts rise from just behind the hotels. In summer it empties out, the slopes turn into flower meadows, and paragliders drift above the grass. Either way the main road, the old Georgian Military Highway, runs straight through the middle, and everything on it, from lorries to cows, goes by at its own speed.

The highway is the story. For centuries this was the one real road through the central Caucasus, linking Tbilisi with Vladikavkaz and Russia, and the Russians strengthened it after they took over Georgia in 1801. The climb from the south is long and steady, up the valley of the Aragvi, with grassy slopes and then bare mountain, and above Gudauri the road tackles the pass, with hairpins, tunnels and snow galleries. The surface is much better than it used to be, though potholes, rockfall and roadworks are a fact of life. The weather is the real boss: fog, sleet and sudden snow can arrive in any month, and in winter the pass is sometimes closed to heavy traffic.

Just beyond the resort, a big curved concrete viewing platform, decorated with a Soviet-era mosaic, sits on the edge of a vast gorge. It was built in 1983 to mark two hundred years of friendship between Georgia and Russia, and today it is mainly a viewpoint, with a long drop into the green valley below and the road wriggling across the mountainside opposite. Stalls sell wool socks, honey and local sweets, and on a clear day the light on the ridge is fine.

Gudauri has a few stations and shops, but supplies thin out quickly, and prices are those of a resort. The nearest proper town to the south is Pasanauri, about twenty kilometres away, with more services, and it is wise to start the climb with a full tank. Bring warm clothes, even in summer, because the wind at this altitude cuts through a mesh jacket, and keep an eye on the cattle, which have no fear of motorcycles and a firm belief in their right of way.
t.stepantsminda@42.7,44.6:
Stepantsminda sits in a green bowl below Mount Kazbek, which at 5,047 metres is one of the great peaks of the Caucasus, and when the clouds part the mountain seems to hang over the roofs. The town was long known by the Russian name Kazbegi, and many signs and maps still use it. The Terek river, called the Tergi in Georgian, runs through the valley on its way north to the Caspian, and a few kilometres further on the gorge narrows toward the Russian border, so this really is the end of the road for most travellers.

The reason most people come is the church on the hill. The Gergeti Trinity Church stands alone on a ridge above the town at about 2,170 metres, a small stone building of the fourteenth century with the great white cone of Kazbek behind it, and it is one of the best known sights in Georgia. A rough track climbs to it, passable on a motorcycle but steep and stony, and a walk of a couple of hours is the traditional approach. Early morning is the best moment, when the mountain is clear and the hill is quiet. Later the clouds often roll in and hide the summit.

The ride from Gudauri is a high, wild stretch, over the Jvari Pass and down through the valley of the Terek, where black slopes, rushing rivers and a few old stone towers fill the view. Heavy lorries heading for the Russian border use this road in large numbers, so there can be queues in the Dariali gorge north of town, and the surface suffers from the traffic. In winter, snow and avalanches can close the road, so check conditions before setting out.

Stepantsminda has a small centre with guesthouses, cafés and shops, and the food is hearty, with khinkali dumplings, cheese bread and grilled meats. Fuel is available in the town, but supplies can run short in busy periods, so do not leave the stop with a nearly empty tank. Gudauri, about twenty-four kilometres back, is the next sizeable place. Nights are cold even in summer, and a warm layer is as useful as a camera.
t.kutaisi@42.3,42.7:
Kutaisi is one of the oldest continuously inhabited cities in the world, and it knows it. This was the capital of ancient Colchis, the land the Greeks said held the Golden Fleece, and in the myth it was here, in the court of King Aeëtes, that Jason and the Argonauts came with Medea's help to take the treasure. Later it was the capital of the kingdom of Georgia and then of Imereti. On a hill above the Rioni river stands Bagrati Cathedral, an eleventh-century church whose controversial restoration cost it its UNESCO status. Just outside the city, the twelfth-century Gelati monastery, with its gold mosaics and the tomb of King David the Builder, is still on the World Heritage List.

The town itself has a lazy, slightly decayed grandeur. Soviet-era buses rattle past Art Nouveau balconies, and the Green Bazaar sells everything from walnuts and churchkhela to pickled vegetables and cheese. The local speciality is imeruli khachapuri, a round flat bread filled with cheese, which beats the boat-shaped Adjarian version for many people. Mid-morning it is a good excuse to stop, and Georgian wine, poured generously, is a standard part of lunch. Not far away the Soviet sanatoria of Tskaltubo, once hotels for workers, are now decaying but still atmospheric.

For a rider, Kutaisi is a base and a gateway. West and north the road runs toward Zugdidi and then up the Enguri valley into Svaneti, one of the great mountain rides of the Caucasus, with its stone towers and high passes. The roads are mostly paved but vary a lot, with potholes, stray cows and drivers who overtake on blind bends, so ride defensively and stay alert for animals on the road in the evening. Weather is mild and often wet, especially in the spring, with summer thunderstorms rolling in from the Black Sea.

Everything you need is here. The city has well over a hundred thousand people and a lot of filling stations, shops and guesthouses, and international flights land at the airport nearby. Fill your tank before heading north, and buy water, bread and snacks, as services thin out fast. Georgian hospitality is real, and a rider who stops to look lost will usually be offered tea, or something stronger.
t.zugdidi@42.5,41.9:
Zugdidi is the unofficial capital of western Georgia's lowlands, a flat green town of seventy thousand people in the region of Samegrelo, near the border of the breakaway territory of Abkhazia and a short way from the Black Sea. It is a warm, humid place, with palms, hazelnut orchards, tea bushes and cornfields, and it looks and feels very different from the mountains it is the gateway to. For riders heading up to Svaneti, this is the last real town and the place to prepare.

The main sight is the Dadiani Palace, a grand nineteenth-century house in a large botanical garden, built for the Dadiani family, the princes who ruled Mingrelia for centuries. It is a museum now, with rooms of furniture, paintings and family relics, and the garden with its old trees and big magnolias is a pleasant place for a walk. The town also has a lively market, where you can buy fruit, nuts, cheese and the strong local honey. Mingrelian food is a point of pride, spicy and rich, with cheese, walnuts and corn, and a dish of cheese with mint called gebzhalia is typical.

The ride to Svaneti starts here, and it is a long one. From Zugdidi, the road runs north across the plain and then enters the valley of the Enguri river, which it follows up into the mountains. Not far along is the huge Enguri dam, one of the tallest concrete arch dams in the world, and from there the road climbs into narrow gorges, tunnels and forests, with the high Caucasus appearing ahead. The surface is variable, and road works are common, so allow plenty of time.

For fuel and supplies, Zugdidi is the place to be thorough. The town has many stations, supermarkets and cafés, and the higher valleys have far fewer. Fill the tank, check tyre pressures, buy water and snacks, and make sure you have cash, since cards are less useful in the villages. If you plan to stay overnight, the guesthouses in town are friendly and cheap. Mornings are the best time to leave, since the lowland heat builds quickly and the mountain road is more enjoyable in the cool.
t.ushguli@42.9,43.0:
Ushguli is a cluster of four small villages at roughly 2,100 metres, high in Upper Svaneti, and it is often described as one of the highest continuously inhabited settlements in Europe. It sits at the head of the Enguri valley, beneath Mount Shkhara, which at over 5,000 metres is the highest peak in Georgia and part of the main Caucasus ridge. Svaneti as a whole is a UNESCO World Heritage Site, and the thing that makes it special is the medieval towers, square, tapering stone defence towers, some up to five storeys, that rise above almost every household. Families used to shelter in them during blood feuds and avalanches, and many still stand.

The setting is extraordinary. Stone houses and towers cling to a grassy slope, rivers run clear and cold below, and in summer the meadows are full of wildflowers, with cattle and pigs wandering through the lanes. There is a small church, Lamaria, with old frescoes, on a ridge above the village, and a path continues up toward the glacier. Life is simple and the winters are long; the villagers have survived for centuries by being self-reliant.

The road to Ushguli is part of the appeal and part of the challenge. From Mestia it runs for about forty-five kilometres, partly paved and partly gravel, over a high shoulder with steep drops and a good many hairpins. It takes two hours or more and can be rough, with mud, rockfalls and stream crossings after storms. Snow closes it in the cold months, and it is generally passable only from late spring to autumn, so check conditions with locals before you commit. The road on toward Lentekhi crosses a high pass and is rougher still. A bike with decent ground clearance and a rider with patience will be rewarded.

The villages have guesthouses where hosts serve kubdari, a local meat pie, along with soft cheese, bread and homemade wine. Go early in the morning, when the light on the towers is soft and the mist lifts from the valley, and stay the night if you can. The place feels different when the day-trippers leave.
t.mtskhetis jvari@41.8,44.7:
Jvari, the Georgian word for cross, stands on a rocky bluff above the point where two rivers meet, the brown Mtkvari and the greener, faster Aragvi. The church dates from the end of the sixth century, and it is a small, dark, stern building, almost square, with a design that influenced much of Georgian architecture later. The reason it stands where it does is a legend: in the early fourth century, Saint Nino, the woman credited with bringing Christianity to Georgia, is said to have raised a cross of grapevine on this hilltop, and the king converted soon after. Georgia calls itself one of the first Christian nations, and this is where that story is anchored.

From the terrace by the church, the view is the real reward. Below, Mtskheta's old streets and the cathedral roofs are laid out in miniature, with the confluence of the rivers shining below like a hinge. The nineteenth-century poet Mikhail Lermontov came here and was inspired to write Mtsyri, the story of a boy who runs away from a monastery, and the setting is still wild enough to explain why. Inside, the church is cool and silent, with candles, icons and a plain stone cross at its centre.

Getting up there is half the fun. A narrow road climbs from the town in a series of tight hairpins, between scrubby oaks and stony ground, and is just wide enough for a car and a bike to pass with care. The surface is sound, but the corners are steep and sometimes dusty or gravelly, and tour buses make the upper section a little congested at peak times. A bike is far easier here than a car. There is a car park at the top and a small shop selling drinks and souvenirs, but not much else.

For fuel, Mtskheta is a few minutes down the hill, and Tbilisi is only twenty kilometres away, with every service. Go early or late, when there are fewer groups and the light is better, and expect the wind to rise in the afternoon. In clear weather you can see the dark line of the Caucasus to the north. Cover your shoulders and be quiet inside, as this is a working place of prayer.
t.historical monuments of mtskheta@41.8,44:
Mtskheta is the old heart of Georgia, and the whole town is listed by UNESCO. For hundreds of years before Tbilisi became important, it was the capital of the kingdom of Iberia, and here at the meeting of the Mtkvari and Aragvi rivers, in the early fourth century, King Mirian converted to Christianity. Archaeologists have found remains of a royal citadel, tombs and Roman-era graves in the surrounding hills, showing how much older the settlement is than the churches. The town is still the seat of the Georgian Orthodox Patriarch, and a place of pilgrimage.

What makes it special is how compact it is. The small streets of the centre, lined with stone-walled courtyards and wooden balconies, lead to the cathedral and a handful of tiny shops selling wine, churchkhela, the walnut-and-grape candy that looks like a candle, and religious icons. Samtavro monastery, with its tombs of kings, sits a short way up the street, and women in headscarves tend the candles. Locals sell tarragon lemonade, bread baked in clay ovens, and fresh grilled meats beside the road. It is touristy but still alive, and on Sundays families come in from Tbilisi to pray and eat.

For riders, Mtskheta marks the start of the Georgian Military Road, the old route over the Caucasus that the Russian army built in the nineteenth century to reach Georgia. It runs north along the Aragvi river past the Zhinvali reservoir and the fortress of Ananuri, then climbs to the Jvari Pass and on to Kazbegi. The surface is reasonable, but heavy lorries, stray cows and sudden fog make it a road that requires attention. In the other direction, the roads toward Kakheti, Georgia's wine country, lead through vineyards and hills.

The town is small, with just over seven thousand residents, but it has several filling stations on the highway and in the centre, and plenty of cafés and restaurants. Traffic on the main road can be heavy, especially on weekends, and parking near the cathedral is limited. There are wide paved areas at the edge of town where bikes are easy to leave. Walk the streets slowly and you will find a much older Georgia than the one you see from the highway.
t.svetitskhoveli cathedral@41.8,44.7:
Svetitskhoveli is the great cathedral of Georgia, and its name means the life-giving pillar. The story goes that after the crucifixion, a Georgian Jew named Elioz brought Christ's robe back to Mtskheta, where his sister Sidonia died of grief clutching it. The robe could not be removed from her hands, so she was buried with it, and a cedar grew from her grave. Saint Nino cut the tree down to make seven pillars for the first church, and the seventh is said to have risen by itself and hung in the air until a prayer brought it down. The present building was raised in the early eleventh century, in a time of great confidence in the Georgian kingdom, and it has been the burial place of many kings.

The cathedral is vast inside, with a high central dome, a floor of worn stone and walls of faded frescoes. The architecture is typical of Georgia, with a cross-in-square plan, blind arcades and delicate stone carving on the outside, including a carved hand said to be the architect's. Candles flicker before the icons, and it is in daily use, with priests chanting. A thick defensive wall, built in the seventeenth century, surrounds the courtyard, giving it the air of a fortress.

The approach by bike is easy. The cathedral stands in the middle of the old town, a short walk from the car park where the roads from Tbilisi arrive, and the surrounding streets are narrow and often cobbled, so it is best to leave the bike and walk. Early morning is the quietest time and the best for photographs, because later in the day tour buses fill the courtyard. Be aware that you need to cover your knees and shoulders to enter, and women usually need a headscarf, which are often lent at the door.

You are in a small town, but fuel stations are close on the main road, and Tbilisi, twenty kilometres south, has everything. The streets near the cathedral hold cafés and wine shops where you can try a glass of amber qvevri wine, made in clay jars buried in the ground in the old way. It tastes of tea and apricots, and it is a very Georgian way to end a visit.
t.rize@41.0,40.5:
There is hardly a hillside around Rize that is not covered in tea. The bushes grow in neat green terraces up to hundreds of metres above the coast, steep enough that pickers use ropes and the road clings to the slope in hairpins. Rize is the tea capital of Turkey, and this is also the wettest part of the country, with cloud and drizzle most of the year, which is exactly why the plants thrive. The town has a pleasant hill park above the centre where you can drink tea at a table with a view of the sea, and a small castle on the ridge above the centre gives a view over the roofs and the sea.

The coast road, the D010, brings you in, but the real interest lies inland. Valleys lead south into the Kaçkar mountains, with villages like Çamlıhemşin and the plateau pastures near Ayder, where the Hemshin people keep traditional wooden houses and stone bridges. Roads there are narrow and often wet, with sharp bends and rockfall after storms, and fog can come down fast. If you plan to ride into the high country, start early and check conditions, because the weather turns quickly and mobile signal fades.

Rize has about ninety thousand people, so there is no trouble with fuel, repairs, or a proper meal. The local cuisine is butter-rich, with muhlama, a molten cheese and cornmeal dish, and fish from the Black Sea. Rize tea is served in small tulip glasses, strong and sweet, and you will be offered more than you can drink. Hotel owners and shopkeepers are often happy to talk about the harvest, which runs from May to September.

The best time to ride is late spring and early autumn, when the days are clear and the air is fresh, though rain can arrive at any time. Winter brings snow to the high passes and the road beyond Ayder may be closed for months. Traffic on the coast road is heavy, so for the smaller valleys plan an early start and take your time on the hairpins.
t.front royal entrance@38.9,-78.2:
Front Royal is where the Shenandoah Valley meets the northern end of Skyline Drive, and a stop here is mostly about getting your head and your tank right before the ridge. The town of about fifteen thousand sits at the confluence of the two forks of the Shenandoah River, with the Blue Ridge on one side and the long valley on the other. It has stations, supermarkets and a small old centre with a bandstand, a courthouse and a couple of good coffee shops, so it makes an easy start.

The riding begins at the park gate, a few minutes up the road. Skyline Drive runs a hundred and five miles along the crest of the Blue Ridge through Shenandoah National Park, and it was built in the 1930s, much of it by the Civilian Conservation Corps, who also cut the stone walls and overlooks that you will pass. The speed limit is a leisurely thirty-five miles an hour, the corners are gentle, and there are dozens of pull-offs looking out across the valley. It is not a road for pace but for patience. The park charges an entrance fee, which a bike pays at a lower rate than a car.

Deer are the real hazard, and they are everywhere, grazing at the edge of the tarmac and sometimes stepping out without warning. Black bears live here too, with one of the densest populations in the East, though you are more likely to see them from a car window than from a bike. In late spring the mountain laurel blooms, and in October the colour is famous and the traffic matches it. Mornings are often misty, with a blue haze that gives the range its name, and fog can come down quickly, so go carefully.

A little history sits under the road. The park was created by the state buying up and clearing hundreds of mountain homesteads, and the people who lived there were relocated, a hard story the visitor centres tell honestly. The town itself saw action in the Civil War, when Confederate scout Belle Boyd carried information to General Jackson, and the Warren Rifles Confederate Museum keeps the memory alive.
