Fuel on the Drive is limited and seasonal, with a few pumps at the larger waysides in the warmer months, so treat Front Royal as the reliable place and arrive with a full tank. Apple Mountain Lake and Shenandoah Farms are small neighbourhoods just beyond town, but the services are all in the middle.
t.skyline drive north@38.8,-78.3:
Somewhere past the first big overlooks, the northern section of Skyline Drive settles into a rhythm that suits a slow day. This stretch lies north of Thornton Gap, where the ridge is narrow and the road switches from one side of the crest to the other, so that the view alternates between the Shenandoah Valley to the west and the rolling Piedmont to the east. On the western side you see the long, dark wall of Massanutten Mountain beyond the river, and on a clear day the valley floor is a patchwork of farms.

The Appalachian Trail follows the same ridge and crosses the road again and again, so you will see hikers with big packs stepping out of the woods and onto the verge, usually looking glad of a road. Give them room. The corners here are easy and the surface is good, but the real caution is for wildlife and for the overlook entrances, where cars slow without much notice. A stop at a pull-off in the early morning, with fog filling the valley like milk, is one of the great quiet pleasures of Virginia.

The forest is oak and hickory with hemlock in the cool hollows, and the understory is full of laurel and fern. In May and June the wildflowers are plentiful, and the roadsides in September turn gold with goldenrod. Autumn colour starts at the high elevations first and works down the mountain over the course of October, so the same road can look different from one weekend to the next. Ravens ride the updrafts above the overlooks, and from time to time a turkey vulture or a hawk passes below you.

Winter closes the Drive in stretches whenever ice or snow arrives, and the gates stay shut until crews have cleared it. In summer, the road is open and busy at weekends. Midweek, the sense of space can be total.

The nearest towns are well down the mountain. Luray lies about eighteen kilometres away to the south-west and Front Royal about twenty kilometres to the north, and Woodstock is further west on the other side of the valley. Fuel on the Drive itself is thin, so fill up in one of the valley towns before climbing, and bring something to drink. A small picnic and a view are all that most days need.
t.stony man overlook@38.6,-78.4:
Stony Man is the second-highest peak in Shenandoah National Park, at 4,011 feet, and the overlook below it is one of the most photographed spots on Skyline Drive. The mountain gets its name from the profile of its cliffs, which look from the valley like the face of an old man lying on his back, with a craggy brow, nose and chin. If you see it or not depends on the angle and your imagination, but the view from the top is easy to appreciate: the Shenandoah Valley opens out to the west, the Massanutten range stands in the middle, and on a clear day the Allegheny ridges stack up to the horizon.

The overlook on the road is a short stop, but the real prize is a walk. A path of about a mile and a half leads from the Skyland area to the summit through oak, hemlock and mountain laurel, and it is mostly gentle, though the final stretch over bare rock needs sturdy shoes. Skyland itself began in the 1890s as a mountain camp for city people, founded by a man who loved the place and wanted to share it. It grew into a resort, and today the lodge still welcomes guests, with big views from the dining room.

Those cliffs are made of ancient greenstone, a volcanic rock from around five hundred million years ago, and in their cracks grow rare plants that have survived on the high ledges since the ice age. Peregrine falcons have returned to some of the Shenandoah cliffs after being wiped out by pesticides, and ravens are common. In spring the whole slope is bright with trillium and wild azalea, and autumn is the busy season for photographers.

For riding, Skyline Drive at this point is gentle, with easy bends and a low speed limit that keeps traffic slow and polite. The park rangers do patrol, and wildlife on the road is a real concern, particularly at dusk. Fog and cloud can swallow the view quickly, which is a pity if you have climbed for it, so check the forecast and go early.

Luray is the nearest town, about eleven kilometres away down the hill, and Stanley is not much farther. Neither is far, but the Drive itself has few places to refuel, so plan your tank before the climb. Skyland has a restaurant and a gift shop in season, and the big overlooks have restrooms and water.
t.luray food@38.7,-78.5:
Luray is the pleasant, slightly sleepy town in the Page Valley that most visitors know for what lies beneath it. In 1878, a group of local men searching for a cave found one, and the Luray Caverns have been one of Virginia's top attractions ever since. The caves are filled with towering columns and curtains of stone, and they hold the Great Stalacpipe Organ, an instrument that taps the stalactites with rubber mallets to produce notes. It is a quirky bit of engineering, and the sound, a soft bell-like tone that echoes through the chamber, is oddly moving.

Above ground, the town sits beside the Hawksbury Creek and the South Fork of the Shenandoah River, with the Blue Ridge on one side and the long ridge of Massanutten on the other. Its main street is lined with brick shops, cafes and diners, and this is a good place for a long lunch and a stretch after the slow miles of Skyline Drive. About five thousand people live here, enough to keep a few bakeries, a couple of decent restaurants, and a handful of antique shops open, and it is easy to find a table at a reasonable hour.

Southern Virginia cooking is the thing to look for. Expect barbecue, biscuits and country ham, fried chicken and apple pie, along with local cider and, increasingly, craft beer. The valley is orchard country, and in autumn the roadside stands sell apples, pumpkins and cider donuts by the bag.

The road up to the mountain begins right at the edge of town, and US 211 climbs through Thornton Gap in a series of long, smooth curves, with the forest closing in on both sides. It is a good road, though it carries lots of traffic in the leaf season, and the wildlife in the Gap is plentiful. Take it slowly in the damp, because fallen leaves and fog catch people out. The valley roads to the south, along the river and through the farmland, are quieter and flatter, and give a different kind of day.

Fuel is easy in Luray, with several stations on the main roads, so this is a good place to fill up before or after the Drive. Parking in town is simple, and the caverns have their own big lot. Mount Jackson and Woodstock, further up the valley, offer more services. Summer weekends can be crowded around the caves, so go early, or on a weekday.
t.front@38.9,-78.2:
Front Royal sits where the north fork of the Shenandoah River slides out of the valley, and it is the northern gate of Skyline Drive, the one hundred and five mile road that runs along the crest of the Blue Ridge through Shenandoah National Park. The town of fifteen thousand is a tidy place with a small-town main street, a bandstand and a long Civil War memory. The Confederate spy Belle Boyd, still a teenager, famously carried information to General Stonewall Jackson here in 1862, and the town changed hands several times during the war.

Skyline Drive itself was built in the 1930s, much of it by young men of the Civilian Conservation Corps, as a motor road that would let ordinary Americans see the mountains. It climbs from the valley to the ridge in a few kilometres, then follows the crest, with overlooks facing east over the Piedmont and west over the valley and the long line of the Alleghenies. The speed limit is low, thirty-five miles per hour, and strictly kept, which suits a road designed for views rather than speed. The curves are gentle and graceful, and the pavement is good, though a few sections can be damp and shaded, and wet leaves in autumn are slippery.

The wildlife is part of the show. Deer are common along the road, and black bears live in the forest, sometimes crossing the pavement at dusk. A visitor centre near the entrance has maps and information. October is the busiest month, as the forest turns red and orange, and weekends can be slow, so ride on a weekday if you can. Spring brings flowering dogwood and redbud, while summer mornings are often misty. Parts of the Drive close in winter or after storms.

Fuel is the key point. Front Royal has plenty of stations, and the Drive has only limited services, which are seasonal, so fill the tank before you go in. An entrance fee is charged at the gate. Local diners and a few cafes along the main street are good for breakfast, and the town makes a pleasant base for a night before or after the ride.
t.dilijan@40.7,44.9:
Dilijan is the town the Armenians call their Little Switzerland, which is a generous description of what is really a small spa town buried in the forest. It sits in the Tavush province, in a green valley of the Lesser Caucasus, at roughly 1,400 metres, with beech and oak woods climbing the slopes all round. It is wetter and cooler than the rest of the country, which is mostly dry plateau, and the sudden greenery after the bare hills of the Armenian highlands is a shock. The air carries a smell of wet leaves and wood smoke.

The old quarter, a short street of restored houses with carved wooden balconies, gives a sense of what a nineteenth-century Armenian town looked like. Craftsmen sell ceramics, carpets and metalwork from the workshops, and the town has long attracted artists, composers and writers who came for the clean air. Mineral water from Dilijan is bottled and sold across the country. The town also has a modern face, with an international school and a growing number of guesthouses, cafes and restaurants.

Nearby are two of the finest medieval monasteries in the Caucasus. Haghartsin, about ten kilometres to the north-east, sits in a forest clearing with a group of stone churches and a refectory dating from the thirteenth century, and Goshavank, at the village of Gosh, is known for its delicate carved cross-stones, called khachkars. Both are beautiful places in a quiet landscape, and bring a sense of centuries of prayer.

The roads around Dilijan are a pleasure. The old road over the mountain toward Lake Sevan climbs through forest in hairpins, and the new highway runs through a long tunnel under the Sevan range. Surfaces are mixed, with good stretches and potholed ones, and Armenian drivers can be unpredictable, so keep your eyes open. Cows, dogs and the occasional herd of sheep take their share of the road. Fog is common in the mornings, and in winter, snow and ice make the roads treacherous.

Dilijan has fuel stations, shops and restaurants, so it is an easy place to stop. Try the local cooking, which includes kebab, fresh vegetables, herbs and the flatbread called lavash, and ask for a cup of strong Armenian coffee. Autumn colours in October can be superb.
t.vanadzor@40.8,44.5:
Vanadzor is Armenia's third city, and it makes no attempt to charm. It sits in a bowl of the Lesser Caucasus, at the confluence of the Pambak and Vanadzor rivers, with mountains on all sides and the old Soviet industrial landscape of chemical plants, apartment blocks and wide avenues in the middle. The city was known as Kirovakan in Soviet times, after a Bolshevik leader, and it took on its present name in 1992. In December 1988, the great Spitak earthquake devastated the region, and Vanadzor suffered serious damage, some of which can still be seen.

For a rider, though, the city is the sensible place to eat, rest and refuel. A hundred thousand people live here, so there are fuel stations, markets and restaurants in good supply, and the city has a surprisingly lively cafe scene on the main street. The central market is a good place to try local produce, with piles of apricots, herbs, cheese and dried fruit, and in the cool of the evening the park fills with families and chess players.

The roads out of Vanadzor lead to some of the best riding in northern Armenia. To the north, the main highway enters the Debed Canyon, a deep gorge with steep cliffs and a river rushing through, and passes through the mining town of Alaverdi, with its monasteries nearby. To the south, the road climbs through forest toward the Dilijan range. The roads are a mix of good tarmac and rough patches, with plenty of heavy lorries, so overtaking needs care. Surfaces break up after winter, and potholes can be deep.

The mountains around the city are forested with oak, hornbeam and beech, and in spring the meadows fill with wildflowers. The weather is changeable, with summer storms and cold winters, and fog in the valleys is common in autumn. Early autumn is a particularly good time, with colourful leaves and clear days.

Because it is a working city, Vanadzor rewards a short walk. The old railway station, built in the Soviet era, has a certain grandeur, and the rows of street vendors sell everything from sunflower seeds to second-hand books. Armenian hospitality is generous, and you will often be offered a glass of something to drink.
t.haghpat@41.1,44.7:
Haghpat is a monastery perched on a ledge above the Debed Canyon, and it is one of those places that makes the long ride worth it. The complex, together with its sister monastery at Sanahin, is a UNESCO World Heritage Site, and it is a masterpiece of medieval Armenian architecture. It was founded in 976, in the reign of the Bagratid kings, by Queen Khosrovanuysh, and expanded over the next three centuries, with a main church, a bell tower, a refectory and a library, all built of dark grey stone with delicate carved decoration.

The setting is as special as the buildings. The monastery sits on a spur of a mountainside, with views across the gorge to forested slopes on the other side, and a cool wind blowing through the courtyard. Inside, the churches are dark, and the smell of candle wax and old stone hangs in the air. Khachkars, the carved cross-stones that are the national art form of Armenia, stand in the grass, each with a unique pattern of lacework in stone. The sound of a choir singing in the church, if you are lucky, is unforgettable.

The monastery was a centre of learning, with a scriptorium where manuscripts were copied and illuminated. The ashulug Sayat-Nova, the eighteenth-century poet and troubadour, is said to have spent time here and is buried at the monastery. His songs, in Armenian, Georgian and Azerbaijani, are still sung across the Caucasus, and the story of a bard at a mountain monastery is a fine one to keep in mind as you sit in the courtyard.

Below the monastery lies the town of Alaverdi, an industrial centre built around a copper smelter, and the contrast between the old stone buildings and the smoking Soviet works is stark. A cable car links Alaverdi to Sanahin, and offers a view down the canyon. The road up to Haghpat is steep and narrow, with tight bends and a rough surface in places, and it is best taken slowly. Parking at the monastery is limited, and the walk from the lot is short.

Alaverdi, about three kilometres away, has fuel, shops and places to eat, and it is the sensible place to prepare before the climb. Dress modestly, and bring a scarf if you are visiting the churches. The best light is in the morning and late afternoon, when the stone seems to glow.
t.alaverdi@41.1,44.7:
Alaverdi is squeezed into the bottom of the Debed canyon, in the north of Armenia, so tightly that the houses seem to be stacked on top of each other up both sides. The river runs below, the railway and the road run beside it, and above rise steep green slopes with cliffs and monasteries. The town grew in the Soviet period around a copper smelter, which worked for decades, and the industry has left a distinctive atmosphere: apartment blocks, rusting pipes, and a feeling of a place that has seen better days but has not given up.

The glory of Alaverdi lies above it. On the plateau overlooking the canyon, the monasteries of Sanahin and Haghpat, both founded in the tenth century, are among the finest in Armenia and are recognised by UNESCO. Their dark stone churches, carved crosses called khachkars and old scriptoria create an atmosphere of deep age, and lamps flicker in cool vaults that smell of wax and stone. Sanahin was the birthplace of the Soviet politician Anastas Mikoyan, and a small museum remembers the Mikoyan brothers, one of whom designed the MiG fighter jets.

For riders, the Debed canyon road is the draw. The route from Vanadzor winds through the gorge, with the river at the bottom and forested cliffs overhead, passing small villages and stone bridges, with tight bends and tunnels. A medieval bridge at Sanahin, with a high arch, spans the river. The surface is generally good on the main road but patchy on the side roads that lead up to the monasteries, which are steep and narrow with tight hairpins. Mist often fills the canyon in the morning, and in winter ice is a hazard.

Fuel is easy at Alaverdi, which has several stations, and there are more at Vanadzor, farther south. In a cafe by the road, order khorovats, grilled meat on skewers, with lavash and fresh herbs. The best time to visit is May to October, with autumn colour in the oak and beech forest. Armenian drivers are fast and overtake freely, so keep your wits about you on blind bends.
t.jvari cross pass@42.5,44.5:
Jvari means cross in Georgian, and the pass gets its name from a cross that, according to tradition, was raised here in the early centuries of Georgian Christianity, high on the saddle of the Greater Caucasus at 2,379 metres. This is the summit of the Georgian Military Highway, the road that the Russians built in the nineteenth century to link Tbilisi with Vladikavkaz on the far side of the mountains. For two centuries it has been the main route between Georgia and Russia, a road of armies, traders, poets and now, in summer, a rising number of motorcyclists.

The climb from the south starts in the broad valley of the Aragvi and rises through villages, with the Gudauri ski resort, perched on an open bowl of grass a few kilometres below the summit, as the last settlement. The road is paved, with a steady series of hairpins that climbs the slope toward the saddle, and at the top, a wide viewing platform and a huge circular monument, a Soviet mosaic from 1983 commemorating the friendship of Russia and Georgia, look out over a deep, green gorge. The mosaic, painted with scenes of national history, is a cheerfully faded piece of Soviet art, and the drop below it is dizzying. You can see the wind turning the clouds.

Be careful with the road. Surfaces vary, with potholes, patches of loose gravel and sections damaged by landslides and winter frost. Lorries labour up the slopes in a line, and overtaking on blind corners is a national habit, so keep to your side and watch the oncoming traffic. Cows and sheep wander across the carriageway. The pass is often closed in winter because of snow and avalanches, and conditions can change quickly even in summer, with cold fog and sudden rain. The best months are June to September.

The Caucasus here are young, steep and wild, with grass slopes dotted with wild flowers in July, and snow lingering in the gullies. Griffon vultures soar on the updraughts, and the air is thin and fresh. Over the pass, the road drops into the Kazbegi region, where the peak of Kazbek rises to more than five thousand metres and the Gergeti Trinity Church sits on a ridge above Stepantsminda.

Services are good for such a high place. Gudauri has fuel stations, small shops, cafés and guesthouses, serving khachapuri, the national cheese bread, and grilled meat, and it is the best place to fill up before the climb or after the descent. Carry a warm jacket, even in summer, because the wind on the saddle is cold.
t.jvari@42.7,42.1:
Jvari is a small town in western Georgia, but its significance is vastly out of proportion to its size, because the largest dam in the country stands a few kilometres upstream. The Enguri Dam, completed in the Soviet era, rises about 270 metres across the narrow gorge of the Enguri river, making it one of the tallest arch dams in the world, a huge curved wall of concrete holding back a long, green-blue reservoir. It still supplies a large share of Georgia's electricity. The dam lies close to the boundary with the breakaway region of Abkhazia, which gives the area a certain tension, though the road to the dam and the mountains beyond is open.

Jvari is, above all, the gateway to Svaneti, one of the most spectacular and isolated regions in the Caucasus. From here the road climbs along the gorge of the Enguri, passing the dam and the reservoir, and continues deep into the mountains toward Mestia and the villages of the high valleys. The Svans have preserved a distinctive language, traditions and architecture, including the stone defensive towers that stand beside many houses, built in the Middle Ages to protect families during feuds. The towers give the villages of Upper Svaneti a skyline like no other, and they are now listed by UNESCO.

For a rider, the road beyond Jvari is both thrilling and demanding. It has been improved in recent years, but landslides, rockfalls, potholes and sections of rough surface are common, especially after rain or the spring thaw. There are tunnels, some of them unlit, and the road clings to cliffs above the river, with long drops. Traffic is mostly local, with minibuses, trucks and cattle, and overtaking can be unpredictable. Check conditions with locals before you set off, and keep daylight on your side. In winter, snow and avalanches close the upper road, and the best months for travel are late May to October.

The country is lush and green, covered in forest of beech, fir and chestnut, with walnut and hazelnut trees along the lower valley, and the air smells of wet leaves and woodsmoke. The river runs a milky turquoise from glacial melt.

The town has a handful of shops, cafés and guesthouses. Fuel stations are present in Jvari, as in most Georgian towns of this size, but supplies in the mountains beyond are limited, so fill up before you go. Tsalenjikha, about twelve kilometres away, has more services. Try a bowl of kharcho, a spicy beef soup, and a plate of fresh bread.
t.lago naki@44.1,40.0:
Lago-Naki is a plateau, a high, rolling upland on the northern edge of the Caucasus, and the road up to it gives you the sense of going somewhere that has not been fully tamed. The plateau lies at around 1,800 to 2,000 metres, in the Republic of Adygea, just next to the Caucasus Nature Reserve, which is a UNESCO World Heritage Site. Behind it, a wall of white and grey mountains rises, with Mount Fisht, nearly 2,870 metres high, and Oshten forming a skyline of snow and rock above the meadows.

The ground here is limestone karst, riddled with caves, sinkholes and dry valleys, and the meadows are alpine, with a short summer of flowers, including rhododendrons, orchids and gentians. Sheep and cattle graze on the plateau, and shepherds' huts and small refuges dot the slopes. The Circassians, or Adyghe, have lived on the northern slopes of the Caucasus for centuries, and the place has a feeling of altitude and quiet. In the evening, the light on the peaks turns pink and gold, and clouds boil up in the valleys.

The road up is not for the faint-hearted. From the valley of the Belaya River, it climbs in many hairpin bends, with steep drops, mixed surface and sudden weather, and the final stretches may be gravel or broken tarmac. Fog is common, and visibility can fall to a few metres. Rain turns clay surfaces to slippery mud, and snow can close the road from late autumn to spring. A dual-sport bike is the sensible choice, and a slow, careful pace the right one. Cattle and sheep sometimes block the road, and tourist jeeps and minibuses add traffic in July and August. Early mornings are best, and September is often the clearest month.

Services are few. The nearest sizeable town is Kamennomostsky, about twenty-eight kilometres away, and that is where you should fill the tank and eat a proper meal before heading up. On the plateau itself, there are a few guest houses, cafés and campsites, with simple food and a lot of tea, but nothing you should count on late in the season. Carry water, warm clothing and waterproofs, and tell someone your plans.

Look at the line of peaks to the south. The reserve beyond is some of the wildest country in Europe, and from here you can feel it.
t.guzeripl@44.0,40.1:
Guzeripl is the village at the foot of the Lago-Naki plateau, where the Belaya River emerges from the Caucasus, and it is the last real settlement before the mountains take over. The valley here is cut deep into the limestone, and the river runs fast and clear and a pale, milky green, between forested cliffs and a few terraces of farmland. The village itself is spread along the river, with houses, orchards and guesthouses, and a base for visitors heading to the plateau, to the river canyons, and to the caves.

Much of the surrounding area is part of Adygea, a small republic with a long Circassian history. The Adyghe, as they call themselves, were once the dominant people along the northwest Caucasus, and in the 1860s, after the Russian conquest, most of them were driven out to the Ottoman Empire, in one of the great tragedies of the nineteenth century. Those who stayed built a modest culture that survives in the cuisine, with cheese, flatbread and spiced meat, and in hospitality, a tradition in which guests are treated almost with ceremony.

The Belaya canyon, a short way downstream, is one of the best natural sights in the region. The river cuts through a narrow gorge, past walls of limestone, and in summer, rafting and canyoning trips run from the villages. The caves of the area, including the huge Azishskaya Cave, which has been developed for visitors, are a few kilometres away, and the whole district is a karst wonderland, full of sinkholes and springs.

The ride to Guzeripl from Kamennomostsky follows the river for much of the way, on a narrow, winding road through forest and meadow, with views of the mountains ahead. The surface is variable, with good tarmac in places and patched or broken sections in others, and rockfalls and washouts are possible after heavy rain. There is a fair amount of tourist traffic in summer, and minibuses and trucks can be slow, so patience helps. Fog and low cloud can obscure the upper valley, and temperatures drop sharply with altitude. The best months are June to September, and autumn colour in the beech forest is memorable.

Fuel is the practical question. Guzeripl has guesthouses, a few cafés and small shops, which cover the basics, though in the high season, rooms are scarce. Walk by the river in the evening, and listen to the water. It is the real sound of the Caucasus.
t.dzhily su@43.4,42.5:
Dzhily-Su is a meadow of hot springs high on the flank of Elbrus, and the name means hot water in the Turkic languages of the Caucasus. The valley, at about two and a half thousand metres, is a broad glacial trough, with mineral springs bubbling up from the ground in several places, some warm and some cold, all rich in iron and carbon dioxide, and the rocks around them are stained orange and rust. The springs are known as narzans, and they are famous throughout Russia, where people have drunk them for centuries for their supposed healing properties. In summer, the spot becomes a base for walkers, horse riders and jeep tours, with simple camps, tents and a wooden bath house.

The setting is dramatic. Above the meadow, the slopes rise to the summit ridges and glaciers of the Greater Caucasus, with Elbrus, the highest peak in Europe at 5,642 metres, appearing on clear days like a huge white dome. The air is thin and cool, with the smell of wet grass and sulphur, and the meadows are brilliant with flowers in July. Cattle and horses graze on the slopes, tended by herders from the Karachay and Balkar peoples, who have lived in the region for centuries and keep alive their traditions of animal husbandry and hospitality.

Getting there is an expedition rather than a ride. The track to Dzhily-Su is a rough mountain road, mostly rock and gravel, climbing from the valleys with steep sections, washed-out gullies and stream crossings, and it is normally done in a four-wheel-drive vehicle with a local driver. A motorbike would be a serious undertaking, with a good dual-sport machine, an experienced rider and a dry day. Rain turns the track dangerous, and the weather in the mountains changes quickly, with fog, thunderstorms, and even snow in summer. The season is short, usually from late June to early September.

The nearest sizeable town is Tyrnyauz, about thirty-one kilometres away by the road, where you can buy fuel, food and supplies, and the villages of Terskol and Elbrus have small shops and cafés. Take water, warm clothes, waterproofs, a repair kit and a plan, and do not travel alone if you can avoid it.

Taste the spring water, if it is safe, and notice the fizz. It is cold, iron-rich, and strange.
t.bermamyt@43.7,42.4:
Bermamyt is a plateau that looks across the whole of the Western Caucasus, and the reason for visiting is simply the view. It lies in Karachay-Cherkessia, at around 2,600 metres, a broad, grassy upland above the valleys of the Kuban and the Malka, and from its edge, on a clear day, the double summit of Elbrus stands white on the horizon, with the long chain of the Main Caucasus Range running off to either side. It is an open, windswept place, with short grass, rocky outcrops and the stone remains of old shepherd huts, and the sky feels very close.

The people of this region are the Karachays, a Turkic mountain people who have herded sheep, cattle and horses on these slopes for centuries. The Karachay horse is a hardy breed, famous for its endurance, and you may see herds grazing on the plateau in summer. In 1943, the Karachays were deported en masse to Central Asia, and they only returned in the late 1950s, so their link to these meadows carries a deep emotional weight. Hospitality is a point of pride, and a visitor on the plateau may be offered ayran, a salted yoghurt drink, and a plate of cheese and bread.

Reaching Bermamyt is a challenge. The usual route is a rough track from the valley, climbing in steep sections, with loose rock and ruts, and it is generally done by jeep or specialist off-road vehicle in summer. Riding it on a motorcycle needs a capable machine, good skills and settled weather. Fog and thunderstorms can come within minutes, and at that altitude it can be cold even in July. The window is short, from late June to September, and the track can close from the first snow.

The nearest sizeable town is Tereze, about twenty-five kilometres away, and Uchkeken is the next best, so fill up before you leave. Carry water, warm clothing, waterproofs and food, and make sure your phone is charged, though coverage may be absent.

Sit on the edge and look at the peaks. They stay in the mind long after the ride.
t.baksan@43.7,43.5:
Baksan is the town where the Elbrus road leaves the plain, and it is a good place to understand how this part of the Caucasus works. It lies on the Baksan River in Kabardino-Balkaria, in the green, fertile belt at the foot of the mountains, with orchards, cornfields and village streets lined with walnut trees. The river itself rises on the glaciers of Elbrus and flows north through a long, steep gorge before it spreads out here, and it is a cold, cloudy grey with glacial silt. About thirty-seven thousand people live in the town, which is mostly Kabardian, a people of the Circassian family, with a strong tradition of horsemanship, hospitality and rich cuisine.

Kabardians have been in the area for many centuries, and their code of manners is famous, with an emphasis on honour, courtesy and respect for guests. Food includes flatbreads, boiled lamb, thick sour cream sauces and a range of cheese, and a friendly stop at a roadside cafe may turn into a long meal. In the surrounding villages, you can still find old stone houses and towers.

Up the valley, a very different science is under way. The Baksan Neutrino Observatory, built in the 1970s deep in a tunnel in the mountainside, was set up to study elusive particles from the sun and the cosmos, shielded from interference by a kilometre of rock, and it continues to operate. It is not a place for casual visits, but the road to it passes through the gorge, and it shows how the mountain landscape serves more than one kind of explorer.

The ride from Nalchik to Baksan and then up the valley is a classic, and the road is mostly good, with wide curves along the river. As the valley narrows, the road climbs in a series of bends, with cliffs, waterfalls and sudden views of the snow peaks. Trucks, minibuses and tourist cars share the road, and the weather in the mountains changes quickly. Summer, from June to September, is the best time, and autumn colours are a bonus. Spring floods and winter snow can cause closures.

Fuel and food are no problem here, since the town is large enough for several petrol stations, shops and cafés. It is the last place for big supplies before the Elbrus region, so top up the tank, and buy water. Eat something local, and enjoy it slowly. The mountains ahead will wait.
t.terskol@43.3,42.5:
Terskol sits at about two thousand metres, at the head of the Baksan Valley, in the shadow of Elbrus, and it has the feeling of a village that was built for the mountains and has stayed small. The houses are mostly wooden chalets and concrete hotels, strung along a road that follows the river, and above them the slopes rise steeply, grey and green, to the ridges of the Main Caucasus Range. On the opposite side of the valley, the peak of Mount Cheget, with its ski lift, stands over the village, and behind everything, on clear days, the twin summits of Elbrus glow white.

The village has long been a base for climbers, skiers and scientists. A high-altitude observatory, with telescopes on a ridge above the settlement, takes advantage of the clear, thin air, and in the Soviet era, the mountaineering camps in the valley trained generations of alpinists. The Elbrus region is also the border with Georgia, and the old passes lead south over the glaciers to Svaneti. The border zone is closed, and you cannot cross, though you can see the peaks of the Georgian side from the high slopes, and permits are required for the frontier areas, so check the rules before wandering off the road.

The road into Terskol is the final stage of the Baksan Valley route from Nalchik, and it is a spectacular mountain ride. Beyond Tyrnyauz, the gorge narrows, the road climbs, and the bends get tighter and more frequent, with the river thundering below. The surface is usually decent, with patches and frost heave, and rockfalls can occur after rain. Cold air flows down from the glaciers, and the temperature drops several degrees in the last few kilometres, so keep warm clothes handy. Summer afternoons bring thunderstorms, so start early. Winter turns the whole area into a ski resort, and the roads can be icy.

The practical points are simple. The village itself has cafés, small shops, hotels and guest houses, serving shashlik, soup and tea, and prices are higher than on the plain. Book ahead in July and August and in the ski season.

Step out of the café in the evening, look up, and let the cold air settle on your face. The peaks are very close.
t.azau@43.3,42.5:
Azau is where the road ends and the cable cars begin. It is a wide, rocky glade at the head of the Baksan Valley, at about 2,350 metres, where the river is still a trickle of grey meltwater and the slopes of Elbrus rise straight from the car park. From here, the main lift system climbs in stages to the high shoulder of the mountain: first a gondola, then a second and a chairlift, reaching the Garabashi station at around 3,800 metres, from which climbers set off for the summit. The towers and cables vanish into cloud on bad days, and on good days, the white dome above you looks near enough to touch.

The mountain is a dormant volcano, the highest in Europe at 5,642 metres on the western summit, with the eastern top a little lower. It is covered with glaciers that feed the Baksan, and every year, the ice retreats a little more. Climbers come from all over the world for a relatively straightforward but serious ascent, and the weather can turn deadly with little warning. For a visitor on a motorcycle, the lift is the more sensible way to see it: a ride to the middle station gives a view across the valley, and a cup of tea at altitude is its own reward. Pay attention to the cold, because the temperature drops quickly, and the wind can be savage.

Azau is also the site of a mineral spring, the Narzan glade, where fizzy water rises from the ground and stains the stones rusty orange. Locals drink it, and it has a sharp, iron taste. Stalls sell woollen hats, socks and souvenirs, and cafés offer hot soup, shashlik and tea, though the prices are those of a resort. In winter, the whole area is ski slopes.

The riding up to Azau is the last stretch of the Baksan road, climbing from Terskol in a few steady bends, with the mountain ahead. The surface is generally good, but expect frost damage, rockfalls after rain, and a lot of tourist traffic in July and August, with minibuses and taxis. Start early, because afternoon cloud and thunderstorms are common. The best window is from late June to September, when the lifts run and the roads are clear.

Parking is limited and busy, so arrive before the crowds. Fill up there and carry what you need. Stand with your back to the car park and look up. Few places give you such a sense of height without effort.
t.chegem@43.6,43.6:
Chegem is a Kabardian town just north of Nalchik, in the fertile belt where the Caucasus foothills meet the plain, and for a rider it is the starting point for one of the best short mountain roads in the region. The Chegem River rises on the glaciers to the south and flows through a deep, narrow gorge before it spreads over the plain, and the town grew where the water emerged. About eighteen thousand people live here, in a mix of old village streets, gardens and Soviet-era blocks, with a neighbouring town, Chegem Vtoroy, almost merging with it. In late summer, the air smells of ripe fruit and hot dust, and the roadside is lined with stalls selling apples, plums and honey.

The people here are mostly Kabardians, part of the Circassian family, with a long reputation for horsemanship, courtesy and cuisine. Kabardian cheese, flatbread and lamb dishes are common, and a visitor who stops for tea may end up invited to a meal. The district also has a Balkar population, a Turkic mountain people whose villages lie higher up the gorges. Their towers and graveyards, some of them hundreds of years old, stand on the slopes, and a few are open to visitors.

Heading into the Chegem Gorge from the town, the road climbs steadily, following the river. The valley narrows, the walls rise, and the road passes through short tunnels and over little bridges, with waterfalls and dark overhanging rock. The surface is generally decent but narrow, with patches, loose gravel and occasional rockfalls after heavy rain. The bends are frequent, and the traffic is a mix of cars, minibuses and local lorries, so overtaking should be done with care. The weather can change rapidly, and fog and thunderstorms are common in the afternoon. The best season is June to September, with September especially clear and calm.

The town itself has fuel and food, since it is large enough for petrol stations, shops, cafés and basic hotels, and Nalchik, only a short distance away, has everything else.

Take a moment at the edge of town to look up at the gorge. The dark walls rise ahead, and the road disappears into them.
t.chegem waterfalls@43.4,43.2:
The Chegem Waterfalls are a group of cascades at the head of a narrow side gorge in the Chegem canyon, and they are among the most visited natural sights in Kabardino-Balkaria. The largest falls drop sixty metres or so over a lip of dark rock in a long, white plume, and the roar of the water can be heard before you see it. In spring and early summer, when the snow is melting, the falls are in full flood, and the mist drifts across the path, so that anyone standing near the foot is soon soaked. Moss and ferns grow on the wet rock, and rainbows form in the spray on sunny afternoons.

The gorge itself is a place of great drama. The Chegem River has cut a deep, steep-sided canyon through limestone and shale, with walls that reach several hundred metres, and in places the road clings to the rock above the river. Balkar villages, with their stone houses and old towers, stand on the slopes above, and the Balkars, a Turkic people who have lived in these valleys for centuries, were deported en masse to Central Asia in 1944 and allowed to return only in the late 1950s. Their memory is strong here, and many of the villages carry the traces of those years.

The road up to the falls is a good mountain road by regional standards, though narrow and winding in places. From the town of Chegem, it climbs through the gorge, past small settlements and viewpoints, with tunnels and bridges, and a few rough or patched sections. In the final stretch, a path leads from a car park to the base of the falls, and there is a cluster of stalls and cafés selling tea, shashlik, honey and woollen goods. Expect crowds at weekends in July and August, and aim to arrive early for a quiet visit. Rockfalls are possible after heavy rain, and the surface can be slippery.

In the afternoon, thunderstorms can build over the ridges, and the road can become muddy, so keep an eye on the sky.

Stand close enough to feel the spray, and then step back. The noise and the cold air are part of the effect.
t.aktoprak pass@43.5,43.0:
Aktoprak is a pass on one of the least-known mountain crossings in the central Caucasus, a road that links the gorge of the Chegem with the valley of the Baksan and the town of Tyrnyauz, and for a rider it is a quiet reward for those who look beyond the usual route to Elbrus. The name is Karachay-Balkar, and the pass lies in the high, rolling country above the Bylym plateau, where the slopes are open and grassy and the villages are widely scattered. The road crosses the watershed in long gentle bends, with views of dark forest in the valleys and, on clear days, white peaks on the southern horizon.

The landscape is a mix of high pasture and rocky outcrops, with sheep, cattle and horses grazing on the slopes in summer, and the occasional herder's hut and stone enclosure. In the villages nearby, the old Balkar farmsteads, with their heavy stone walls and flat roofs, have survived on the steep slopes. The wild flowers of July and August are remarkable, including gentians, primulas and orchids. Because the pass is not heavily used, you may have long stretches of the road to yourself, with only the sound of the wind and the clink of cowbells.

The condition of the road varies. There are good sections, with newer tarmac, and others where frost heave, potholes and gravel are common, and in some places, the edge of the road is unprotected. Fog can fill the pass in minutes, and rain can create mud and standing water. Landslides and washouts are possible in spring and after storms, so check the situation if you can before setting out. The season is short, typically from June to October, and winter snow can close the road. Take your time, and keep an eye out for livestock.

Tyrnyauz, about twelve kilometres from the pass, is the nearest town of size, and it is a curious place: a Soviet-era mining city, built to extract tungsten and molybdenum, with a faded, half-empty look and a great scar of a quarry above it. It has fuel, shops and cafés, and it is the sensible place to stop before or after the crossing. The village of Bylym, very near the pass, has only the basics.

Pull over where the road crests, and look both ways. The change in the landscape between the two sides is striking.
t.blue lakes@43.2,43.5:
The Blue Lakes are a group of karst lakes in the Cherek Gorge, south of Nalchik, and the most famous of them is a hole in the ground filled with water the colour of turquoise. The lower lake, called Tserik-Kel in the local language, is a nearly round sinkhole, and it is said to be one of the deepest karst lakes in the world, with a vertical shaft going down to depths of several hundred metres. The water is astonishingly clear and cold, with a constant temperature of about nine degrees, and its blue colour comes from sulphur compounds and fine particles. Divers have explored the shaft, and the lake has an almost hypnotic quality, especially on a sunny morning when the light penetrates to the sunken tree trunks on the sides.

There are several other lakes in the group, including smaller ones that are greener or milkier in colour, and some are rich in hydrogen sulphide, which gives them a smell of rotten eggs. The local people believe the lakes have healing properties, and in summer you will see families picnicking by the shore. The area is a protected natural monument, and swimming is generally not permitted, so take photographs instead.

The road to the lakes is a short detour from the Nalchik highway. It runs up the Cherek Gorge, through villages and orchards, with rocky walls closing in, and then a smaller road leads to the lake itself. The surface is generally decent, with occasional gravel and potholes, and the last stretch is a short walk from a car park. In summer, the area is busy, with minibuses, taxis and tour groups, and the café stalls do a good trade in tea, shashlik and souvenirs. Go early or on a weekday for peace. Rain can make the road muddy, and fog sometimes hangs in the gorge.

Babugent, the nearest village, has a small shop and a few guest houses, and Kashkhatau, about eleven kilometres away, is bigger. For a full tank, you should fill up in Nalchik or one of the larger towns on the plain.

In the evening, when the crowds thin out, the lake turns a darker blue, and the silence returns. It is a remarkable place to stand and look.
t.fiagdon@42.8,44.3:
The Fiagdon is a river in North Ossetia, running down from the high Caucasus through a deep, narrow valley, and the village of Verkhny Fiagdon sits at about the point where the road begins to feel properly remote. The valley is one of several side valleys that run south from the plain around Vladikavkaz, each with its own character, and this one is known for stone towers. The Ossetians, who speak an Iranian language and descend from the medieval Alans, built defensive towers and burial vaults in these gorges, some dating back hundreds of years, and they stand on the slopes above the road, grey and square, with their narrow windows and flat roofs.

Ossetian culture has a quiet, proud character, shaped by mountains, feuds, and hospitality. Three pies at a table is a local tradition, a custom that holds that every meal should include three round pies, offered to the three saints, and the meat and cheese pies of the region are justly famous. Ossetian beer, brewed from barley and hops at home, is an old ritual drink, and in the villages, guests are welcomed with food whether they are hungry or not.

The road into the Fiagdon valley is narrow, and in places it winds along the edge of a steep slope above the river. The surface varies, with patches of good tarmac, broken sections and gravel, and landslides and washouts are possible after heavy rain. The bends are tight and frequent, and the views are superb, with forested slopes, cliffs and the white peaks of the Main Range in the distance. Traffic is light, mostly local cars and lorries, but you should expect livestock on the road. Fog and thunderstorms are common in the afternoon. The best months are June to September, and early autumn is lovely, with clear light.

Services are thin. The nearest sizeable town is Alagir, about twenty-four kilometres off, and Mizur, a village on the way, has basic shops. There are small guest houses in some villages, but it is wise to arrange accommodation in advance.

Stop at a tower and look at the valley from there. It is easy to imagine why the Ossetians built here.
t.dargavs@42.8,44.4:
Dargavs is known as the City of the Dead, and the name is accurate. On a bare slope above the Gizeldon Valley in North Ossetia stand about a hundred small stone buildings, like a village of tiny houses with pointed roofs, and each one is a family tomb. Inside, wooden boats once served as coffins, and skeletons and old bones can still be seen through the doorways, lying on shelves and stone benches. The crypts date from roughly the sixteenth to the eighteenth centuries, though some may be older, and they are the best known of the several necropolises in the Ossetian mountains.

Nobody knows exactly why the Ossetians built tombs in this way. Some explanations point to old beliefs about the afterlife and the journey of the dead, and to the Alanian heritage, and others suggest the plague or the harsh climate. A legend says that the tombs were used to isolate plague victims, who were walled in and left to die, but historians treat that story cautiously. What is certain is that the site is eerie, windswept and quietly impressive, with the white peaks of the Main Range rising behind. The hamlet of Dargavs is a few stone houses nearby, and visitors have to pay a small fee and sometimes ask permission to enter the tombs, a request that should be taken seriously, since this is a sacred place for many people.

The road from Vladikavkaz, about thirty kilometres away, climbs through villages into the Gizeldon Valley, and the final stretch to Dargavs is narrow and steep, with hairpin bends and a rough surface. The tarmac is patchy, with potholes and gravel, and landslides are possible after heavy rain. The views are excellent, particularly as you gain height, and a few viewpoints allow you to look out over the valley and the plain. Cloud often wraps the hills in the afternoon, so aim for the morning. Spring and autumn are quiet seasons, and in winter, snow can block the road.

The village has a small café or two in season, but not much else.

Walk up among the crypts, and keep your voice low. Whatever the truth of the stories, the place invites silence.
t.tsey@42.8,43.9:
The Tsey Gorge is one of the great mountain valleys of North Ossetia, a long, steep, forested cleft that runs south from the plain toward the high ridge of the Caucasus, ending in a glacier. The road follows the Tseydon River up from Alagir, through woods of beech, birch and pine, with the cliffs closing in and the air growing cooler, until the valley opens into a broad glade with a handful of hotels, a small ski area, and a view of the Skazsky Glacier hanging above. Mount Adai-Khokh, at 4,408 metres, stands at the head of the gorge, and its icy flanks gleam on clear days.

The valley has a sacred side. In the forest above the road stands the Rekom shrine, an ancient holy site of the Ossetians, with a chapel and a grove of trees where horned animals, deer and ibex, were once honoured, and the place was for centuries a destination for pilgrims. The traditional religion of the Ossetians blends Christianity with older beliefs, and shrines such as this are still visited on festival days. Visitors should be respectful, and some of the old customs, including limits on who may enter certain parts, are observed.

The ride up is among the best in the region. The road is narrow, with many bends, and climbs steadily along the river, with forested slopes on either side and the odd tunnel or bridge. The surface is generally good, since it serves the resort, though frost heave and rockfalls are possible, and the upper stretch can be steep and tight. In the morning, the valley is cool and shaded, and by midday, clouds often gather around the peaks. Traffic includes tourist minibuses and cars, and there is a checkpoint, as the area lies near the border zone, so keep your documents handy. Summer is the best season, from June to September, and in winter, the road is used by skiers.

Services are limited, and the nearest sizeable town is Alagir, about thirty-nine kilometres away, where you should buy fuel and supplies. The settlement at the top has hotels, cafés and a chairlift, though the choice is modest, and prices are those of a resort. Book ahead for July and August.

Look up at the glacier from the glade, and listen to the river. The air is clean and cold, and smells of pine.
t.mamison@42.7,43.8:
The Mamison Pass is the highest road crossing in the Ossetian mountains, and at 2,829 metres it is one of the great pass roads of the Caucasus. It runs from the upper valley of the Ardon River, in North Ossetia, over the Main Caucasus Range to the Rioni headwaters in Georgia, and for centuries it was used by shepherds and traders who carried salt, wool and iron between the northern and southern slopes. The approach on the Russian side passes through the Mamisonskoye valley, a long, narrow trough of steep slopes, meadows and rock, with the white wall of the main range ahead, and the air at the top is thin and cold.

The pass is also a border. The region is a sensitive one, with a military presence, and checkpoints are common, so be patient and polite. The mineral springs near the head of the valley, known for their healing properties, are also a feature of the area, and there is a small resort with bath houses.

The road itself is a mix of good and bad. Lower down, it is a decent mountain highway, with wide bends and strong views, but higher up, the surface deteriorates, with potholes, gravel and washouts. Landslides and rockfalls can occur at any time, especially after rain, and the road can be closed by snow from October to May. In the high section, fog and cloud can fill the valley in minutes, and thunderstorms in the afternoon are common, so start early. The wild flowers of July are magnificent, and the high meadows are alive with sheep and cattle.

There are no services near the top, so fill up in Mizur or in a larger town on the plain, and carry water, food and warm clothing. The nearest large town is Alagir, a considerable distance away, and the villages in the valley have basic shops.

At the top, the wind is usually strong. Look south over the rim, and see the mountains of Georgia rolling away.
t.mindo@-0.1,-78.8:
Down the western slopes of the Andes, where cold Quito air turns into warm, wet forest, lies Mindo. It is a small village at roughly 1,200 metres on the edge of the cloud forest of the Pichincha province, and it has built a reputation as one of the best birdwatching places in Ecuador. Hundreds of species live in the surrounding reserves, from toucans and tanagers to hummingbirds that whirr at feeders, and the famous Andean cock-of-the-rock gathers here to display at dawn.

Two roads lead there from Quito, a little over thirty kilometres in a straight line and much more on the ground. One drops through the old road via Nono, narrow, damp and full of tight curves through mossy forest, with potholes and landslide scars that demand attention. The other follows the main highway toward the coast before turning off to the village on a better surface. Both give you a tremendous change of climate in an hour, from the cool plateau to humid, green hillsides draped in mist, so be ready for rain and slippery patches at any time of day.

Beyond birds, the area is full of other things. There are butterfly farms, waterfalls reachable on forest trails, ziplines and tubing on the river, and small chocolate producers who will show you how cacao turns into a bar. Orchids grow on the tree trunks, and the air smells of wet leaves and earth. The best time for riding and walking is the morning, since the cloud usually closes in by afternoon, and the dry months from about June to September give better odds of clear skies.

Mindo has several small guesthouses and cafés, and most visitors come from Quito for the day or stay a night or two. Fuel is the thing to remember: the village is small and the better bet is to fill the tank in Quito before heading down, since there is no large town in between. Bring insect repellent and a rain jacket, and keep a close eye on the road on the way back up, when cloud and truck traffic make the climb slow.
t.banos ecuador@-1.4,-78.4:
Baños sits in a crack in the Andes with a volcano breathing down its neck, and that is the secret of its charm. The town, whose full name is Baños de Agua Santa, lies at roughly 1,800 metres where the Pastaza river leaves the highlands, with the cone of Tungurahua rising directly above. The name of the volcano means throat of fire in Kichwa. After a long eruption phase beginning in 1999, which forced people to evacuate for a time, the mountain has been alternately quiet and restless, and you should check the current status before you go.

People come for the hot springs, fed by the volcano's heat, and the waterfalls, and a reputation as the adventure capital of Ecuador. The basilica holds the Virgin of the Holy Water, credited by the locals with protection from the volcano, and the walls are covered with paintings of miracles. Sweet shops pull melcocha, a stretchy cane-sugar toffee, on hooks in the shop windows, and the smell of cooking sugar drifts down the main streets. At night, steam rises from the pools.

The ride out is the famous part. The road east follows the Pastaza gorge down through a string of tunnels and past waterfalls to the Amazon basin, dropping by roughly a kilometre of altitude, with hairpins, cliffs and ferny rock faces. The Pailón del Diablo, where a large cascade thunders into a narrow chasm, is the best known of the falls. Cyclists share the road on weekends, as do buses and lorries, so ride with your wits about you, and expect wet tarmac at almost any time of year.

Baños lies about twenty-seven kilometres from Ambato, the big city to the north-west, and Pelileo, a town of around sixteen thousand, is closer, but the town itself has fuel stations and the services of a place that lives on visitors: hostels, restaurants, motorbike rental shops. Weekends and holidays are packed, so arrive early or come midweek. Rain is likely in the afternoon, and the morning is the best time for the road. Try a plate of trout or a sugar-cane drink from the stalls.
t.puyo@-1.5,-78.0:
Puyo is where the Andes finally give up and the Amazon takes over. The town is the capital of Pastaza province, at about 950 metres on the edge of the rainforest, and when you arrive after the long descent from Baños, the air feels like a warm, wet towel. The town grew from a mission and a base for oil exploration in the twentieth century, and it still serves as the commercial centre for a huge area of forest, rivers and indigenous communities of the Kichwa, Shuar and Achuar peoples.

For a rider, the destination is really the road, and Puyo is where the Route of the Waterfalls ends. After the gorge, the road flattens, runs beside the Pastaza and its tributaries through banana plantations and green slopes, with the occasional lorry carrying timber or cattle. Rain can arrive within minutes, so keep waterproofs handy and expect the surface to shine and the visor to fog. In the dry months, the heat is thick and damp, and it is better to be moving than waiting.

In town, the Omaere ethnobotanical park shows the medicinal plants and traditional houses of the local peoples, while the riverside and malecón offer a gentler walk. The jungle is close, and tour operators arrange trips to communities along the rivers, with canoe rides and guided walks in the forest. The food is different too, with fish cooked in leaves, called maito, yuca, plantain and a fermented drink made from cassava called chicha, which you will usually be offered in a village.

Puyo is a town of about twenty-five thousand, so fuel, hotels and workshops are all easy to find, and Palora, a smaller town further south, is the next place of any size in that direction. Take mosquito repellent, as evenings bring insects, and a change of clothes, as everything feels damp. The road back up toward the highlands is a memorable one in the late afternoon, when mist forms in the valleys and the climb feels like leaving another world behind.
t.chimborazo refuge@-1.5,-78.8:
Here is a fact that sounds made up and is not: the summit of Chimborazo is the farthest point on the Earth's surface from the centre of the planet. Because the Earth bulges at the equator, this 6,263-metre volcano, only a degree and a half south of the line, stands a couple of kilometres further out than Everest does. It is the highest peak in Ecuador, a broad, glaciated dome that is dormant, and the refuge gate lies on its flanks in the Chimborazo Fauna Production Reserve.

The road up is a high-altitude treat. From Riobamba or the Guaranda highway, you climb through the dry, cold plateau known as the Arenal, an area of sand and volcanic ash, across a landscape that feels more like the moon than the equator. Vicuñas, reintroduced to the reserve, graze on the tussock grass and are very often seen close to the road, along with the small herds of llamas and alpacas kept by local families. The pavement leads to a gate and then a gravel track toward the refuge at about 4,800 metres, so conditions and rules about access may change, and it is important to check them.

The mountain has a long place in exploration history. Alexander von Humboldt tried to climb it in 1802, reaching a height of about 5,600 metres, which was thought to be a world record at the time, and Edward Whymper made the first successful ascent in 1880 with the Carrel cousins. Today, mountaineering is a serious business, and even the refuge walk should be taken seriously, because altitude sickness and sudden storms are real dangers.

The weather turns quickly. Clear dawns bring great views of the snowfield and its neighbour Carihuairazo, but cloud, hail and wind arrive early in the afternoon, so ride up in the morning, wear several layers, and be ready for fingers that stop working. Bring water, energy snacks, and give yourself a day or two at altitude beforehand.
t.cuenca ecuador@-2.9,-79.0:
Cuenca is a city of domes, rivers and hats, and it gets under your skin. Its full name, Santa Ana de los Cuatro Ríos de Cuenca, refers to the four rivers that run through the broad valley at 2,550 metres, and the historic centre, founded in 1557 by the Spanish on the ruins of the Inca city of Tomebamba, is listed by UNESCO. The cathedral's blue and white domes rise over the main square, and streets of red-tiled houses with wrought-iron balconies run down to the Tomebamba river and its grassy banks.

The famous hats are a good story. What the world calls Panama hats are actually made in Ecuador, woven from toquilla straw, and Cuenca is one of the main centres of the trade, with workshops and a small museum where you can see how the fibres are prepared and woven by hand. They were shipped to Panama and worn by workers building the canal, which is how the wrong name stuck. Markets sell flowers and fruit, and the pace of life is deliberately slow.

For riders it is a base with good options in each direction. West of the city the road climbs toward Cajas National Park, with cold páramo and lakes. South runs the road to Loja, and east and north lead to quiet farming villages such as Llacao and Nulti, where narrow roads wind through hills of crops. The best riding is early in the day, when the traffic in the city is lighter and the mountain air is crisp. Take care on cobbled streets, which become slippery in the rain.

A city of nearly three hundred thousand people has everything, from fuel stations to motorcycle workshops and plenty of places to eat. Try mote pillo, a dish of hominy and scrambled egg, or a bowl of locro soup, and finish with a cup of local coffee in one of the courtyard cafés. The altitude is moderate, the climate mild, and the evenings are cool, so a light jacket does well. Spend a full day walking the old centre, because the best of it is invisible from the saddle.
t.cajas@-2.8,-79.2:
Cajas looks like a place that nobody finished. The national park, west of Cuenca, is a high tableland of rock, bog and water, scattered with more than two hundred lakes left behind by glaciers, and the land sits mostly above 3,500 metres. Tussock grass and cushion plants cover the slopes, and in sheltered folds you find small woods of polylepis, the paper-bark trees that grow higher than any other tree on Earth, their twisted trunks peeling in red flakes.

The road through is a main route between Cuenca and the coastal city of Guayaquil, and its highest point is around 4,000 metres or a little more. That makes it a spectacular and sometimes unpleasant ride. Mist hangs on the tops for most of the day, rain is possible at any time, and the temperature can fall to a few degrees above freezing. The surface is paved, but fog reduces visibility to a few metres and lorries grind slowly, so ride with lights on and lots of caution, especially on the descent toward the lowlands, where the road falls in long, wet bends through cloud forest.

The best moment is early, when the light is clear and the lakes are still. Laguna Toreadora, near the visitor centre, is the best known, with a short loop trail around the shore. Trout fishing is popular in the lakes, and a simple café near the park serves hot soup and trout, which a cold hand will appreciate. Andean condors are rare but possible, and you may spot caracaras, hummingbirds and even a spectacled bear if you are very lucky.

Cuenca, about twenty-eight kilometres to the east, is the place for fuel, and there is nothing at the park itself, so fill the tank beforehand. Small villages such as Cañar lie much farther south. Bring layers, waterproofs and warm gloves, whatever the weather in town, because the climate changes completely within half an hour of the city. Stop at the park office for current information on trails and conditions.
t.loja@-4.0,-79.2:
Loja is the quiet intellectual of Ecuador. Tucked into a green valley at about 2,100 metres in the far south, it has a reputation as the country's capital of music and the arts, with a conservatory and a long tradition of poets and composers. The city was founded in 1548 and is home to a respected university, so the streets have a youthful, studious feel. It has a calm centre of arcades and plazas, and a castle-like gate at the northern entrance to the city, the Puerta de la Ciudad, which is the favourite photo stop.

The surroundings are surprisingly rich in nature. Podocarpus National Park rises just to the east, protecting cloud forest, páramo and a huge variety of birds and orchids, and it connects to forest on the Amazonian side. The region has a long coffee tradition, and Loja's cafés are a decent excuse to stop. Locals eat repe, a thick green banana soup, and cecina, a thin salted pork, as well as the sweet cakes sold in the bakeries.

For motorcyclists, Loja marks the end of the long highland road that runs the length of Ecuador, and the beginning of the southern mountains. Heading south, the road toward Vilcabamba is smooth and winding, crossing ridges with wide views, while the road north to Catamayo and the airport drops into a dry, warm valley with sugar cane. To the east the road to Zamora descends into the Amazon basin in a long series of bends and tunnels, though conditions need checking. Mornings are clear and fresh, afternoons often cloudy.

Loja is a city of about a hundred and twenty thousand, with fuel, workshops and a large choice of food, and Catamayo and Zamora, with eighteen and fifteen thousand people, are the next centres. The climate is mild but changeable, and rain comes in short heavy bursts in the wetter months, so bring waterproofs. People are famously polite, and most are happy to point you in the right direction if you stop and ask.
t.vilcabamba@-4.3,-79.2:
Vilcabamba has a reputation that is bigger than it is. The small town in a sheltered valley south of Loja, at about 1,500 metres, was once marketed as the Valley of Longevity, with stories of residents living to well over a hundred, though researchers who checked the records found such claims did not stand up. What is true is that the climate is hard to fault: mild, sunny and dry for most of the year, with cool nights, which is why the valley has drawn a steady stream of foreign settlers and a laid-back community of artists, retirees and hikers.

The mountains give the place its look. Behind the village rises Mandango, a ridge shaped like a sleeping figure, which is a popular walk, and the edges of Podocarpus National Park reach nearby with cloud forest, waterfalls and orchids. Birdwatching is excellent, and the valley is a good place to see hummingbirds in gardens. Horse riding, hot springs and herbal medicine have all become part of what visitors do, and the central plaza has the relaxed feel of a village where nobody is in a hurry.

The ride from Loja takes about thirty kilometres, and it is one of the nicest short roads in the south. It climbs out of the city, crosses a ridge, and winds down through eucalyptus, farmland and small settlements into the valley, with good tarmac, steady bends and wide views. Traffic is light, apart from the occasional bus, and the best time is the morning, when the sun picks out the folds of the hills. Dogs and animals are an occasional hazard on the road.

For practical needs, Vilcabamba is small, and the safer approach is to fill the tank in Loja, though there may be a pump in the area, so ask locally. Guesthouses and cafés are plentiful, with vegetarian food and fresh juices, thanks to the visitors, and local coffee and cheese are good. Take a swim if your accommodation has a pool, and expect warm days and cool evenings. Go slowly through the village, where pedestrians and pickups share the narrow streets.
t.historic centre of santa ana de los rios:
High in the southern Ecuadorian Andes, at about 2,500 metres, Cuenca was founded by the Spanish in 1557 on a grid plan, on the site of an Inca city called Tomebamba, which was itself built over an earlier Cañari settlement. The colonial centre, with its cobbled streets, whitewashed houses with wooden balconies, churches and plazas, was inscribed by UNESCO in 1999, and the blue-tiled domes of the new cathedral are the city's landmark. The Tomebamba river runs through the city, lined with parks and old houses perched on the bank.

Cuenca is also the home of the so-called Panama hat, woven from toquilla straw, which got its name because it was shipped through Panama and worn by the workers building the canal. Several workshops in the city show the process, from weaving to blocking and finishing. The Pumapungo museum and archaeological park displays the remains of Inca Tomebamba, and the markets sell flowers, fruit and local specialities.

The riding around Cuenca is spectacular. The road west to the coast crosses the Cajas national park, a high páramo landscape of lakes, grasslands and rocky peaks, climbing to over four thousand metres before descending steeply to the lowlands, through cloud forest and banana plantations. To the east, roads lead down into the Amazon basin, through deep valleys and over passes. The surfaces vary, with landslides common in the rainy season, and the altitude affects both rider and machine. The drier months, June to September, are the best time to ride.

Cuenca is a city of nearly three hundred thousand people, with fuel, mechanics, hotels and restaurants. The food is a highlight: try hornado, roast pork, and mote pillo, hominy scrambled with eggs, and drink the local coffee. The markets are colourful and lively, and the hat workshops let you see the weaving and buy a hat made by hand. Allow time to acclimatise to the altitude before riding the high passes, and carry warm clothing, as the weather in the Cajas can change from sunshine to freezing fog in minutes.
t.grigoleti@42.1,41.7:
Grigoleti is a strip of pine woods and black sand on Georgia's Black Sea coast, squeezed between the sea and the great reed beds of Lake Paliastomi, a few kilometres north of the resort of Ureki and a short hop south of the port of Poti. It is a holiday place for Georgian families rather than foreign tourists, with guesthouses among the trees, wooden cafés and a beach that stretches as far as you can see. The sand here, and even more at Ureki, is dark and magnetic, full of iron-rich minerals washed down from the mountains, and locals swear it does wonders for aching joints. After a long day in the saddle feel free to test the theory.

This is the edge of ancient Colchis, the land where, in Greek myth, Jason and the Argonauts sailed to steal the Golden Fleece. The river Rioni, which the Greeks called the Phasis, meets the sea at Poti, and Greek colonists really did trade along this shore. The wet lowland behind the coast is now protected as part of Kolkheti National Park, a landscape of peat bogs, alder forest and lagoons, and it sits on one of the major migration routes for birds of prey between Europe and Africa. In autumn the skies over Batumi, further south, fill with raptors.

The main coast road from Poti south towards Kobuleti and Batumi passes right by, and it is mostly flat and straight, but Georgian traffic will keep you awake. Overtaking is a national sport, minibuses stop wherever they like and cows stand on the asphalt with total serenity, especially around dusk. Roads in good condition can suddenly have deep potholes. The best riding in the region is inland: up into the hills of Guria behind Ozurgeti or north into Samegrelo, where the forests of the Colchic rainforest climb steeply into the Caucasus foothills.

Poti is the nearest real town, with fuel, markets and banks, and Ureki has smaller petrol stations along the main road. Food on the coast is simple and good: khachapuri, grilled fish, fresh cheese, and the Megrelian dishes from just up the road, which come with walnuts and a properly fiery kick. Summer is hot and humid, so think about the early morning and the evening for riding, and leave the middle of the day for the shade of the pines.
t.subsection quebrada huatuchi plaza del i:
Far down in the southwest of Ecuador, in the province of Loja near the border with Peru, the old Inca highway crossed a dry and broken country of ridges and ravines on its way between the Andes of Ecuador and northern Peru. The subsection near the Quebrada Huatuchi is one of the stretches of the Qhapaq Ñan identified and protected here, part of a route that linked Inca settlements on both sides of the present border, including the ruins of Aypate on the Peruvian side. Out here the stone paving, retaining walls and drainage of the road can still be traced across the hillsides.

The landscape is quite unlike the green highlands further north. This is the realm of the Tumbesian dry forest, with ceiba trees swelling like bottles, cacti, thorn scrub and seasonal streams that roar in the wet months and vanish in the dry season. Hummingbirds and parrots move through the trees, and the light in the late afternoon turns the slopes gold. Mornings at altitude can be cool, but by midday the valleys are hot.

Riding in this corner of Loja is rewarding but remote. Main roads linking Loja, Catamayo, Cariamanga and Macará are paved, winding and scenic, with long climbs over ridges and drops into warm valleys, though landslides and broken sections are common after heavy rain. The tracks toward the Inca road sections are often dirt, sometimes rough and steep, and best tackled on a bike that can handle it. Distances look short on the map but take time.

Cariamanga, about twenty five kilometres away, is the nearest proper town, with fuel, small restaurants and basic lodging, and it sits beneath a striking cone shaped hill. Catamayo, further north, has the regional airport and more services, and Loja city, beyond it, is a pleasant colonial city known for its music. In the villages expect simple food: soups, rice, plantain, and the strong local coffee that grows on these slopes.

Carry plenty of water, a spare tube, and enough fuel to return, as stations thin out quickly on the side roads. Ask locally about the state of the tracks before setting off, and avoid riding after dark. The reward is a sense of travelling a route that people walked long before there were any engines here at all.
t.segment san jose llamacanchi las limas@-:
The Inca road did not end at the Ecuadorian border; it ran on through the Andes of southern Ecuador towards Cuenca and Quito, and segments of it survive in the province of Loja, among them this one between San José, Llamacanchi and Las Limas. It is a remote stretch in hill country near the Peruvian border, where the Andes are lower and drier than further north, and the road crosses ridges and valleys covered with scrub, pasture and patches of seasonally dry forest. It belongs to the Qhapaq Ñan World Heritage site, which spans six countries.

The landscape is surprisingly varied. In the rainy season, from roughly January to April, the hills turn green, rivers swell and the dry forest bursts into leaf. In the dry months, the land becomes brown and dusty, and the forests lose their leaves, revealing the twisted forms of ceibo trees with their swollen green trunks. Higher up, the ridges are cooler and often cloud-capped, with farmland and small villages.

The riding is for those who like adventure. Roads in this part of Loja are often narrow, winding and unpaved, with steep gradients, loose gravel and sharp bends. Surfaces can deteriorate quickly after rain, with mud and landslides, and some routes may become impassable. Traffic is light, mostly trucks, buses and local pickups. A dual-sport bike with good tyres is the right tool. Cariamanga, the nearest town, is reached via a paved road from Loja that is a fine ride in its own right, with long climbs and views over deep valleys.

The region has a long history. Before the Inca, the Palta people lived in these mountains, and the Inca incorporated them into their empire in the fifteenth century. After the Spanish conquest, the area became a quiet rural backwater, known for cattle, coffee and sugarcane. Today, the towns are small and friendly, with central plazas, churches and markets.

Cariamanga, about twenty-five kilometres away, has fuel, food and basic accommodation. Ayabaca, across the border in Peru, is another option, though border formalities apply. Carry extra fuel and water if you plan to explore the back roads. Local food includes cecina, thin slices of salted pork, and repe, a hearty green banana soup that is a staple of Loja.
t.pitshora@42.2,41.8:
Close to the Black Sea coast of western Georgia, north of the port city of Poti, the land dissolves into marsh. This is the Colchic lowland, where the Rioni and smaller rivers have built a wide plain of peat bogs, alder swamps and lakes, and Pitshora is one of the wetland areas protected here as part of the Colchic Rainforests and Wetlands World Heritage site, listed in 2021. The rains are heavy, the air is warm and humid, and the vegetation is lush in a way that feels almost tropical, surprising if you think of the Caucasus as dry mountains.
