This is the ancient land of Colchis, where, according to Greek myth, Jason and the Argonauts came in search of the Golden Fleece. The story may preserve a memory of real trade between the Greeks and the peoples of the Black Sea coast, and some scholars connect the fleece with the old practice of using sheepskins to catch gold particles in mountain streams. Greek colonies were founded along the coast, and Poti grew up near the site of ancient Phasis.

The wetlands are an important habitat for birds, especially during migration, when huge numbers pass along the Black Sea coast between Europe and Africa. Herons, pelicans, cormorants and birds of prey are common, and the peat bogs, some of the oldest in the region, support rare plants and insects. The Kolkheti National Park, centred on Lake Paliastomi near Poti, offers boat trips through the wetlands.

The riding in western Georgia is an adventure. The main roads are generally paved but can be rough, with potholes, livestock wandering freely and local drivers who overtake with abandon. Cows lying on the asphalt are a classic Georgian road hazard. The roads along the coast are flat, but inland, the mountains of Svaneti and Racha offer some of the most spectacular riding in the Caucasus, on roads that range from new asphalt to rough gravel. The best season is late spring and early autumn, as summer can be hot and humid in the lowlands.

Poti, about twelve kilometres away, has fuel, shops and restaurants. Khobi and Ureki, a beach resort famous for its black magnetic sand, are nearby. Georgian food is a highlight: try khachapuri, cheese-filled bread, Megrelian style with extra cheese on top, and spicy dishes with walnut sauce. Georgian hospitality is legendary, so be prepared for generous meals and toasts.
t.segment mamamag mamamag@-2.8,-79.2:
West of Cuenca the Andes lift quickly, and the Mamamag label sits on the edge of that rise, about twenty-four kilometres from the city, where the cultivated valleys give way to cold, open páramo. The nearest real town is Cuenca itself, a university city of cobbled colonial streets at roughly two and a half thousand metres, and anything you need, from fuel to a decent soup, you should sort out there before you climb.

This stretch belongs to the Qhapaq Ñan, the Inca road system that ran for thousands of kilometres along the spine of the continent. The Incas conquered the Cañari people here in the late fifteenth century and built a northern capital, Tumipampa, on the site of today's Cuenca; from it, tracks fanned out to the highlands and down towards the Pacific. The segments that survive are often modest, a paved strip a couple of metres wide, stone steps where the slope turns steep, drainage channels beside it, and they reward people who look at the ground rather than the horizon.

The riding up here is serious in a quiet way. The main road west towards the coast climbs through Cajas National Park, a plateau of glacial lakes, tussock grass and polylepis trees, and it goes over four thousand metres. At that height engines lose power, and you will feel the thin air yourself, with headaches and slow thinking if you push too hard. Weather turns without warning. A sunny morning can become sleet and thick cloud by noon, and the surface can be wet with fog even when it has not rained. Wear more layers than seems sensible and keep your speed down in the cloud, because visibility drops to a few metres.

Come in the drier months, roughly June to September, and start early. The light on the lakes in the morning is remarkable, and the páramo smells of wet earth and wild herbs. Locals sell hot drinks and trout from roadside stalls near the park entrance, which is worth a stop.
t.segment santa martha santa martha@-2.9,-:
If Mamamag is the top of the climb, Santa Martha is the other end of the story: the foothills where the Andes tip into the coastal plain, thirty-odd kilometres from Naranjal and a long way from anywhere that feels like highland. The air is thicker and wetter here, and the vegetation changes from tussock grass to ferns, bamboo and the dense green of the western slopes.

This is another piece of the old Inca highway, the Qhapaq Ñan, which linked the high settlements around present Cuenca with the lowlands, where cacao, cotton and other goods were traded up the mountains. The Cañari and the Incas before the Spaniards moved loads on foot and on llama trains, which explains the stone paving and the careful drainage on the steepest sections.

On a motorcycle, the descent from Cajas towards Naranjal is one of the most dramatic changes of climate you can ride in a single morning. Corners come in long series, the cloud forest closes in and then drops away, and the temperature climbs so quickly you will want to stop and peel off the layers you put on at the top. Damp surfaces and landslide debris are real hazards, particularly in the rainy season from about December to April, when sections of the road can be closed or reduced to one lane. Trucks heading for the port at Guayaquil use the road, so overtaking calls for patience on the tight bends.

Naranjal is a banana and cacao town of about thirty thousand people and is the place to refuel, eat rice and fish at a simple place near the market, and get out of the heat. Ecuador's coastal lowlands are among the world's biggest banana exporters, and you will pass plantation after plantation with the fruit bagged in blue plastic. Come in the drier months for the better visibility on the mountain section, and start early, because afternoon cloud sits low over the pass and the lowlands bring thunderstorms in the heat of the day. Water is available in every village, but carry your own bottle for the climb.
t.subsection achupallas ingapirca@-2.3,-78:
Achupallas is a high village in Chimborazo province, about sixteen kilometres from Alausí, and the walking trail named after it, which runs south towards Ingapirca, is one of Ecuador's best-known treks. For motorcyclists the point is the landscape and the road beside it: bare páramo at over three thousand metres, with the volcanic cone of Sangay on a clear day, and little else but sheep, lupins and the odd shepherd's hut.

Ingapirca, at the other end of the trail, is the biggest Inca site in Ecuador, though it is smaller and more intimate than the Cusco monuments. The Cañari people had a sacred place here long before the Incas arrived, and the Inca builders left their stonework beside the older foundations, so the elliptical Temple of the Sun, with its beautifully fitted blocks, stands next to Cañari remains. The trail between the two places follows what was once a stretch of the Qhapaq Ñan, the imperial highway that linked Quito and Cusco, and parts of the old paving survive on the walk.

The way in is to join the Pan-American Highway south of Riobamba and riding the long, winding descent into Alausí, a railway town on a steep hillside. The famous Nariz del Diablo line leaves from here, and the town is lively on weekends with tourists and schoolchildren. Alausí, with a little over fourteen thousand people, is the nearest sensible place for fuel and lunch, and Cañar, further south, has pumps too. Take a spare layer for the tops: the air at this height is cold even in sunshine, mornings start freezing, and afternoon cloud and drizzle are common. The surface on the main road is mostly good, but the side tracks to the high villages can be rough gravel, deeply rutted in the wet.

Mornings are clearest, July to September are the driest months, and from February through May the cloud tends to sit on the hills. Altitude matters too. If you are coming up from the coast, give yourself a night in Riobamba or Alausí before you go higher, because headaches and tiredness arrive quickly at the top of the páramo. Ingapirca itself has a small museum and a modest village with simple food, and there are cheerful cafes on the road near the ruins.
t.colchic rainforests and wetlands@41.7,42:
Rain is the first thing you notice on Georgia's Black Sea coast, which gets some of the heaviest rainfall in the Caucasus and grows a green, tangled forest to match. The Colchic forests and wetlands lie between the sea and the foot of the Lesser Caucasus, behind the resort town of Kobuleti and inland from the lanes of Ispani, with Chakvi, a small coastal town of eight thousand people, about eighteen kilometres away and Batumi not much further. UNESCO listed the Colchic rainforests in 2021 as a remnant of the temperate forests that once covered this part of the world, with trees such as alder, hornbeam, beech and the evergreen cherry laurel, hung with lianas and ferns.

Colchis is a name from myth. This is where Jason and the Argonauts sailed to steal the Golden Fleece, and the river Phasis, today the Rioni, gave its name to the pheasant, which the Greeks first met on its banks. Real history was less romantic: Greek traders had colonies on this coast, and the region later passed to Rome, Byzantium and the Ottomans. In the nineteenth century the Russians introduced tea and citrus here, and the hills above Chakvi hold some of the first tea plantations in the Russian Empire.

The wetlands are the quiet side of the place. Peat bogs, sphagnum mats and shallow lakes near Ispani and further north around Lake Paliastomi are a key stop for migrating birds, and in spring and autumn, raptors and storks stream along the coast. Boardwalks cross the bog at Ispani, which makes it easy to see sundews and dragonflies without sinking in, and the whole place smells of wet leaves and peat.

On a motorcycle the coast road from Batumi north through Kobuleti is mostly flat and fast, with heavy traffic in summer, and the roads that climb into the hills towards Chakvi and Churia are narrower, wetter and often patched, with a mix of cobbled villages and fallen branches. Mist hangs in the valleys, and a dry day can turn into a downpour within minutes, so waterproofs are not optional. The best months are May, June and September, when it is warm but not too crowded or humid.

Fuel is easy along the main road, with stations at Chakvi, Kobuleti and Batumi, and the towns offer khachapuri, a cheese-filled bread boat topped with an egg, and fish grilled on the beach. Tea is served in tiny glasses, often with jam.
t.churia@42.3,41.7:
Poti, on the Black Sea coast of Georgia, stands at the mouth of the Rioni, the river the ancients called the Phasis, and this is the legendary land of Colchis, where Jason and the Argonauts sailed in search of the Golden Fleece. Churia lies a short way inland, in the lowlands of Samegrelo, among maize fields, hazel groves and wetlands. The area is part of the Colchic Rainforests and Wetlands, a UNESCO site added in 2021, which protects a remnant of the ancient forests that once covered much of the coast, with alder swamps, peat bogs and rare ferns.

Kolkheti National Park, with Lake Paliastomi at its heart, is a paradise for birds, and the autumn migration brings thousands of raptors and waterfowl along the Black Sea flyway. The climate is subtropical, warm and humid, with heavy rain, and the ground is often wet. In summer the heat can be oppressive, with mosquitoes in the wetlands, so go in spring or early autumn. The smell of the place is damp earth, woodsmoke and wild flowers.

The Mingrelian cuisine of this region is among the most distinctive in Georgia. Look for gomi, a firm cornmeal porridge served with cheese, satsivi, a walnut sauce over chicken or turkey, and spicy adjika. Roadside stalls sell churchkhela, strings of walnuts dipped in grape must, and the hospitality is formidable, with toasts and wine at the slightest excuse. Poti, a port city of about forty-seven thousand people, has fuel and plenty of restaurants.

For riders, the roads here are flat and fast, but drivers can be unpredictable, and cows and pigs wander on the highways. The main road between Poti, Senaki and Kutaisi, the E60, carries heavy lorries, and the surface is a mix of good asphalt and potholes. Kutaisi, an hour or so inland, has the medieval monastery of Gelati, founded in 1106 by King David the Builder, with its golden mosaic of the Virgin and Child. Plan for sudden downpours, and carry water in summer.
t.segment san antonio san antonio@-2.9,-79:
What I can say is that the point lies on the steep western slope of the Andes, in the country between the highlands near Cuenca and the coastal plain, with Naranjal the nearest real town, thirty-odd kilometres off on the lowlands.

The Inca built their road to link Cusco with Quito, and the stretch through what is now Azuay passed through Tomebamba, the second city of the empire, close to modern Cuenca. Roads like this one were paved with flat stones, with steps on the steep ground and drains set to carry rain away, and parts of it are still walkable. The segments that run down to the coast were used for carrying goods such as shells and cotton, a trade that the Incas controlled tightly. A walk on an original stretch, in mist, with the páramo grass bending in the wind, gives a feeling of old purpose.

The riding in this region is serious and spectacular, though it demands care. From Cuenca, the road to the coast climbs through Cajas National Park, a high moorland of lakes and tussock grass at more than three and a half thousand metres, where fog and rain are regular, then drops through cloud forest in a long series of bends to the hot banana and cacao lowlands. The temperature shift is dramatic, and the road is often damp, with landslides in the rainy season and occasional roadworks. Wear warm layers on the top and carry rain gear all the time.

Services are thin in the hills. There is fuel in Cuenca and in Naranjal, and small villages along the way have food stalls and basic shops, but petrol stations are not frequent, so fill up before the climb. Dry months from June to September give the clearest views, though the páramo is never entirely dry. If the weather turns nasty on the high section, wait for a break rather than riding blind in the fog.
t.segment aypate el arco@-4.7,-79.6:
High above the dry coast of northern Peru, the Andes rise into a cold, wet world of páramo and cloud forest, and in the highlands near Ayabaca sits Aypate, an Inca administrative centre that few visitors ever see. It was one of the major stops on the Inca road network in this part of the country, linked to the great highway that ran north toward Quito, and the Qhapaq Ñan road system was listed by UNESCO in 2014. The stone terraces, plazas and buildings lie scattered on a windy hilltop, with the mist drifting through, and the sense of remoteness is extraordinary.

The segment named Aypate to El Arco is a rural stretch in the Ayabaca district of the Piura region. Roads here are rough, steep and often unpaved, and conditions change with the weather. In the dry months, roughly from May to October, tracks are firmer, and in the rainy season landslides and mud are a real risk. This is a place for a capable bike, a patient pace and local advice, and for riders who are happy to turn back if the weather turns. Temperatures at altitude can be cool even when the lowlands are hot.

Ayabaca, about eighteen kilometres away, is a town of around five thousand and is the nearest place for supplies, food and a bed. Fuel in a small highland town is not always certain, so carry what you need, and plan to refill in Sullana or Piura on the way up. Each October the town hosts one of the largest religious pilgrimages in northern Peru, devoted to a figure known as the Señor Cautivo, and thousands of people walk up from the coast.

The mornings can be luminous, with the whole landscape clear and sharp, before the cloud thickens. Take a good map, tell someone your route, and give yourself time to sit and look at the stones, because the Inca did not choose this site by accident.
t.nabada@42.2,41.7:
Georgia's Black Sea coast has a wet, green corner that few people think of when they think of the Caucasus. The Rioni river, the ancient Phasis of the Greeks, empties into the sea here, and around its mouth lies the Kolkheti lowland, a flat, humid country of alder swamp, peat bog, reedbeds and shallow lakes. Lake Paliastomi lies just south of Poti, and the Colchic rainforests and wetlands, listed by UNESCO in 2021, preserve a remnant of the forests that once covered the whole plain. This is the land of Colchis, where the Argonauts came for the Golden Fleece, according to the myth, and on a misty morning with the trees draped in lianas it is easy to believe in it.

Riding here is flat and straightforward, with fairly good main roads and slower, patched lanes through villages. The hazards are of a different kind. Cows, pigs and dogs wander onto the carriageway without warning, drivers overtake with optimism, and in rain the road surface can hold deep puddles. Summers are hot and sticky, with thunderstorms in the afternoon, while winters are mild and wet. Spring and early autumn are the best seasons, and the autumn migration brings huge numbers of birds, including raptors and storks passing along the coast on the way to Africa.

Poti, about eleven kilometres away, is a port town of nearly forty-seven thousand people, with fuel, markets and a good deal of Soviet-era grit. Its cathedral, finished in the 1900s, was modelled on Hagia Sophia in Istanbul, and it served for some time as a theatre during the Soviet years. Khobi, farther inland, is smaller. Along the roadside, stalls sell hazelnuts, mandarins, tea and honey, and in the restaurants you will meet the cornbread, cheese and walnut sauces of western Georgian cooking. Try a plate of khachapuri, the cheese bread that varies in shape from region to region.

Bring insect repellent, and a poncho, and slow down. The wetlands are best seen from a boat on the canals or a short walk on a wooden path, and the quiet, steamy atmosphere is unlike anything else in the country.
t.segment ciudadela vinoyaco grande@-3.7,-:
The Inca built a road through the Andes of Ecuador as they did elsewhere, and in the south of the country a stretch of it runs through the hills near Saraguro, north of the city of Loja. This is a section of the Qhapaq Ñan, the great Andean road system recognised by UNESCO in 2014, and the segment from Ciudadela to Vinoyaco Grande follows a paved or cobbled path across high grassland and over low ridges, with stone steps in the steep places and drains to keep the water off. Saraguro is known for its indigenous people, the Saraguros, who wear black clothing, the men in knee-length trousers and flat hats and the women with shawls and long pleated skirts, and who keep a strong tradition of farming and festivals.

The land is high, cool and green. This is the páramo country, and the fields of maize and potato, the eucalyptus woods and the open pasture climb to over three thousand metres. Mist drifts in during the afternoon, and rain is frequent. Cattle graze, women spin wool as they walk, and from some points on the ridge the line of the old road can be traced across the slope. Podocarpus National Park, a vast area of cloud forest near Loja, is among the richest places for plants and birds in South America, with hummingbirds, spectacled bears and orchids.

Ecuador's main north-south road, the Panamericana, runs through Saraguro, and it is a good ride, with long curves, mountains and views, mixed with trucks and buses. The surface is generally sound, with potholes after rain, and fog on the passes can be sudden and thick. The back roads to the sites are gravel or dirt. Altitude affects engines and riders alike, and nights can be cold. The dry season, from June to September, is the best time, though weather in the Andes can change in an hour.

Loja, twenty-nine kilometres away, is a city of over a hundred thousand, with fuel stations, workshops, markets and restaurants, and it is known for its music and universities. Saraguro has fuel and basic services. Try a plate of cuy, roasted guinea pig, or a humble but hearty locro, a potato and cheese soup, and a cup of local coffee, since Loja province is known for its beans. Carry cash and water, and respect local customs by asking before photographing people, especially women in traditional dress.
t.segment hierba buena hierba buena@-2.7,-:
The Inca road in Ecuador came down from the high Andes to the coast, and in the south the line passes through hills above the lowlands near Naranjal, a banana and cacao town in the province of Guayas. This stretch, called Hierba Buena in the listing, belongs to the Qhapaq Ñan system, which UNESCO recognised in 2014, and it sits on the western slopes where the cold páramo drops through cloud forest into warm, humid foothills. The segment is paired with another called Botija Paqui, which suggests a path used by travellers and traders linking highland and coast.

What I can say is that the landscape here is dramatic. The western Andes of Ecuador are steep and wet, with waterfalls, tree ferns, moss-covered trunks and mist, and in the lowlands below you find bananas, cacao, rice and shrimp ponds as far as the eye can see. The Cajas National Park, with its hundreds of lakes, lies on the high edge, and the contrast between its cold moorland and the tropical plain is striking.

The roads from Cuenca down to Naranjal are among the best-known descents in the country. They fall in long curves through cloud forest and farmland, with fog, landslides and heavy trucks as the main hazards, and a surface that can be patchy after the rains. The wet season, from December to May, is the hardest, with slides closing sections, and the dry months bring better visibility. Side roads to the Inca remains are rough, and a dual-sport bike is the safer choice.

Naranjal, about twenty-three kilometres away, has about thirty-two thousand people, with fuel stations, a market and plenty of small restaurants, and it is the practical base. Cuenca, on the high side, is a handsome colonial city with a UNESCO centre. Try a plate of encebollado, a fish and onion soup that is the national hangover cure, or a ripe banana snack, and a cup of fresh cacao drink. Carry rain gear and insect repellent, bring cash, and check conditions with locals before attempting any unpaved route.
t.sangay national park@-1.8,-78.3:
Sangay is one of the most active volcanoes on Earth, a cone of a little over five thousand two hundred metres that has been erupting more or less continuously for centuries. It stands in the eastern Andes of Ecuador, at the centre of a national park that was listed as a World Heritage Site in 1983, and the park covers a remarkable range of habitats, from glaciers and páramo down through cloud forest to Amazonian rainforest. The altitude difference between the top of the mountain and the lowest part of the park is more than four thousand metres.

The park is home to mountain tapirs, Andean bears, pumas and a rich bird life, including the Andean condor. The tapir, a shy and rare animal of the high forests, is one of the symbols of the place. The area is remote and rugged, and most of it can only be reached on foot, with permits and a guide, but the road from Riobamba to Macas, which crosses the northern part of the park, gives a view of the landscape from the saddle.

That road is among the most atmospheric in Ecuador. From Riobamba it climbs into the páramo, with views of Chimborazo and other peaks behind, then crosses a high pass in cold mist and wind before dropping steeply to the east, through cloud forest, waterfalls and tropical vegetation. The air changes from alpine to jungle in a couple of hours, and the temperature rises with every kilometre. The road has many bends, and in places the surface is damaged by landslides and rain, so go carefully and be ready for sudden fog, rain and cold.

Riobamba, the nearest large town, lies about forty kilometres away, with over a hundred thousand people, so fill the tank there before the climb, since stations are not frequent on the high section. The town is a good base, with a market, hotels and the old railway station, and the local dish, hornado, roast pork with potatoes, is a hearty meal. Bring warm and waterproof clothing, even on a sunny morning.

The best season for views is the drier months in the highlands, from June to September, but the weather here is unpredictable at any time of year. Start early to have clear mountain views, before the clouds build in the afternoon.
t.segment caragshillo canaro tuncarta@-3.6:
The Qhapaq Ñan, the royal road of the Incas, ran for thousands of kilometres from Colombia to Chile, and in Ecuador it climbed along the spine of the highlands between Quito and Cusco. Cobbled or terraced sections survive in the high country, usually away from the modern highway, and a number of them were added to the World Heritage list in 2014 as part of the multinational road system.

Names like Caragshillo and Tuncarta tell you that this is Kichwa-speaking country, and the word Cañaro points to the Cañari, the people who held these southern valleys before the Incas arrived and who resisted them fiercely before eventually becoming useful allies. The Saraguro people, with their black wool ponchos and broad felt hats, are the best-known community of the area, and local tradition holds that their ancestors were moved here by the Incas from far away, though the details are debated.

Do not expect the wide, polished road of the postcards. These segments are often stone paths a couple of metres wide, grass-grown, with steps where the slope steepens, and they are made for feet and llamas, not wheels. The motorbike rides that link them keep to the modern roads and approach on gravel tracks that can be slick in the rain, so allow extra time and take care in cloud. The highland weather is changeable: bright, cold mornings, afternoon cloud and sudden showers are the norm, and the air at this altitude, well over two thousand metres, is thin and cool.

The Pan-American Highway runs through Saraguro and is the backbone of travel here, a mountain road with long curves, steady gradients and many trucks, and the views over green ridges and cultivated slopes are good. The town has fuel and simple food, and a bowl of hot soup and a plate of rice and potatoes with a cup of sweet coffee is the right fuel for the day.

Early morning gives the clearest air and the best light on the hills.
t.peaks of otter@37.4,-79.6:
Three rounded summits stand out of the Virginia Blue Ridge here, and the Parkway slides in beneath them beside a small lake that mirrors the lot. Sharp Top is the pointed one, at around 1,150 metres, with a bare rock crown that you can reach on foot or by a seasonal shuttle bus; Flat Top is slightly higher and, true to its name, flatter; Harkening Hill makes up the trio. The Peaks of Otter area is one of the most loved stops on the whole Blue Ridge Parkway, and it is easy to see why, because the setting is compact, green and calm in a way many bigger overlooks are not.

Getting here from Rockfish Gap is the real reward. The Blue Ridge Parkway is a ridge road designed for slow travel, with a 45 mph limit, no commercial traffic and no intersections to speak of, and it follows the crest of the mountains with long, rhythmic bends and constant views down into farmland and out toward the next ridge. The surface is generally good, though tree roots and frost can leave patches rough, and fog is common, sometimes thick enough that the dividing line disappears. In autumn the hardwoods go orange and red, and the parkway fills with leaf-watchers, so aim for a weekday. Deer step out without warning, especially at dusk.

The place has a human story too. There was a farm in the hollow in the nineteenth century, the Johnson Farm, which you can visit, and a small inn has stood near the lake for generations, serving meals to travellers. Bedford, down in the valley about fourteen kilometres away, is a gentle town best known for the National D-Day Memorial, built there because Bedford lost proportionally more young men on the Normandy beaches than almost any other American community. It is a quiet, moving place and worth an hour if you have the time.

There is a lodge and restaurant at Peaks of Otter and a campground nearby, and a visitor centre with maps and displays on the natural history. A short loop around the lake takes only ten minutes and gives a nice reflection of Sharp Top in the water. Pack a warm layer, because even in summer the mountain air is cool, and in spring and autumn a sudden drop in temperature can arrive at sunset.
t.quilotoa@-0.9,-78.9:
Quilotoa is a hole in the Andes, and what a hole. The caldera is about three kilometres across, with steep walls dropping hundreds of metres to a lake the colour of jade, and the rim sits at roughly 3,900 metres above sea level, high enough that the air thins and the wind cuts. The volcano collapsed in a huge eruption several hundred years ago, throwing ash across the region, and the crater filled with water over time. It is a spectacle that photographs poorly and stuns in person, since the colour of the lake shifts with the light from turquoise to deep green to an almost metallic blue.

The ride up is a long climb on the Quilotoa Loop, a ring of roads in Cotopaxi province that links a string of Indigenous Kichwa villages, high plateaus and deep canyons. Most of the route is paved now, but some sections remain gravel, and landslides and washouts can occur in the rainy season. The road climbs through terraced fields, patches of eucalyptus and open páramo grassland, with small farms at astonishing heights and women in felt hats herding sheep and llamas. At Zumbahua, a small market town on the way, a Saturday market draws people from the surrounding communities, and the colours of the ponchos and skirts are a pleasure.

Altitude is the main practical issue. If you have come up from Quito, which sits at about 2,800 metres, or from the coast, the thin air at nearly 4,000 can cause headaches, breathlessness and nausea, and the engine will feel it too, losing power and running a little rich. Take it slowly, drink water, and do not rush the walk along the rim. Temperatures are low, even at midday, and fog can fill the crater within minutes. Wear warm layers and gloves, and be ready for rain, hail or even a dusting of snow.

The nearest town of any size is Pujilí, about twenty-six kilometres away, and Latacunga, farther east, has proper fuel stations and supplies. Fill up before the climb and carry a spare layer. Early morning, before the cloud rolls in, gives the clearest view into the crater.
t.zumbahua@-1.0,-78.9:
Zumbahua is a high-altitude village of adobe and corrugated iron, built on a plateau at roughly 3,500 metres in the western Cordillera of the Ecuadorian Andes, and on Saturday it comes alive. The weekly market draws indigenous Kichwa families from all the valleys round about, who walk or ride in from far above the tree line to sell potatoes, barley, wool, guinea pigs and bundles of herbs, and to buy salt, cloth and plastic bowls. The women wear felt hats and woollen shawls in vivid pinks, reds and greens, and the animals have their own section of the market, with sheep and pigs being bargained over in loud, cheerful voices.

The area is also known for its painters. In the nearby community of Tigua, local artists paint scenes of village life, fiestas and the surrounding páramo on stretched sheepskin, a style that grew in the 1970s and is now sold in galleries across the country. The paintings are bright, naive and full of detail, with condors, llamas and little figures dancing in the fields. A few studios in the area welcome visitors, though they are not always easy to find.

For a rider, the road is the thing. From Latacunga, the highland city to the east, the road climbs through Pujilí and up onto the páramo, a cold, wind-beaten grassland covered with tussocks and sudden patches of potato and barley fields, which lie on the slopes like a patchwork quilt. Zumbahua is the last substantial village before the road goes on to the Quilotoa crater, about twelve kilometres to the north. The surface is mostly paved, with rough patches, potholes and the odd animal on the road. The altitude takes its toll on engines and riders, so expect less power and take care not to rush. The weather can swing from sun to hail within an hour, and the nights are cold enough for frost.

Services here are basic. There is no real fuel station worth relying on, so fill the tank at Latacunga or Pujilí and carry a margin. A handful of simple hostels and eateries serve soup, rice and eggs, and the cheapest hot meal of the day is usually a bowl of chicken soup with potatoes. Altitude headaches are common, and a cup of coca tea or a slow walk helps.

Visit on a Saturday morning if you want the market, but arrive early and park carefully, because the narrow streets fill quickly.
t.chugchilan@-0.8,-78.9:
Chugchilán sits on the far side of a canyon, which in the Andes means you can see it for an hour before you reach it. The village is at about 3,200 metres, above the deep gorge of the Toachi river, and it has long been a stop on the Quilotoa Loop, the circuit of villages and crater lakes that winds through the western Cordillera south of Quito. Its houses cluster around a small plaza, and the surrounding land is a patchwork of fields, steep pasture and dark scraps of cloud forest that cling to the sides of the canyons.

Travellers come here for the walking and the scenery, and it has become one of the main bases on the loop. The community runs a small cheese factory, which was started with outside help to give local families an income, and its cheese and other local products are sold in the village. Many of the hostels offer communal dinners and hearty breakfasts, with a wood fire in the evening to fight off the chill, and the whole place has the mood of a small, friendly outpost at the end of the road.

The road from Quilotoa to Chugchilán is the kind of ride you remember. About twenty kilometres of winding highland road, paved in some sections and rough in others, it follows ridges and dips into side valleys, with big views over the canyon and the slopes of the Cordillera. The surface varies, with gravel patches, landslides after rain and animals walking on the road, so keep to a modest speed. Fog often rolls in by early afternoon, and the temperature can fall sharply, so start early and carry a rain jacket and warm layer. The route carries on past Chugchilán toward Sigchos, with the canyon always at your side.

Chugchilán has little in the way of services. There is no reliable fuel in the village, and the nearest dependable pumps are in Latacunga, so top up there before you leave and carry a spare. A few small shops sell basics, and hostels can usually feed you if you ask in advance. Mobile coverage is patchy, so tell someone your plans.

The mornings are the best time, when the air is cold and clear and the canyon lies in blue shadow before the sun reaches the bottom.
t.sigchos@-0.7,-78.9:
Sigchos is a market town in the foothills where the high páramo slides into warmer, greener country, and it feels like the end of one world and the start of another. The town sits at around 2,800 metres, on the western edge of the Ecuadorian Andes, with the Toachi canyon dropping away to the north and the road running down toward the subtropical valleys of the coast. It is the last proper settlement on the Quilotoa Loop, and for riders coming round from Chugchilán, it marks the point where the cold, windswept heights give way to terraces of maize, sugar cane and fruit trees.

Local life revolves around farming and cattle. Highland dairy farms produce milk and cheese, the fields are steep and worked by hand, and the surrounding hills are dotted with isolated houses and small chapels. t.al hada hairpins@21.4,40.3:

t.al hada@21.4,40.3:

t.sultan murat plateau@40.7,40.1:

t.uzungol@40.6,40.3:

t.caykara@40.7,40.2:

t.cape hatteras lighthouse@35.3,-75.5:

t.ocracoke@35.1,-76.0:

t.stony man@38.6,-78.4:

t.big meadows@38.5,-78.4:

t.cherkessk@44.2,42.0:

To the south, the Greater Caucasus rises in a long wall of snow peaks, with Mount Elbrus, the highest in Europe at 5,642 metres, in the neighbouring republic and visible from some spots on a clear day. The Teberda river cuts through spruce-clad gorges, and the valleys are green and cool in summer.

The people of the region are Karachays, Circassians, Russians, Abazins and Nogais, and the local food reflects a mix, with khychiny, flatbreads filled with cheese and potato, and shashlik, grilled skewered meat. Ayran, a salty yoghurt drink, is offered in cafes, and the mountain honey is excellent. Hospitality is a real tradition in the Caucasus, and a polite visitor may be invited for tea.

The road up the valley is a good one for a rider. Smooth tarmac, wide bends and the sound of the river alongside give way to steeper sections with hairpins as the valley narrows. Livestock, cows and sheep, often wander onto the road, and local drivers overtake boldly, so keep your speed under control. Rockfalls and mudflows are possible after heavy rain and in spring, and snow can close high roads outside summer. The best season is June to September.

Cherkessk has fuel stations and shops, with more in nearby Psyzh and Druzhba, but the road into the mountains offers fewer options, so fill the tank before you go. Border zones are close in this region, and it is wise to carry your passport and check local rules for permits.
t.yerevan@40.2,44.5:
Yerevan is a pink city. The stone that built it is volcanic tuff, in shades from rose to apricot to grey, and when the evening light hits the apartment blocks and the opera house it glows as if lit from inside. It is one of the oldest continuously inhabited cities in the world, founded as the fortress of Erebuni in 782 BC, and yet most of what you see was laid out in the Soviet years by the architect Alexander Tamanian, in a ring plan around a great central square. A little over a million people live here, about a third of the country, and the capital feels like the engine room of Armenia.

Ararat is the other presence. On a clear morning the twin cone of the mountain stands on the southern horizon, enormous and snowy, and every Yerevan resident seems to know exactly which window gives the best view. It lies across the border in Turkey now, which gives it a certain ache in Armenian eyes. It is also the reason so many riders wake early here: the haze builds through the day and the mountain disappears by mid morning.

Riding out of the city is a matter of choosing your exit and being patient. Traffic is assertive, lane markings are suggestions, and tram-sized marshrutka vans stop without warning. Once you are through the suburbs, the roads fan out in every direction: north towards the Debed canyon and its medieval monasteries, east over the Selim Pass and down to Lake Sevan, south through the Ararat plain. All of them climb quickly into mountains of volcanic rock, with corners that often arrive without a warning sign and surfaces that change from fresh tarmac to potholes in the space of a kilometre.

Practicalities are straightforward. Petrol stations are all over the city and on the main roads out; many also sell coffee, and some of them still give you a free glass of water, which tells you a lot about the country. Eat well before you go: lavash fresh from the tonir oven, grilled lamb, dolma, apricots from the market. In the cool of the evening, join the crowds at Republic Square for the fountains and the music. Spring and autumn are the best seasons; July and August are hot in the valley, and the passes can hold snow into May.
t.archaeological site of ani@40.5,43.6:
The first thing to understand about Ani is that you stand in one country and look into another. The ruined city lies on a promontory above the Akhurian River, and that river is the border between Armenia and Turkey, shut since 1993. The ruins themselves are on the Turkish bank, while the nearest Armenian towns, Maralik and the villages around it, are twenty kilometres or more away across open plateau. A rider coming from the Armenian side can get close enough to see the walls and the cathedral dome across the gorge, and that is a strange, quiet, rather moving experience in its own right.

In the tenth and eleventh centuries this was the capital of the Bagratid kings of Armenia, and the stories about it grow with the retelling: the city of a thousand and one churches, a population that may have rivalled the great cities of Europe, a crossroads on the Silk Road. The cathedral, finished around the year 1001 to a design by the architect Trdat, was a marvel of its time. Then came the Seljuks, the Georgians, the Mongols in 1236, and finally an earthquake in 1319, and the city was left to the wind and the swallows. What survives is a scatter of red and black basalt churches standing in grassland, still lovely, with faint frescoes peering out of the apses.

The landscape here is high, bare steppe at something over 1,500 metres, rolling and windy and treeless, with the deep cut of the gorge below. The roads across it from Gyumri and the south are wide and fast in places and broken in others, and between villages you may see nothing but sheep and a distant tractor. Weather turns quickly on this plateau: bright mornings, afternoon thunderstorms in early summer, and a long hard winter when the whole area is under snow. Late May to early October is the usable window.

There is nothing at the border viewpoints, so bring water and fill the tank in a larger town before heading out; this part of Armenia is thinly served, and the closest reliable stations are in the bigger towns of the region rather than the villages named on the map. A flask of coffee and a picnic of bread and cheese fit the place better than a restaurant would. Stay a while, and let the bells of memory ring: for Armenians, Ani is both the proof of a golden age and a place they can see but cannot reach.
t.cathedral and churches of echmiatsin and:
Armenians call this the Mother See, and the phrase is meant literally: Echmiatsin is the spiritual centre of the Armenian Apostolic Church, the seat of the Catholicos, the place the faith is governed from. The cathedral stands on the edge of Vagharshapat, a flat town of about forty thousand on the Ararat plain west of Yerevan. Tradition holds that Gregory the Illuminator, after the king converted around the year 301, saw a vision of Christ descending with a golden hammer to mark where the church should rise. That vision gave the place its name: Echmiatsin means the descent of the only-begotten. The present building has been rebuilt and added to many times, but its bones date to the fifth century and the core to even earlier.

The setting is deliberately calm. Walled gardens, tall cypress and plane trees, a courtyard of cross-stones called khachkars carved by generations of masons, and a museum with relics said to include a fragment of Noah's Ark and the Holy Lance. Your boots will be loud on the stone in a place where people speak softly. Dress for a church: cover shoulders and knees, and take your helmet off long before the gate.

The ride in from Yerevan is simple and rather dull in the best sense. It is a straight, busy highway across the flat plain with orchards, apricot trees, vineyards, roadside stalls of melons and peaches, and a clear sight of Ararat to the south on a good morning. You pass close to the airport and the ruins of the seventh-century church of Zvartnots, a circular pillared ruin worth a short detour if you have the time. Traffic gets heavy near Yerevan, and drivers are not patient, so keep your mirrors busy.

Vagharshapat is large enough for everything practical: fuel stations on the approach roads, cafes around the main street, bakeries selling warm bread and sweet gata. Lunch of grilled meat, fresh herbs and tomatoes that taste like tomatoes costs very little. Midday heat in summer is fierce on the plain, with temperatures well into the thirties, so go early or late. In April, when the fruit trees are blossoming and the mountain is still white, the whole plain looks like a postcard from a gentler world.
t.saint hripsimeh church and st shoghakat:
This stop is for the stone itself. Hripsime church is one of the oldest buildings in Armenia still standing as it was built: a compact, square-planned church topped by a drum and a conical dome, finished in 618 under the Catholicos Komitas, and so well proportioned that architects have been copying the plan for fourteen centuries. It sits in a green enclosure on the western side of Vagharshapat, a short ride from the cathedral at Echmiatsin, and its tuff walls have gone the colour of dark honey.

The story behind it is a hard one. Hripsime was, by tradition, a Roman Christian woman who fled to Armenia with a group of companions to escape the attentions of the emperor, and was martyred by the pagan king Tiridates around the turn of the fourth century. The church marks her burial place. A few hundred metres away is the second church, Shoghakat, dedicated to others of the group and rebuilt in 1694; the name means ray of light. It is small, plain and lovely, with a worn feel, and a very different mood from the rest of the complex.

Inside Hripsime you step down into a dim, cool space with a vertical sweep of tiny windows, a lit candle, and, beneath the altar, a crypt where the martyr is said to rest. Local visitors come in a steady trickle, often kissing the doorframe, lighting a candle, and leaving without a word. Treat it that way. It also means that photography is best done outside, in the early morning or late afternoon, when the light rakes along the walls and brings out their carved details.

Riding here is easy and gentle: flat, straight roads through the orchards and vineyards of the Ararat plain, light traffic on the side streets, and signposts in the Armenian script that you will learn to read by the second day. Vagharshapat has fuel, small shops, and plenty of places for a thick Armenian coffee, boiled in a little pot and served with the grounds. Come back through town on a Sunday and you might hear the bells and see weddings queueing at the door, with the groom's party honking all the way down the street.
t.monastery of geghard and the upper azat:
Geghard is cut into a cliff. Some of its chapels are built out of the mountain, others hollowed from it, and the effect is of a monastery that grew out of the rock instead of being placed on it. It sits at the head of the Azat gorge, about forty kilometres east of Yerevan, in a narrow valley where the walls rise vertically on three sides and the stream chatters below. The name means the spear, from the relic of the lance that pierced Christ, brought here by the apostle Thaddeus according to tradition and kept for centuries before being moved to Echmiatsin. The monastery was founded in the early Middle Ages, but most of what you see dates to the thirteenth century, when the princely Proshyan family built the rock-cut chapels. Together with the upper Azat valley it is a UNESCO site.

Inside, the main rock-cut chamber is dark, cool and very echoey, and the acoustics are the reason musicians and choirs love it. If anyone is singing when you arrive, stand still. Outside, small caves in the cliff hold khachkars and carved crosses, and pilgrims tie scraps of cloth to the trees.

The ride is one of the pleasures of Armenia. From Yerevan you go through Garni, a larger village of nearly seven thousand with fuel, shops and the only Greco-Roman temple standing in the country, a colonnaded first-century building above the gorge. From there the road narrows, climbs gently, and follows the Azat past basalt columns, orchards, and little stalls selling dried fruit and fruit leather. Surface and traffic are friendly enough, though tour buses fill the last stretch at midday, so aim for early morning or late afternoon. Watch for loose gravel on bends and for the occasional cow in the road.

Garni is the last place for fuel, so top up there. Goght, closer to the monastery, has a few small shops and cafes, and in season there are women on the approach road baking gata and lavash for visitors. A picnic by the river, with bread, cheese and herbs, is better than any restaurant. Mid-autumn brings gold into the poplars, and the place is beautiful, but winter can leave the road icy for days at a time.
t.cuenca@-2.9,-79.0:
Cuenca stands at about two and a half thousand metres in the southern Andes of Ecuador, where the air is thin and cool, and the rivers run down from the high moorland of El Cajas toward the Amazon basin and the Pacific. It is the third city of the country, a place of red-tiled roofs, whitewashed walls and wrought-iron balconies that was granted World Heritage status in 1999 for its well-preserved colonial grid, laid out in the sixteenth century on the site of an Inca settlement. The Tomebamba river runs along the southern edge of the old town, and its banks are lined with old houses with balconies hanging over the water.

The cathedral, known as the New Cathedral, rises above the main square with blue and white domes that are visible from almost everywhere in the town. It was built over many decades in the late nineteenth century and was never fully completed. Cuenca is also associated with a well-known product, the so-called Panama hat, which is in fact an Ecuadorian invention woven from the toquilla palm and exported from the port of Panama to workers building the canal. The best hats are still woven in the region around Cuenca, and several workshops in town let you watch them being finished and blocked.

The riding in and out of Cuenca is demanding in the best way. The roads climb and drop through Andean valleys with steep slopes, tight bends and sudden changes of weather, and the surface varies from fresh asphalt to potholed patches. To the west, Cajas National Park rises above four thousand metres, with lakes, peat and rocky ridges, and the road crossing it can be cold, wet and foggy even when the city is sunny. Pack warm clothing and waterproofs. Altitude can affect you and your engine, so ride sensibly and carry water.

As a city of nearly three hundred thousand, Cuenca has fuel stations, workshops, markets and plenty of places to eat, including the local specialities of mote pillo, a dish of hominy and eggs, and roasted guinea pig, known as cuy. Mornings are clear and crisp, and afternoons often bring rain. The air smells of woodsmoke, cut flowers from the flower market and warm bread. It is a delightful place to finish a long ride from the high volcanoes, or to start one.
t.western caucasus@44.0,40.0:
This is the core of one of the last large mountain regions in Europe where nature has been left more or less alone, and it is a World Heritage property because of that. The Caucasus Nature Reserve covers a vast area of peaks over three thousand metres, alpine meadows, beech and fir forests and glacier-carved valleys, and the area is also known for its plant life, with species found nowhere else.

The animals are the story. European bison were wiped out in the wild in the 1920s, with the last wild animals of the Caucasus shot, and the reserve took part in the work of bringing them back from zoo stock, so that herds now live in the mountains again. Brown bears, lynx, chamois and the Caucasian tur, a goat with huge curved horns, live here, along with a rich bird life including the Caucasian snowcock and golden eagle. The road from Maykop in Adygea climbs through Kamennomostsky to the Lago-Naki plateau, a high limestone upland with caves and meadows, and the last part is steep and rough, sometimes gravel, and often wrapped in cloud. Weather changes fast, with fog, hail and cold even in July, and snow can come early in autumn. The reserve interior is restricted and a permit is needed for any entry, and parts of the area lie in a border zone.

Fuel is available in Kamennomostsky and the larger towns, but in the mountains there is almost none, so fill up before climbing. Because current travel conditions and permit rules for foreigners in Russia are uncertain and change, check them thoroughly before you plan a ride here. Local mountain honey and cheese are worth buying from roadside stalls.
t.shenandoah rockfish gap@38.0,-78.9:
Rockfish Gap is a mountain pass in name only, a low saddle in the Blue Ridge where Interstate 64, the town of Waynesboro, and two of the most famous scenic roads in America all meet. The idea was a road for driving slowly, which is why the speed limit hardly ever exceeds 45 miles per hour, commercial traffic is banned, and there are no traffic lights or billboards. It is the longest linear park in the US.

Humpback Rocks, a few miles on, has a farm museum and a short, steep hike to a rocky viewpoint. In spring, flowering dogwoods and rhododendron turn the roadside white and pink, and in October, the maples and oaks give the ridge one of the best displays of colour on the east coast. It has fuel, restaurants and motels, and you should fill your tank here, since there are very few fuel stops directly along the Parkway, and you may need to leave the road to find one. t.kislovodsk@43.9,42.7:
Kislovodsk is a spa town in the northern Caucasus foothills, among the old resorts known as the Caucasian Mineral Waters, and it carries an air of nineteenth-century elegance. About a hundred and thirty thousand people live here, in a valley sheltered by hills, and the town is famous for its clean air, its mild climate and its mineral springs. The name means sour water, from the fizzy, iron-rich spring called Narzan, which Caucasian highlanders called the drink of the giants.

The town began as a Russian fortress in 1803, and soon the aristocracy caught on to the healing waters. Pushkin visited the region, and Mikhail Lermontov set parts of A Hero of Our Time in the Caucasian spa towns, with scenes of duels and romances beside the springs. The Narzan Gallery, a grand colonnaded hall where visitors sip the water, is a gracious place to see how it was done.

Doctors prescribed measured walks along its marked trails as a treatment, and the idea of the health walk, or terrenkur, is still part of the culture. The air is fresh and cool among the pines, and you can reach viewpoints and old pavilions by well-kept paths.

The road toward the Dzhily-Su valley climbs into the mountains, passing through rolling green pastures and then into rocky terrain with mineral springs and waterfalls. The Bermamyt plateau, a high meadow with views over the whole range, is reached by a rough road.

The surfaces in the hills vary, with some smooth asphalt, rough patches and gravel on the plateau routes, and the weather changes quickly, with fog and thunderstorms in summer. Cattle roam across the roads, and in the villages there are dogs and sheep.

Kislovodsk has fuel stations, shops and many cafés and restaurants, and the local food includes shashlik, flatbreads with cheese and the sweet pastries of the Caucasus. Summer is warm and pleasant, autumn is golden, and winter brings snow to the hills.
t.teberda@43.4,41.7:
Teberda is a mountain resort in the western Caucasus where the air smells of spruce and cold stone, and the first thing that strikes you is how green and tidy a high mountain village can be. It lies in the valley of the Teberda river, in Karachay-Cherkessia, ringed by peaks of two and three thousand metres. Caucasian bison were reintroduced here after almost vanishing in the twentieth century, and chamois, ibex and brown bears live in the high valleys. The flora is rich, with rhododendron, pine and fir, and wildflowers cover the slopes in early summer. A small museum in the village displays specimens and photographs, and it is a good introduction before heading into the hills.

Most visitors walk, and there are well-marked trails to waterfalls, to glacial lakes and up to viewpoints under the glaciers of Alibek, whose cold green stream rushes through a forested gorge. The surface is generally decent but can have sections of potholes and rockfall debris, and in the spring and early summer snowmelt can wash across the road. Cattle and horses graze freely in the villages, and drivers on the narrow bends tend to hug the middle.

Fuel stations are in the valley and in Karachayevsk, the larger town, so it makes sense to top up there before climbing. Teberda has small shops, cafés and guesthouses, and the local food includes khychiny, flatbreads filled with cheese and potato, and ayran, the sour drink made from yoghurt. Summer is cool and fresh, the best weather runs from June to September, and snow closes the high roads in winter.
t.dombay@43.3,41.6:
Dombay is a high mountain basin at about 1,600 metres, where the Teberda valley opens into a green bowl surrounded by some of the most dramatic peaks in the western Caucasus. The name is said to mean bison in the Karachay language, and local legend ties it to herds that once grazed the meadows. The peaks around it are serious: Dombay-Ulgen, a pyramid of rock and ice, tops 4,000 metres, and glaciers hang above forests of spruce and pine.

In winter, Dombay is a ski resort, with a cable car that carries passengers high up the slope to terraces at over three thousand metres, where skiers and snowboarders descend runs above the treeline. In summer the same lifts take hikers and sightseers up to views over a sea of summits. A vast panorama extends from the top station, with the ridges of the main Caucasus range fading into the haze. The village itself is a straggle of wooden chalets, hotels and cafés, with a lively and relaxed atmosphere.

The valley is full of walking routes. A short walk leads to a waterfall, another to a glacier lake with emerald water. The nearby Alibek and Gonachkhir valleys offer longer days among rocks and snow. The weather is changeable, and clouds can wrap the peaks in minutes, so carry a waterproof layer even in July.

The surface is mostly asphalt, with patches of potholes, and in the valley bottom the road narrows between trees. In the old days, the historic Military Sukhumi Road ran from here over the Klukhor Pass to the Black Sea, a rough mountain route built in the nineteenth century, though the modern border situation keeps the high crossing out of reach for travellers.

There are small fuel stops at the foot of the valley, but not in the village itself, so fill up before climbing. You can eat at the cafés in Dombay, where grilled meat, dumplings and flatbreads fill the menus, and the tea is served with local honey. In early summer, the meadows bloom with wildflowers, and in September the larches and birches go yellow. By November, snow lies thickly and the ski season begins.
t.nalchik@43.5,43.6:
Nalchik is the capital of Kabardino-Balkaria, a republic where the northern Caucasus rises abruptly from a rolling plain, and its setting is one of its main pleasures. The city sits at the foot of the mountains with the long white wall of the Caucasus range on the southern horizon, and on a clear day the twin summits of Elbrus appear far above everything else. The name is from the local word for horseshoe, nal, and the town began in 1818 as a Russian fortress on the frontier. Kabardians, a Circassian people, had long been known for horsemanship, and the horse culture remains central in the region. Balkars, a Turkic mountain people, live in the high valleys, with their own language and traditions. The two communities share the republic, and their cooking, music and festivals add depth to the region.

The city's heart is a large park, which was laid out in the early nineteenth century and has a pleasant mix of old trees, fountains and a small lake. People walk there in the evening, and it is a good place to sit for an hour. The town also has springs and spa facilities, and a long reputation as a health resort.

The roads south of Nalchik are the lure. The Baksan valley road runs up toward Elbrus, climbing through forested gorges to the high villages at the foot of the mountain, with the final stretch ending at Azau, where cable cars rise onto the slopes of the highest peak in Europe. To the west, the Chegem gorge is a deep, narrow canyon with a series of waterfalls that drop in high white ribbons from the cliffs, and the road beyond leads up to Eltyubyu and the high meadows. Surfaces are generally good on the main roads and rougher on the side routes, and rockfalls and washouts can occur after heavy rain.

Everything a rider needs is in Nalchik, including fuel, mechanics and hotels. Local food includes khychiny, pastries filled with cheese, and a hearty dish of boiled meat with a sauce of garlic and sour cream. The best seasons are late spring and early autumn, and summer afternoons can bring sudden storms in the mountains.
t.kingston@18.0,-76.8:

About a million people live in the city and its surrounds, and the first thing to remember is that Jamaica drives on the left, so if you arrive from Europe you are fine and if you arrive from anywhere else, take the first roundabout very carefully. The best months for a clear mountain view are December to March, when the afternoon cloud sits higher.
t.blue and john crow mountains@18.1,-76.6:

t.maikop@44.6,40.1:
Maikop is the capital of Adygea, a small republic that sits like an island inside Krasnodar Krai, and it is the last proper city before the northern edge of the Caucasus starts to climb. With around 144,000 people it feels more relaxed than most regional capitals of its size, laid out on a wide grid of tree-lined avenues on the Belaya River, which comes down brown and fast from the mountains in spring. It is one of the more satisfying slow reveals in southern Russia. Traffic in the city is ordinary, and the best advice is to be out by mid-morning so the hills are ahead of you for the day.

The city has a deeper past than its tidy streets suggest. A Russian fort was founded here in the 1850s, towards the end of the Caucasian war, and around the area there are Bronze Age burial mounds, among them the famous Maikop kurgan, whose gold and silver finds are held in St Petersburg. Archaeologists use the name Maikop culture for an early civilisation of the northern Caucasus, so you are riding through a landscape with real prehistoric importance, even if you will not see it from the saddle.

Adygea itself is home to the Adyghe people, a Circassian group, and their language, cheese and hospitality are the first things you notice. The local soft cheese is worth buying for a roadside lunch, and you will find it in the markets and in small cafes. Food here is hearty and unhurried.

The route out heads up the Belaya valley, with beech and oak forest closing in, the river getting clearer and the road narrowing into a proper mountain ride. A rider who arrives early and leaves with a full tank, warm layers for the plateau and some local cheese in the pannier has done it right.
t.dakhovskaya@44.2,40.2:
Dakhovskaya is a village on the Belaya River in the foothills of the Western Caucasus, and the name matters less than what it marks: the point where the broad valley south of Maikop narrows and the mountains stop being a view and become a place you are inside. The village is small, and the nearest sizeable settlement is Kamennomostskiy, six kilometres away, which is where you will find shops and fuel if the tank is low. Abadzekhskaya lies further north along the river.

The ride in from Maikop is gentle at first, with the river on one side, orchards and meadows, then beech forest taking over as you gain height. Past Kamennomostskiy the road bends along the river and the valley walls steepen, with limestone cliffs appearing above the trees. This is the approach to the Lago-Naki plateau and the Guzeripl road, and the surface and traffic change with the season. In spring, meltwater turns the Belaya milky and loud. In summer, tour buses and jeeps share the road, and in autumn the beech turns copper and the air smells of damp leaves, which is the best of the year to ride here.

Geology is the star of this stretch. The Belaya cuts through limestone, and in places the rock walls close to form narrow gorges where the water turns turquoise. Nearby is the Rufabgo waterfall area, a series of cascades in a wooded gorge that has been a walking destination for generations. The forests around here are among the best preserved in the Caucasus, part of a vast reserve system that protects bison, bears, lynx and some of Europe's oldest beech stands. You are unlikely to see any of the larger animals from the saddle, but the sense of wild country is real.

The area also has a long history of human use. Dolmens, those stone burial chambers of the late Bronze Age, are scattered around the western Caucasus valleys, and the people who built them left no written record. Locals will point out that the village has been a gateway for shepherds heading to the high pastures for centuries, and they still do, driving flocks up in summer.

Practical advice is simple. Carry fuel from Maikop or Kamennomostskiy, bring a warm layer even in July because the plateau above is much colder, and watch for livestock, gravel and rockfall on the bends. This is a place to slow down and listen to the river.
t.mineralnye vody@44.2,43.1:
Mineralnye Vody is the front door to the North Caucasus. The name means mineral waters, and the town grew up around the railway junction and later the airport that serves the spa towns of Kislovodsk, Pyatigorsk, Essentuki and Zheleznovodsk, a group known since the nineteenth century as the Caucasian Mineral Waters. About seventy-six thousand people live here, and many more pass through it on the way to the mountains or the sanatoria.

For a rider it is a landing pad and a supply point, and it does that job well. Fuel, cafes, car hire, hotels and mechanics are plentiful, and the roads around are flat and straight over open steppe. Ahead, on a clear morning, you may see the Caucasus ridge floating on the southern horizon, and on the very best days the twin white cone of Elbrus rises above it, a sight that makes you immediately want to turn the bars south. The ride toward Kislovodsk, Dzhily-Su and the Elbrus approach starts here, and so does the Dombay route. Early morning light is the best for the long view.

The region's history is bound up with the springs. Russian officers and doctors found the healing waters in the early nineteenth century, and the spa towns became fashionable for the aristocracy and for writers. Lermontov set parts of A Hero of Our Time in Pyatigorsk and died there after a duel in 1841, and Pushkin and Tolstoy both visited the region. The sanatorium culture grew in the Soviet era and still draws visitors. Locals will tell you that the water tastes of iron and eggs, and they are not being unfair.

The land around is also unusual. A group of small volcanic laccoliths, steep hills of hardened magma that never reached the surface, stand up from the steppe like loaves, and the best known, Mount Beshtau, is visible in the distance and gave Pyatigorsk its name, meaning five mountains. This is a rare piece of geology, and the sight of the hills against the plains is memorable.

Practical advice is to stock up here. The roads south have fuel at the larger towns, but supplies thin out in the valleys, and prices rise. Check the weather for the mountains before leaving, because the steppe can be warm and clear while the high valleys are wrapped in cloud.
t.arkhyz@43.6,41.3:
Arkhyz is a high green valley in the Western Caucasus, the kind of place where the road ends in front of the snow, and it has been a mountain resort since the Soviet period. It sits in Karachay-Cherkessia, at the head of the Bolshoy Zelenchuk river, with the village of Nizhny Arkhyz nearby and the nearest town of any size, Storozhevaya, almost forty kilometres back down the valley. That distance matters: fuel and a real shop are down the road, not up it.

The ride in is one of the better runs in the region. From Cherkessk the road follows the Bolshoy Zelenchuk upstream, first through open farmland and villages, then narrowing between forested slopes as the valley tightens. Corners are mostly flowing and open, with the surface generally decent and the scenery improving every few kilometres until the peaks stand ahead. In summer, tour buses and cars slow things on weekends, and in spring, rain and meltwater can leave gravel and washouts, so keep an eye on the tarmac. Autumn is the quiet and golden season.

Arkhyz has a long history and a few real surprises. Above the village, on a hillside, stand the Zelenchuk churches, among the oldest Christian monuments in Russia, dating to the tenth century and attributed to the Alans, a people who ruled this region in the early medieval period. Whether or not you stop to look, it changes how you see the valley: this was a corridor of the Silk Road branches and a Christian kingdom long before the Russian army arrived. The Special Astrophysical Observatory also sits nearby, its great white dome a strange sight in a wild valley.

Nature is the real draw. The surrounding mountains hold glaciers, alpine lakes, spruce and fir forest, and flowers in summer meadows. Chamois and tur live on the higher slopes, bears in the forest, and eagles ride the thermals above. The air is thin, cold and clean, and the river is loud with meltwater.

Practically, fill the tank before the climb and bring warm layers, because the valley is much cooler than the plains. Small guesthouses and cafes serve simple local food, such as grilled meat, fresh bread and cheese pies. It is a place to arrive early, stay quiet and watch the light move along the ridges.
t.eltyubyu@43.2,43.2:
Eltyubyu sits in the Chegem Gorge in Kabardino-Balkaria, a deep cut in the northern flank of the Central Caucasus where the Chegem River has carved its way through pale rock and left a long, narrow valley with mountains on both sides. It is a small place, and the nearest proper town is Tyrnyauz, some twenty-four kilometres away, so this is somewhere to arrive with a full tank and a plan. Bylym and Verkhnyaya Balkariya lie in other valleys around.

The road in is among the more dramatic in the region. The Chegem Gorge squeezes in tightly, with cliffs almost touching the road in places and waterfalls tumbling from the rocks after rain. Beyond the gorge, the valley opens into a wide bowl of meadows, with snow peaks standing at the head. The tarmac is narrow and broken in sections, with corners that tighten without warning, and rockfall, livestock and oncoming trucks can all be in the same bend. Ride it slowly, in good light. Late spring through early autumn is the usable season, and a rain-soaked afternoon can bring mud and gravel.

The Balkars, the mountain people of this region, have lived in these valleys for centuries, building stone towers for defence and shelter. The ruins of those towers stand on some slopes, and they give the landscape a human scale that is rare in the high Caucasus. The Balkar people also suffered a bitter chapter in 1944, when they were deported to Central Asia, and were allowed to return in the late 1950s. Many villages in the upper valleys are echoes of that return, and it is worth riding through them with some quiet respect.

The nature is wild. Chegem has famous waterfalls, tumbling over rock faces in the gorge, a sight that draws visitors in summer. Higher up, the meadows are covered in wildflowers, and the air smells of cut grass, sheep and cold stone. Mountain peaks reach well above three thousand metres on the skyline, and in clear weather the contrast between green meadows and white snowfields is striking.

You will find small guesthouses and basic cafes serving Balkar food, such as khychiny, which are flatbreads filled with cheese, potato or meat. Water is plentiful, but fuel is not, so fill in Tyrnyauz or lower down. Bring warm clothing, because the weather turns quickly.
t.upper balkaria@43.1,43.5:
It is a remote corner. Babugent and Zhemtala are the nearest settlements down the valley, and the nearest real town of any size, Kashkhatau, is about twenty-four kilometres away, so plan fuel before you climb.

The ride is a pleasure for anyone who likes quiet mountain roads. The Cherek valley climbs steadily between steep, forested walls that open into wide pastures, with the Cherek river tumbling white beside the road. The tarmac is narrow and patchy in places, with frost heaves, potholes and the occasional landslide, but traffic is light and the corners are mostly open and flowing. A dawn start gives you cool air, soft light on the ridges and empty road. In summer, midday brings heat in the lower valley and cloud in the upper, so keep a jacket handy.

The people here are Balkars, a Turkic mountain people who have herded sheep and cattle in these valleys for centuries. Their stone towers, which stand like chess pieces on the slopes, were built as refuges and watchtowers, and the oldest are several hundred years old. In 1944 the whole Balkar population was deported to Central Asia, and they were not allowed home until the late 1950s. The memory is still present in the villages, and a Balkar household will often welcome a rider with tea, bread and cheese, which is a lesson in how people can hold history and hospitality together.

The surrounding nature is spectacular. Close to this valley lie the Blue Lakes, a group of karst lakes whose water is a startling turquoise, and the nearby mountains rise past four thousand metres, with glaciers visible on clear days. Alpine meadows are alive with flowers in July, and the air smells of crushed grass, woodsmoke and cold water.

For practical purposes, treat this as the end of the road. Fill the tank in Kashkhatau or lower, carry water and snacks, wear layers, and leave time for the way back. Mobile coverage can disappear in the upper valley, so tell someone your plan.
t.akhaltsikhe@41.6,43.0:
Akhaltsikhe means new fortress, and the fortress is the first thing you see: Rabati Castle, a large, restored walled complex on a rise above the Potskhovi river, with a golden-domed mosque, a church and a few towers, floodlit at night. The town of about seventeen thousand people lies in the south of Georgia, in the region of Samtskhe-Javakheti, where the green valleys of the Kura river meet the dry, high plateaus that run toward Turkey and Armenia. Vale, a smaller town, lies to the south.

As a stop, Akhaltsikhe is hugely useful. It has fuel, cafes serving khachapuri and kebabs, markets, guesthouses and mechanics, and it sits at the junction of several of Georgia's best mountain routes. West from here, the road climbs over the Goderdzi Pass toward Adjara and the Black Sea, rising to over two thousand metres through forest, meadows and a final stretch of rough gravel and broken tarmac, with fog and rain common on the western slope. South, the road to Vardzia follows the Kura valley through a country of dry gorges, ruined castles and small farms, with good tarmac and gentle bends. Early summer and September are the best times, and traffic is generally light.

The history here is deep and complicated. The area was the heartland of the Jaqeli princes, who ruled as semi-independent lords under the Georgian crown, and in the sixteenth century it fell under Ottoman control, which lasted until the Russian conquest in 1829. That layered past is visible in Rabati, where Orthodox, Muslim and Armenian buildings stand within the same walls. The population has long included Georgians, Armenians and Muslim Meskhetians, many of whom were deported in 1944 under Stalin, a painful memory that still resonates in the region.

Just a short ride south is Vardzia, the great cave monastery carved into a cliff face in the twelfth century, under Queen Tamar, with hundreds of rooms, a church with frescoes and tunnels. It is among the most striking sights in the Caucasus, and the approach through a quiet gorge adds to the drama. In the other direction, the thermal springs and mineral waters of Borjomi, famous across the former Soviet Union, lie a short distance to the north.

The landscape is a mix of orchards, pastures and dry hills, and the air smells of woodsmoke, fruit and baking bread. Wine, cheese and honey are good, and hospitality is generous.

Fill the tank here, since fuel is sparser on the mountain roads. Bring a warm layer, particularly for Goderdzi, and check the pass conditions, as it may close in winter.
t.mecca outskirts@21.4,40.0:
This one needs a plain word before anything else. Mecca is the holiest city in Islam, and the area around it, the sacred territory known as the Haram, is closed to non-Muslims. Road signs mark the points where non-Muslim traffic is directed to bypass roads, and the rules are enforced at checkpoints. If you are not Muslim, plan to start your ride from the Taif side or well outside the boundary, and look carefully at where the signed limits run before you go anywhere near here.

The landscape is the reason people ride this way at all. The Hijaz escarpment is a wall of dark rock rising abruptly from the Red Sea plain of Tihama to the highlands, and the road from the Mecca basin to Taif climbs it in a long series of hairpins and sweeping bends, gaining over a thousand metres in a short distance. The Mecca basin below sits in blistering heat, easily forty degrees in summer, while Taif at around eighteen hundred metres is often cool and sometimes foggy. The lower ground smells of hot rock and dust and fuel, the upper ground of juniper and, in season, roses.

Saudi roads are generally wide and well surfaced, but the drivers deserve attention. Speeds are high, lane discipline is flexible, and heavy trucks and pilgrim buses crawl the slopes and make overtaking a gamble. Speed cameras are widespread and fines are real, so keep your documents and your licence handy and obey the posted limits. In the pilgrimage season, particularly around Hajj, traffic around Mecca can be gridlocked for hours.

Fuel is not a worry on the main highways, since stations are frequent, and the nearest community of any size, Al Hadā, sits up the mountain with cafes and small shops. Carry water, especially in the lower heat, and wear proper ventilated riding gear, as sun and wind can drain you faster than you notice. The best time to ride is the cooler months from November to March, early in the morning, when the escarpment is quiet and the air is clear.
t.taif@21.3,40.4:
Taif is the cool lung of Saudi Arabia, a city of half a million set on the crest of the Sarawat mountains at something like eighteen hundred metres. After the furnace of the Red Sea lowlands the first lungful of air here is a small shock, and in winter the nights can really bite. For centuries the town has been the place where Hejazi families went to escape the summer, and the royal court still moves up here in the hot months.

Its great product is the rose. Taif roses are grown on small terraced farms in the hills above the city, picked by hand at dawn in a short season around April, and distilled into rose water and an oil that is prized across the Gulf. If you arrive at the right time, the smell drifts down the valleys and into the shops of the old souq, where you can buy a little vial without needing a long conversation. Pomegranates, figs, honey and grapes also come from these slopes, and you will find them in the market stalls.

History runs deep. Before Islam, the plain near Taif hosted the annual fair of Ukaz, where poets recited and tribes traded, and the city later became a prize in the early wars of the Prophet's lifetime.
