The old quarter, with its coral-and-stone houses and wooden shutters, has had a hard time against modern construction, but pockets remain. Taif is open to visitors of every faith, unlike Mecca, so there is no restriction on stopping here, and the downhill road toward the plain is the reason many riders arrive.

The approach from the plain is the ride's high point. Whichever way you take it, it is a long climb through rock walls, tunnels and hairpins, and the road down toward Al Hadā has a cable car running beside it for part of the way. Slow trucks and a lot of cars in summer weekends make overtaking an exercise in nerve, and visibility drops when the cloud rolls in, which happens more often than visitors expect. Fuel and food are everywhere in the city, with plenty of petrol stations on the outskirts, and the evenings, with the heat gone and families out in the parks, are the best part of the day.
t.of@40.9,40.3:
Of is a name that sounds like an exclamation, and the town has had its fun with it. It is a busy Black Sea town of about thirty thousand people at the mouth of the Solaklı river, in the province of Trabzon, wedged between a steep green coast and the sea. The hills behind it are covered with tea bushes, hazelnut groves and dense forest, and almost everything is wet, because the eastern Black Sea gets some of the highest rainfall in Turkey.

The people here are proud of their local identity, with a strong regional dialect and a reputation for toughness and wit. The coast road is busy, with lorries, minibuses and plenty of roadside fish restaurants, and it can be a slow start. But the interest begins when you turn inland and climb up the Solaklı valley toward Çaykara and the famous Uzungöl, a lake formed by a landslide, surrounded by wooden guesthouses and spruce forest. Beyond that, the road keeps climbing.

The D915 is the route that gives this ride its name. It leaves the humid coast and mounts the Pontic Alps by a series of tight, linked bends, known as the Derebaşı bends, with the tarmac doubling back on itself again and again up a forested hillside. The road then crosses a high pass above the tree line at well over two thousand metres, where the vegetation changes to alpine meadows and the air gets thin and cold. Fog is common, and snow can arrive early and linger late, so the pass can close for long periods in winter.

Before you go, take fuel and food in town, since Of has everything and the road above has little. The tea is strong and served in small tulip glasses, and the local specialities include kuymak, a molten cheese and cornmeal dish, and fresh anchovies from the Black Sea, which are eaten fried, in bread or in a rice pilaf. Early summer, when the meadows are flowering, is wonderful, but expect rain at any time. Waterproofs are a necessity, not an option, and a warm layer is wise for the top of the pass.
t.bayburt@40.3,40.2:
Bayburt is a high, dry, windswept city on the upper Çoruh river, and after the green wetness of the Black Sea side it feels like arriving in another country. It sits at roughly fifteen hundred metres, in a plateau landscape of bare brown hills, wheat fields and clear skies, and its thirty thousand residents are used to winters that are long, cold and snowy. A castle dominates the town, a large fortress on a rocky ridge with walls that have been rebuilt many times, by Byzantines, Seljuks and Ottomans, and the view from the ramparts takes in the whole valley.

Bayburt is on an old trade route that connected Trabzon and the Black Sea with Erzurum and Persia, and in the Middle Ages it was part of the great caravan trail. Marco Polo is said to have passed through on his journey east, and the old stone bridge over the Çoruh is a reminder of the traffic that once flowed here. The city is associated with Dede Korkut, the legendary bard of the Oghuz Turks, and there is a monument in his honour. Nearby, the village of Baksı has an unusual museum of contemporary art, built on a hillside by a local artist.

Riding in from the coast, you cross the pass and come down into a wide, open landscape where the road runs fast and straight for long distances. The surface is mostly good, but the weather at altitude can be unpredictable, with strong winds, sudden storms, and cold even in July. The descent from the pass offers dramatic views, particularly late in the afternoon when the low sun lights the slopes. Expect farm vehicles and herds of sheep.

Fuel stations and shops are plentiful, since Bayburt is the main town on this part of the route, and there are simple restaurants in the centre serving lamb, soup and flatbread. The local sweet, a rich dessert of grape molasses and nuts, makes a good snack to carry. Warm clothing is wise even in summer, and in autumn it can be genuinely cold at dusk, so check the forecast before riding the high section back to the coast.
t.chesapeake city@39.5,-75.8:
Chesapeake City is a tiny, tidy canal town on the Maryland shore, in the narrow neck of land between the Chesapeake Bay and the Delaware River, and it exists because someone had the idea of cutting a channel across the peninsula. The Chesapeake and Delaware Canal, opened in 1829, links the two waterways, saving ships a long voyage down the bay and around Cape Henlopen. It was enlarged and straightened in the twentieth century, and still carries a great deal of shipping, so the sight of a huge container ship gliding past the end of a village street is normal here.

The old town is split by the canal into a north and a south side, each with Victorian houses, small shops, cafes and inns that look over the water. It is pleasant to walk, especially in the evening, when the lamps come on and the lock-keeper's old pump house, now a small museum, catches the light. A tall, arching bridge carries the road high over the canal, with a long view of the water and the countryside on both sides, and it is a good start to the ride.

From here, the byway heads south through the Upper Eastern Shore, a flat, quiet countryside of farm fields, tidal creeks, hedgerows and little towns. The roads are gentle and winding, with a good surface, mostly modest speeds, and plenty of places to pull over. You are never far from water, and the landscape changes with the season, from green fields in spring to golden stubble in autumn. Wildlife is part of the show, with herons, ospreys, geese and swans, and deer at dusk.

The town is small, with fewer than a thousand people, so for fuel head to Elkton, about nine kilometres away, where you will find stations and shops. In town, cafes and taverns serve Chesapeake favourites: crab cakes, steamed blue crabs seasoned with Old Bay, oysters in season, and cold beer. Summer is warm and humid, with biting insects near the marshes, and the best months for riding are May, June, September and October, when the air is cooler and the light softer. Weekday mornings are especially calm.
t.easton maryland@38.8,-76.1:
Easton is the county seat of Talbot County and the unofficial capital of Maryland's Eastern Shore, a handsome town of about seventeen thousand people on the flat, creek-slashed land between the Chesapeake Bay and the Choptank River. It is a place of brick courthouses, tree-lined streets, galleries and boutiques, and an old hotel on the main street, and it has an air of quiet prosperity. For a rider at the end of a day, it is a comfortable place to get off the bike and find a good meal.

The shore's story is one of water. Waterfowl, oysters, crabs and fish brought the first settlers, and the culture still revolves around the bay, with its working boats, old boatyards and hunting traditions. In November, the town hosts a large waterfowl festival, with decoy carving, painting and retriever demonstrations. Nearby, the Third Haven Quaker Meeting House, built in the seventeenth century, is among the oldest surviving wooden religious buildings in the country, and visitors can see its simple, plain interior. Frederick Douglass, born into slavery in Talbot County, is also tied to the area, and several sites in the region tell his story.

The roads around Easton are the opposite of mountain riding. They are flat, straight and quiet, running between fields of corn and soybeans, through marshes and past old farmhouses, with long bridges over the creeks. It is gentle, meditative riding, ideal for a late afternoon, when the light turns gold on the water. Wind off the bay can be brisk, and in summer the air is hot and sticky, with mosquitoes and greenhead flies near the marshes. Speeds are generally low, and local police pay attention.

A short ride from Easton is Saint Michaels, a sleepy harbour town with a maritime museum and a lighthouse, where many people go for lunch and a walk. For food, order crab, the blue crab of the Chesapeake, steamed and cracked with a mallet at a paper-covered table, or a crab cake, which here is mostly crab and little filler. Everything you need, including fuel, is available in Easton itself, and the evenings are pleasant on a restaurant terrace.
t.whalebone junction@35.9,-75.6:
Whalebone Junction takes its name from a whale skeleton that once stood here, and it is not much to look at now: an intersection and a few shops on a narrow strip of sand between the Atlantic and Roanoke Sound. But it matters, because this is the point where the roads from the mainland meet NC 12, the highway that runs down the Outer Banks, and from here you head south into Cape Hatteras National Seashore, with ocean on one hand and sound on the other.

The Outer Banks are barrier islands, long, low ridges of sand constantly shifted by storms, tides and wind, and living on them has always been precarious. This stretch of coast has seen hundreds of shipwrecks, and the area is nicknamed the Graveyard of the Atlantic. It is also where the Wright brothers flew the first powered aeroplane in 1903, a few miles north near Kitty Hawk and Kill Devil Hills, where a memorial stands on the dunes. Just south of the junction, the black and white striped Bodie Island Lighthouse stands among the marshes.

The ride is flat and open, with long straight runs broken by gentle curves, the dunes rising on one side and the marsh on the other. It is a pleasure when the air is clear, but wind is the dominant feature, and crosswinds can be strong enough to push a motorcycle across the lane. Sand drifts across the road after storms, so watch for patches, and in places the road is close to the water and may be flooded by high tides and hurricanes. Summer weekends bring dense traffic from beach visitors, so early morning is best.

You can fill the tank at the stations in Nags Head, a few kilometres north of the junction, and at Kill Devil Hills, and you should do so, since services thin out as you go south. Seafood is excellent, with shrimp, oysters, soft-shell crab and local fish served in simple cafes. The bridge across Oregon Inlet takes you onto Hatteras Island, and free ferries run beyond it, across to Ocracoke. In summer, mosquitoes and biting flies can be a nuisance, and autumn brings calm, warm days and fewer crowds, which makes it the best time to ride.
t.cedar island@35.0,-76.3:
Cedar Island is the end of the road, in a way that is surprisingly pleasant. It is a quiet, flat, marshy tongue of land on the far eastern edge of the North Carolina mainland, at the end of a long road through pine woods and salt marsh, and it faces the Pamlico Sound. Here the highway meets the ferry terminal, where boats leave for Ocracoke island, and the whole place feels like a pause between two worlds.

This part of the coast is known as Down East, and its communities have fished, crabbed and built boats for centuries. Many of the families are descended from the early settlers, and you may hear an old accent here, sometimes called the Outer Banks brogue, that retains a few echoes of older English. Wood duck decoys and boat building are traditional crafts, and the little villages along the road have a plain, weathered look. Cedar Island National Wildlife Refuge protects marsh and woodland, and in winter the sky fills with ducks and geese.

The ride in is long, flat and pretty, passing through tiny settlements, across salt marsh and over small bridges, with Core Sound on one side. There is not a lot of traffic, but the wind can be strong, and in summer the marsh breeds clouds of biting insects, so keep the visor down. Heavy rain and storm surge occasionally flood low parts of the road. The ferry to Ocracoke takes a couple of hours, and in summer it is wise to reserve a place, since motorcycles are normally accommodated but the boats fill up.

Services here are minimal, so arrive with a full tank, since stations are scarce. The larger towns of Beaufort and Morehead City, along the coast to the west, have all the fuel, food and lodging you could need. If you plan to take the ferry, check the schedule and the weather, because crossings can be cancelled in high winds and storms. Bring water, some snacks and a good book, because you may have a wait. The sunsets over the marsh, with the light turning gold and then pink across the water, are often spectacular, and the birdlife is rich throughout the year.
t.front royal@38.9,-78.2:
Front Royal is the northern gateway to Skyline Drive, a small Virginia town of about fifteen thousand people in the Shenandoah Valley, where the north and south forks of the Shenandoah River meet. The Blue Ridge rises to the east, a long wall of forest that goes violet at dusk, and the main street has a mix of old brick buildings, antique shops, diners and a town green with a gazebo. It is a convenient and friendly place to prepare for the mountains.

Like most of the valley, it saw a lot of fighting during the Civil War. In May 1862, Stonewall Jackson's army struck the Union garrison here in a surprise attack that opened his famous valley campaign, and control of the town changed hands many times afterwards. A small museum recalls the story. The area was also home to Mosby's Rangers, a Confederate guerrilla band that harassed Union supply lines, and the surrounding countryside is known as Mosby's Confederacy.

Skyline Drive begins just outside the town and climbs along the crest of the Blue Ridge for a hundred and five miles through Shenandoah National Park, with the valley on one side and the Piedmont on the other. Built in the 1930s with the help of the Civilian Conservation Corps, it has a speed limit of thirty-five miles an hour, and the pace is part of the pleasure. The curves are smooth and easy, the surface is good, and about seventy overlooks give views over the valley, where mist often pools in the mornings. There are very few places to buy fuel on the drive, so fill up in Front Royal before entering.

Black bears are common in the park, and deer wander across the road, particularly at dusk, so keep your speed down. In autumn, the leaves turn from late September to late October, and the Drive can be crowded on weekends. Spring brings wildflowers and a fresh green. Fog can be thick, and the road may close in winter because of ice. Bring a jacket, since the temperature on the ridge can be ten degrees lower than in the valley, and a rain layer is wise, since afternoon thunderstorms are common in summer.
t.rockfish gap@38.0,-78.9:
Rockfish Gap is a low saddle in the Blue Ridge Mountains, and it has a history that outweighs its modest size. It was a natural crossing from the Piedmont to the Shenandoah Valley long before roads were built, and in the nineteenth century a turnpike and then a railway tunnel used it. Today, Interstate 64 passes through it, and it is where Skyline Drive ends and the Blue Ridge Parkway begins, so the gap is a kind of hinge between two of the great scenic roads of the eastern United States.

In 1818, a commission chaired by Thomas Jefferson met at a tavern at the gap to choose the site for a state university, and agreed on Charlottesville, which led to the founding of the University of Virginia. The Appalachian Trail also crosses here, and hikers walking from Georgia to Maine pass through on their way. If you see a tired, bearded stranger with a heavy pack and a gleam in his eye at the roadside, he is probably two thousand miles into the trip.

For riders, it is a sort of finish line. The southern end of Skyline Drive winds down gently from the high ridge toward the gap, through hardwood forest, with views over farmland to both sides. At the gap, the Blue Ridge Parkway starts at milepost zero and runs south for four hundred and sixty-nine miles to the Great Smoky Mountains, and many riders continue straight on. Speed limits are low on both roads, and the pace is relaxed, which suits the long, looping, hilltop curves.

Waynesboro, a small city of over twenty thousand just below the gap, has fuel stations, supermarkets, restaurants and motels, and it is the sensible place to refill and rest. There is little fuel on the Parkway itself, so fill up before leaving. Weather in the Blue Ridge can change quickly, with fog and rain, and the Parkway sometimes closes in winter. Autumn is the busiest and most colourful time, while spring brings wildflowers and cool mornings. In summer, the ridge is a good place to escape the heat of the lowlands.
t.jvari pass@42.5,44.5:
The Jvari Pass is the high point of the Georgian Military Highway, the road that has linked Tbilisi and the north Caucasus for centuries and that the Russian empire paved and straightened in the nineteenth century. At 2,379 metres, it divides two worlds: south of the summit the Aragvi river runs down towards Mtskheta and the Georgian heartland, while on the north side the waters head toward the Terek and Russia. The name simply means cross, and the monument at Gudauri, a short way down, was built in the Soviet era to celebrate friendship between the two nations. Politics have moved on; the view has not.

Gudauri itself is a ski resort, and the whole upper valley feels like one. From the south you climb out of the green valley of Pasanauri in a string of bends, and the road gets steeper and more open as the trees give way to grassy slopes. Above Gudauri you have wide, easy corners and big sky, with cloud often rolling over the ridge at lunchtime. Trucks are a real feature of this road, particularly lines of lorries heading for the Russian border, and you will spend a few corners behind a diesel plume. Overtake with care; the surface can be patched and uneven, and the edge is often unprotected.

The weather changes quickly up here. Fog, rain, and even snow outside high summer are normal, and in winter the pass closes or restricts traffic when storms blow through. Mornings are clearest, and early autumn gives the most stable days with the hillsides turning gold. Wear layers, because the temperature at the top may be a surprise after a warm valley.

For a rest, Gudauri has cafes, small hotels and viewpoints, and the paragliders launching from the slope above the resort are worth ten minutes of your attention. Fuel is available in Gudauri during the season, but the sensible plan is to start with a full tank from Mtskheta or Pasanauri, or to refill farther north at Stepantsminda, beneath Mount Kazbek. The long ridge to the north is the Greater Caucasus, and on a clear day, with snow in the high gullies, you will understand why people have been arguing about who owns this road for a very long time.
t.goderdzi pass@41.7,42.5:
Goderdzi is the quiet cousin of Georgia's famous passes. It crosses the Meskheti range, also called the Shavsheti, at about 2,025 metres, connecting the green, humid coast of Adjara to the dry, high plateau of Samtskhe-Javakheti inland. The change in a single morning is startling. Coming from the Black Sea side you ride through steep tea-country hills, dense beech and spruce forest, rhododendron thickets and fog, and then you pop out onto open alpine meadows where the air is thin and cold and the sky is wide.

The road has long had a reputation for being rough, and sections were unpaved for years. Much of it has been improved in recent times, but conditions vary, and it makes sense to ask locally before you set out. Expect some tight bends, a few potholes, tractors and cows. Weather changes fast; the western slope catches much of the moisture from the Black Sea, so fog and rain are common, while the eastern side is often drier and brighter. Winter closes the pass under deep snow, and it is generally best from early summer through early autumn.

The area around the summit is wild and beautiful: grass slopes covered with wildflowers in early summer, summer pastures dotted with shepherd huts, and in the distance the ridges rolling off in layers. Goderdzi also has a ski resort, which gives a few cafes and hotels in season. The villages on the Adjaran side, such as Khulo, have a mostly Muslim population, a legacy of the Ottoman centuries, and the old timber houses and small mosques sit among terraced hillsides.

For fuel, do not count on anything at the top. The east side has Diokhnisi and the larger town of Akhaltsikhe not too far beyond, while on the west you can resupply in Khulo or Keda. Fill the tank at either end. If the weather is clear, spend a few minutes at the pass for the view, and eat whatever the local cafe offers, usually good bread, cheese and a strong tea or coffee. It is not the most famous pass in the Caucasus, but it is often the one riders remember most fondly because it was empty.
t.borjomi@41.8,43.4:
Borjomi has been selling its water for longer than most countries have had a currency. The town sits in a narrow, wooded gorge of the Kura River, in Samtskhe-Javakheti, and the mineral spring that bubbles out of the ground here has been famous across the Russian empire and the Soviet Union for the better part of two centuries. The water is warm, salty, slightly sulphurous and very much an acquired taste. Locals will tell you it cures nearly everything, and the green bottles appear in shops from Tbilisi to Tashkent.

The town is a pleasant mix of Soviet-era sanatoria, wooden villas and busy cafes along the main street, all squeezed between steep forested slopes. At the end of the main street is the Mineral Water Park, where you can taste the spring for a small fee and where a path leads up through the trees toward warm sulphur baths. The Romanov family fell for the place too. A summer palace at nearby Likani was built for a grand duke in the 1890s, and the royal connection helped make Borjomi fashionable. Beyond the town, the huge Borjomi-Kharagauli National Park offers hiking, bears and some of the best beech and fir forest in the Caucasus.

The riding in and out is relaxed. The road follows the river gorge with gentle bends, tree cover and cool air, a nice contrast to the hot plains further east. Tarmac is generally decent, though trucks use the same route, and speeds are moderate. The turn toward Bakuriani climbs out of the gorge into higher pine country, and this is a ride for a leisurely lunch rather than fast corners.

As a stop, Borjomi is very well provided. It is a town of about fourteen thousand people, so there is fuel, pharmacies, supermarkets, and plenty of restaurants, including places serving grilled trout, khachapuri and local cheese in a leafy setting. It is a sensible place to refuel body and bike before the climb. Parking for motorcycles is easy, and many guesthouses will let you park in a yard. Come in early autumn when the leaves turn, or in summer when it is shaded and cool, and leave your expectations of fast, empty roads at the door.
t.bakuriani@41.8,43.5:
Bakuriani is a mountain town that has spent its whole life being a place to escape to. At around 1,700 metres in the Trialeti range, in the pine forests above Borjomi, it was a summer retreat for the Russian aristocracy and later a Soviet winter-sports training ground, and the grid of wooden dachas and chunky concrete hotels tells both stories. In summer it is sleepy, scented with resin and woodsmoke. In winter the population balloons and skiers fill every cafe.

The road up from Borjomi is the reason to come. It leaves the gorge of the Kura, climbs in long, steady bends through dense spruce and fir, and the temperature drops a few degrees each time you look at the gauge. The tarmac is generally good, with gentle gradients and only the odd rough patch where meltwater has done its worst. There is little traffic outside the ski season, and the corners are the kind that reward a relaxed rhythm instead of aggression. Early mornings in summer are cool and clear; autumn brings red and gold in the undergrowth.

Another way to arrive is also worth mentioning. A narrow-gauge railway, locally nicknamed Kukushka, the cuckoo, has been chugging between Borjomi and Bakuriani since the beginning of the twentieth century, and it still runs, slowly, wheezing through the forest. You will see it from the road in places, and it makes a charming photograph if your timing is right.

Bakuriani itself has all that a rider wants for a short break: small shops, cafes with wood stoves, bakeries, and guesthouses where the owner cooks dinner and talks politics. Fuel is not abundant here, since this is a small town of about two and a half thousand, so the safe plan is to refill in Borjomi, about fifteen kilometres below. Lifts and trails above town lead to open meadows and ridges, with views toward the Lesser Caucasus on clear days. In the shoulder seasons, late spring and late autumn, it can be quiet to the point of closure, so check that your cafe is open before you plan lunch around it.
t.vardzia@41.4,43.3:
Vardzia is a whole town carved into a cliff. High above the Kura River, in the arid, rocky country of southern Georgia near the Turkish border, the face of Erusheti mountain is honeycombed with hundreds of rooms, passages, chapels and cells, the legacy of a monastery complex that was built in the twelfth century under King Giorgi III and his daughter, Queen Tamar. The idea was defence as much as devotion: a hidden refuge in the rock, tucked into the border zone against Mongol and Turkish threats. At its height it is said to have held thousands of rooms spread across many levels.

An earthquake in the late thirteenth century sheared off the outer part of the cliff and exposed the interior, which is why you now see the caves open to the air like the cells of a honeycomb. In the middle of the complex, a rock-cut church of the Dormition still has fragments of wall paintings from Tamar's time, including portraits of the royal family, and monks have returned to live here in recent decades. You can climb the stairs and tunnels, but wear shoes with proper grip, bring a torch if you can, and expect cool damp air inside after the dry heat outside.

The ride from Akhaltsikhe follows the Kura valley through dry hills, orchards and old villages, with fortresses on the heights. Khertvisi, a striking old citadel at the junction of two rivers, stands on the way and deserves a few minutes. Corners are broad and easy, the surface is mostly decent, and the valley glows golden in the late afternoon. Livestock on the road is the main hazard, followed by the odd bus taking its half of the middle.

There is nothing in the way of fuel at Vardzia itself. Akhalkalaki, to the northeast, and Aspindza and Akhaltsikhe, to the north and west, are the sensible places to fill up. Near the site, you will find small cafes and guesthouses serving simple meals. Summer can be hot and crowded with tour buses, so aim for early morning or late afternoon, and consider spring or autumn when the light is soft and the cliffs are almost empty. A modest entrance fee is usual.
t.avenue of the volcanoes point 2@-0.7,-78:
South of Quito the highway passes below Cotopaxi, one of the highest active volcanoes in the world, a nearly perfect cone that rises to about 5,900 metres and wears a cap of glacier ice. On a clear morning the sight from the road is stunning, with the white peak floating above a sea of cloud. The mountain has erupted many times in recorded history, and the most recent period of activity began in 2015, so the national park has been subject to closures and access limits. Check conditions before you head for the entrance.

Machachi is the nearest sizeable town, about twenty-four kilometres away, with Latacunga further south, and both have fuel and food. At this spot there are no services of note, though the park area has a small museum and a visitor centre, and some haciendas offer lunch and rooms. The haciendas, old estates converted into guesthouses, are a good place to rest and eat well, often in stone buildings with fireplaces. Fill the tank in town before you go.

The land here is the paramo, the high Andean grassland, a cool, windswept landscape of tussock grass, cushion plants and small lakes. Wild horses run on the slopes, and with luck you may see an Andean condor soaring above the ridges, or a fox slipping through the grass. The air is thin and cold, and the wind can be sharp, so dress warmly and carry waterproofs. At night temperatures fall below freezing.

The road itself is the highway, paved and generally good, but the side roads into the park are cobbled or gravel, and they become slippery in rain and fog. Altitude affects riders and engines alike, and the climb to the high car park is steep. Take it slowly, rest often, and be ready to turn back if the cloud closes in, because Cotopaxi can hide itself for days. Early morning, before the cloud builds, is the best time to see the peak, and the soft pink light on the snow is worth getting up for.
t.quilotoa loop point 2@-1.0,-78.9:
Out in the high country west of Latacunga the farms get smaller, the fields steeper, and the road begins to climb towards the great barren plateau of the western cordillera. This section runs through open paramo and patchwork fields, with the horizon scored by deep valleys. The towns of Pujili and Saquisili lie behind, a day's walk if you had to, but at the pace of a bike they are far enough that fuel is a real concern. Check the tank, because little is on offer here.

Indigenous communities live along this road, mostly Kichwa people who farm potatoes, barley and quinoa on slopes that would defeat anyone else. Their houses, built of adobe and thatch, sit among the terraces, and women in felt hats and bright shawls walk the road with children and loads. The Tigua area further along is known for its paintings, brightly coloured scenes of village life painted on sheepskin, which began as a local art and are now sold across the country. If you meet a gallery open at the roadside, it is a rewarding stop.

The riding is gently demanding. The road is generally paved or well-compacted, with sweeping gradients and the odd stretch of loose gravel, and it twists along the shoulder of the valleys. Dogs, sheep and cattle wander onto the road, so keep the speed down in villages, and slow for blind bends. In the wet season, landslides and potholes appear without warning, particularly after heavy rain, and visibility can drop in cloud.

The altitude, above three thousand metres, means chilly mornings and sharp winds, and the sun burns even when the air is cold. Take a good layer, gloves and a neck warmer. Local food is simple and sustaining: potato soup, corn and cheese, with a glass of hot sweet tea, a good treat when you reach a village. The mood is calm, a kind of slow Andean rhythm, and the sky seems very large. Keep an eye on the weather, because storms can build quickly in the afternoon.
t.quilotoa loop point 3@-0.9,-78.9:
Quilotoa is the reason people come. The crater of an extinct volcano, about three kilometres across, holds a lake of astonishing colour, a turquoise to emerald green that shifts with the light and the minerals dissolved in it. The rim sits at about 3,900 metres, and the drop to the water is some three hundred metres, with a steep path that zigzags down for those who want to touch it. The climb back up is far harder than the descent, so take it slowly, or hire a mule for the way up.

The caldera was formed by a huge eruption roughly eight hundred years ago, and the collapse of the summit created the basin that later filled with water. The crater is still volcanically alive, with bubbles of gas rising and a faint sulphur trace at times, and locals tell stories of a creature or a spirit in the depths. The village of Zumbahua nearby holds a lively Saturday market, where indigenous families trade potatoes, wool and livestock, and the hats and ponchos are a sight in themselves.

The nearest towns are Pujili and Saquisili, and neither is close, so the usual caution applies: no real fuel here, though small guesthouses and cafes around the rim serve soup, trout and hot drinks. They are simple, cold and warmly welcoming, and many have fires. Staying overnight at the rim, you wake to a view few places can match, and the night sky is brilliant.

The wind sweeps the rim hard, so a windproof jacket is essential, and weather swings from hot sun to hail in an hour. Fog can erase the lake entirely, and visitors sometimes arrive to see nothing but white. If that happens, wait; it often lifts. The road to the rim is paved on the main approach but narrow and sometimes potholed, with dogs and livestock. Take care on the cobbled village streets, which are slippery in rain. Early morning is the best time, when the water is calm and the colours deepest, and the crowds have not yet arrived.
t.quilotoa loop point 4@-0.8,-78.9:
Chugchilan is a small village on the edge of a canyon, the sort of place where a day's ride ends with soup and a fire. The valley of the Toachi River drops away below the village in green folds, and the farmland on the far side is cut into a patchwork of squares, with the occasional white house and a thread of smoke. At about 3,200 metres the village is cold in the evening, and the sky clears after dusk to reveal a thick scatter of stars.

There are a handful of lodges and hostels, several of them community-run, with simple rooms, hot meals and wood stoves, and the people are warm and hospitable. A cheese factory in the village, started by an aid project, makes a local cheese that appears in several of the lodges. Fuel is not sold here in any reliable way, and the nearest towns are many kilometres back, so make sure to carry what you need.

The road from Quilotoa is a good one, if narrow, running along the rim of the Toachi canyon in a series of gentle bends with big drops and brilliant views. The surface varies from smooth paving to rough patches, and in the wet season it can turn greasy. Dogs and animals are common, and corners can have livestock or children on them. Keep a steady pace, and sound the horn on blind bends if you must.

The culture here is Kichwa, with Spanish overlay. Villagers wear felt hats and wool ponchos, and keep their language and festivals alive. Corn and potatoes are the staples, and the Sunday market, when it takes place, is lively. The mountains in the evening glow orange, and the air smells of woodsmoke and cattle. Rain is common in the afternoons, and the cloud sometimes sits in the canyon for hours. A good plan is to ride in the morning, with the clearest views, and stop at a lodge for lunch and a hot drink before heading on.
t.quilotoa loop point 5@-0.7,-78.9:
Sigchos is a modest market town set on a green ridge, and arriving feels like returning to the world of roofs, shops and things that look like a town. The road here drops from the high paramo into a warmer, softer valley, where sugarcane and fruit trees start to appear among the maize. The altitude is lower than at Quilotoa, so it is noticeably warmer and the air feels thicker, a relief after the rim.

The town is small, with a central plaza, a church and a handful of shops, and it is a useful stop for a meal and a break. There are small restaurants serving soup, rice and grilled meat, and a stall or two selling fruit juice. Fuel may be available in the town, though the supply is modest, and the nearest big towns are far back, so be ready to carry spare fuel or ride on with care. Carry cash.

The ride in is among the finest of the loop. The road winds along the contour of the valley, crossing streams and passing through villages, with big views over the folded green hills. The corners are mostly gentle, and the surface is decent, though rain can bring landslides and rock fall. Cattle, dogs and the occasional bus appear around bends, and the road is narrow in places. Take it steadily and enjoy the scenery.

The area is a meeting of highland and subtropical climates, which means a wide range of crops and birds. Hummingbirds visit the roadside flowers, and the hillsides are patched with cloud forest. The culture is a mix of mestizo and indigenous, with a strong tradition of farming and cattle. In the afternoon the cloud often rolls up the valleys, so start early to enjoy clear views. From here the road leads on towards the highway, and a return to Latacunga closes the circuit, a day of stunning scenery and a fine test of a rider's patience and stamina.
t.near waynesboro@38.0,-78.9:
Rockfish Gap is a low saddle in the Blue Ridge above Waynesboro, Virginia, and it is one of the great meeting points of American motorcycling. Here, on the crest of the ridge, the Skyline Drive ends its 105-mile run south through Shenandoah National Park, and the Blue Ridge Parkway begins its 469-mile journey south to the Great Smoky Mountains. Interstate 64 crosses the gap too, along with the Appalachian Trail, and on a summer weekend you will see riders from every state stopping for photos at the milepost zero sign.

The views are wide in both directions. To the west lies the Shenandoah Valley, a broad green valley of farms and small towns between the Blue Ridge and the Alleghenies, and to the east the land falls away to the rolling Piedmont, towards Charlottesville and Thomas Jefferson's Monticello. On the ridge just south of the gap stands Swannanoa, a white marble mansion built in 1912 by a wealthy businessman in the style of an Italian villa, a strange and striking sight in the forest.

The two roads are made for slow, scenic riding. The Skyline Drive has a speed limit of 35 miles per hour, an entrance fee for the national park, and more than seventy overlooks, with views over the valley and the mountains, and black bears and deer are common along the road. The Blue Ridge Parkway has a limit of 45, no commercial traffic and no billboards, and it winds along the crest with gentle curves and wide views. Both roads are often closed in winter when snow and ice cover them, and fog is frequent on the ridge, sometimes so thick you can barely see the road. A few kilometres south on the Parkway, Humpback Rocks has an old farmstead and a steep trail to a rocky summit with a great view.

Fuel is the practical issue. There are very few fuel stations on the Skyline Drive and none directly on the Parkway, so you need to leave the road to fill up. Waynesboro, just below the gap, has fuel, food and services, and it is wise to fill up here before heading south or north. Afton, on the eastern side, has a few places to eat.

Spring, with wildflowers and dogwood, and autumn, with the hardwood forests ablaze in red and gold, are the best seasons. Fill the tank, grab a coffee, and choose your direction.
t.near tutamandahostel@-0.2,-78.5:
The strange label is a hostel name that a map database has turned into a town; the real place here is Quito, the capital of Ecuador, stretched along a narrow valley at about 2,850 metres, almost exactly on the equator, with the volcano Pichincha rising directly above the western side of the city. Quito is long and thin, perhaps forty kilometres from end to end but only a few wide, squeezed between mountains, and it has a population of nearly two million.

The old town is one of the best preserved colonial centres in the Americas, and in 1978 it was among the first places in the world to be listed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site. Its churches are astonishing, especially La Compañía, whose interior is covered in gold leaf, and the streets around the Plaza Grande are full of life, with street vendors, shoe shiners and old men sitting in the sun. A cable car, the TelefériQo, climbs the slopes of Pichincha to nearly four thousand metres, with views over the city and, on clear days, the volcanoes. About twenty-five kilometres north, the Mitad del Mundo monument marks the equator, though GPS shows the true line is a short distance away.

The Avenue of the Volcanoes is the name the German explorer Alexander von Humboldt gave to the long valley that runs south from Quito between two chains of the Andes, lined with snow-capped volcanoes. Cotopaxi, at nearly 5,900 metres one of the highest active volcanoes in the world, is the most famous, with a perfect cone of snow, and others like Chimborazo, Tungurahua and the Illinizas rise along the way. The Pan-American Highway runs through the valley, and smaller roads climb to the national parks and mountain villages.

Riding in Quito is a challenge. Traffic is heavy and chaotic, with buses, taxis and trucks, and the steep, winding streets can be confusing. The altitude affects both you and your bike, and the weather changes quickly, with sun in the morning and rain in the afternoon. Once you leave the city, though, the roads are spectacular, with mountain passes, deep valleys and views of the volcanoes.

Quito has fuel, food and every service, and the city has excellent restaurants, from street food to fine dining. Try locro de papa, a creamy potato soup with cheese and avocado, and take time to acclimatise before heading for the high passes.
t.near front royal@38.9,-78.2:
Mile zero of Skyline Drive is just outside Front Royal, and from here the road climbs onto the crest of the Blue Ridge and stays there for a hundred and five miles. This northern end is where you pay at the entrance station, pick up a map, check the speed limit, which is thirty-five miles per hour for the whole length of the drive, and accept that you are here for the views, not the pace. The first few miles climb quickly through oak and hickory forest to the first overlooks, with the Shenandoah Valley spreading out below to the west and the Piedmont rolling away to the east.

Front Royal is a small town of about fifteen thousand at the confluence of the North and South Forks of the Shenandoah River. During the Civil War, it was the scene of a battle in 1862, part of Stonewall Jackson's famous Valley Campaign, and the Confederate spy Belle Boyd, who passed information to Jackson, lived in the town. Today it is a gateway town for the park, with motels, restaurants, outfitters for canoeing on the river and a historic main street. The Skyline Caverns, just south of town, are known for their rare white crystal formations.

Skyline Drive was built in the 1930s, largely by the Civilian Conservation Corps, a New Deal programme that employed young men during the Depression. It was a scenic road designed for motorists, with gentle curves, stone walls and seventy-odd overlooks. The creation of the park had a darker side: hundreds of families who lived in the mountains were moved out, some by force, and their homes were demolished. The remains of their farms, stone walls and old orchards can still be found in the forest.

The riding is gentle, scenic and slow. The asphalt is well kept, and the curves are smooth and flowing, but the speed limit is strictly enforced, and there are plenty of hazards: deer, bears, wild turkeys, cyclists, and tourists stopping suddenly at overlooks. Fog is common in the mornings, and the road can be closed in winter because of snow and ice. The best times to ride are spring, when the wildflowers bloom, and autumn, when the leaves turn red and gold, usually in mid to late October, although that is also when the traffic is heaviest. Front Royal has fuel, food and everything else, so fill up here before heading into the park, as services along the drive are limited.
t.near luray@38.6,-78.4:
Skyland is where Skyline Drive reaches its highest point, at about 3,680 feet, and also where the story of the park really began. Long before there was a national park, a man named George Freeman Pollock ran a mountain resort here, with cabins, a dining hall and entertainments for city folk escaping the summer heat of Washington, and he became one of the most vocal campaigners for creating a national park in the Blue Ridge. Today Skyland is a lodge with rooms, a restaurant and a taproom, and its dining room windows look straight out over the Shenandoah Valley.

Just north of the lodge, Stony Man mountain rises to more than 4,000 feet, and a short and easy trail leads to its summit, a rocky outcrop with one of the best views in the park: the valley below, the town of Luray, the long ridge of Massanutten Mountain in the middle of the valley, and the Alleghenies on the horizon. From certain angles, the cliffs of the mountain are said to look like the profile of a bearded man, hence the name. Hawks and ravens ride the updrafts along the cliffs, and in the evening the sunset over the valley is spectacular.

The drive here is at its most dramatic, with the road running along the crest and overlooks on both sides. The curves are smooth and gentle, the surface good, and the speed limit of thirty-five miles per hour means you have plenty of time to enjoy the views. Watch for black bears, which are common in this part of the park, especially in late summer and autumn when they are feeding on acorns and berries, and for deer, which seem to have no fear of traffic. Weather at this height can be cooler and wetter than in the valley, with fog, rain and wind, and the temperature can drop quickly in the evening.

Down in the valley, about ten kilometres away, the town of Luray is famous for its caverns, the largest in the eastern United States, with huge chambers of stalactites and stalagmites and a so-called Great Stalacpipe Organ, which produces musical tones by tapping the formations with rubber mallets. Luray has fuel, motels, restaurants and shops. To reach it, leave the drive at Thornton Gap and follow US 211 down the mountain, a winding descent through the forest. Inside the park, Skyland has food and lodging, but fuel is limited, so plan accordingly.
t.near stanley@38.5,-78.4:
Big Meadows is the largest open space on Skyline Drive, a broad, grassy clearing on top of the Blue Ridge at around 3,500 feet, and on a summer evening it fills with deer, grazing quietly in the long grass while families watch from the edges. It is not a natural meadow in the strict sense: it has been kept open for centuries, first by Native Americans, who burned it to attract game, then by settlers who grazed cattle on it, and today the park mows and burns it to keep the forest from taking over. Wild blueberries grow here in late summer, and the meadow is full of wildflowers in spring and early summer.

This is the heart of Shenandoah National Park, and it was here, in 1936, that President Franklin D. Roosevelt dedicated the park in front of a large crowd. The Byrd Visitor Center, named after the Virginia senator Harry F. Byrd, has exhibits on the history of the park, including the story of the families who were moved off the land to make way for it. Nearby, Big Meadows Lodge offers rooms and meals in a stone and timber building from the 1930s, and the campground is one of the most popular in the park.

A short but steep trail leads down to Dark Hollow Falls, a pretty waterfall cascading over greenstone rocks, and another trail runs from the area to Rapidan Camp, the summer retreat of President Herbert Hoover, who fished for trout in the streams and hosted visiting dignitaries in the rustic cabins. The camp has been restored, and the park runs ranger-led tours there in season.

For riders, Big Meadows is a natural place to stop: it has food, toilets, water, shade and space to stretch out on the grass. The drive here is smooth and gently curving, with the speed limit of thirty-five miles per hour and wildlife on the road. In autumn, the trees around the meadow turn red, orange and gold, and the views from the overlooks nearby are spectacular. The nights can be cold, even in summer, so bring a warm layer if you plan to camp. For fuel, the nearest towns are Stanley and Luray in the valley to the west, or Harrisonburg further south, and services inside the park are limited and seasonal.
t.near elkton@38.4,-78.5:
Swift Run Gap is where US 33 crosses the Blue Ridge, and where Skyline Drive passes over it on a bridge at about 720 metres, or 2,365 feet. It is one of four entrance stations to the park, and it is a natural break point, with the road dropping west to Elkton and the Shenandoah Valley, and east to Stanardsville and the Virginia Piedmont. The gap itself is a low saddle in the ridge, forested with oak, hickory and maple, and the drive on either side climbs back up to the high ridges in long, smooth curves.

The gap has a place in Virginia legend. In 1716, the colonial governor Alexander Spotswood led an expedition of gentlemen, servants, rangers and Native American guides over the Blue Ridge here, the first organised English party to see the Shenandoah Valley. They drank toasts to the king on the far side, and Spotswood later gave each member a small golden horseshoe, and the group became known as the Knights of the Golden Horseshoe. The story has been embroidered over the centuries, but it marks the moment the valley was opened to settlement from the east.

US 33 is a good road in its own right, with sweeping curves and steep gradients as it climbs from the valley to the gap and down the other side. It carries more traffic than Skyline Drive, including trucks, but the riding is more varied, and the views are good. Elkton, about eight kilometres west, is a small town on the South Fork of the Shenandoah River, with fuel, food and a few shops, and Harrisonburg, a university town, is further west. To the east, the road runs through the Piedmont toward Charlottesville, home of the University of Virginia and Thomas Jefferson's Monticello.

Along the drive just north of the gap, Lewis Mountain was once the only area of the park open to Black visitors during the era of segregation, with its own lodge, campground and picnic grounds. The park has worked in recent years to tell this part of its story. In the evening, the light on the ridges is lovely, with layer after layer of blue hills fading into the distance, the haze that gave the Blue Ridge its name. Bring a warm layer, since the temperature drops quickly after sunset, even in summer.
t.kholmogory@64.2,41.7:
Mikhail Lomonosov, the fisherman's son who walked to Moscow in the winter of 1730 and became Russia's first great scientist, poet, chemist and founder of its first university, was born on an island in the Northern Dvina just outside Kholmogory. His home village now carries his name and has a museum devoted to him, with displays on his life and the Pomor world he came from. For Russians the story of the boy who followed a fish convoy to the capital and changed the country's intellectual life is a kind of national legend.

Kholmogory itself is a quiet village of about four thousand people, but it was once among the most important places in the Russian north. Before Arkhangelsk was founded in the late sixteenth century, this was the main trading town on the Dvina, the seat of governors and archbishops, and the point where English and Dutch merchants came to trade. When the port moved downstream, Kholmogory slowly faded, leaving a few old churches, a cathedral and a sense of past grandeur in a modest setting. The area is famous for two things: a breed of black-and-white dairy cattle, and delicate bone carving, a craft that has been practised here for centuries.

The Dvina valley around Kholmogory is broad and flat, with meadows, channels, islands and forest. In spring the river floods, sometimes dramatically, and in summer the meadows are full of wildflowers and cattle. The roads here follow the valley, mostly flat, with long straights, occasional bends and a surface that varies from good to poor. Traffic is light, but watch for farm vehicles and loose animals. In summer, the white nights mean long, bright evenings, while mosquitoes near the water can be fierce.

The village has a shop or two and simple cafes, and fuel should be available along the main road, though it is worth filling up in Arkhangelsk, about seventy kilometres north, before setting out. The Lomonosov museum is a short ride away, and makes a good stop for anyone interested in Russian history. Take time to wander the old churches, look out over the river, and imagine the merchant ships that once tied up here.
t.gonachkhir gorge@43.3,41.7:
High in the Teberda valley, where the road from Karachayevsk up to Dombay crosses a narrow stretch of gorge, the Gonachkhir River comes in from the west, carrying meltwater from the glaciers along the main Caucasus ridge. Here the old Military Sukhumi Road, built in the nineteenth century to link the North Caucasus with the Black Sea coast, branches off up the Gonachkhir valley toward the Klukhor Pass and the border with Abkhazia. The pass, at roughly 2,780 metres, saw fierce fighting in 1942, when German mountain troops reached the passes and were driven back.

The landscape is classic Caucasus. Steep slopes of spruce, fir and pine rise on both sides, with granite crags and snow-streaked peaks above, and the river roars over boulders far below the road. The Teberda Nature Reserve protects much of the surrounding land, home to bears, chamois, lynx and the West Caucasian tur, a wild mountain goat. In spring, the meadows are covered in wildflowers; in autumn, the beech and birch turn gold against the dark conifers, and the first snow dusts the peaks.

As the finish of a ride up from Teberda toward Dombay, this is a dramatic end. The road climbs steadily through the valley, with tight bends, steep gradients, and some narrow sections where rockfalls and landslides are common after heavy rain. The surface is generally paved, but can be rough and broken in places, and you will share it with buses, taxis and minibuses ferrying tourists up and down. Beyond the junction, the road toward the Klukhor Pass becomes rougher and passes into a border zone, so check rules and permits before heading further.

At the junction itself you will find little beyond a roadside stall. Teberda, a small resort town a short ride down the valley, has fuel, shops and simple cafes, and Karachayevsk, further down, has more. Dombay, a few kilometres up the valley, is a ski resort with hotels, restaurants and cable cars that run in summer too. Stop for a while at the junction, listen to the river, look up at the peaks, and feel the scale of the mountains around you; this is one of the great valleys of the Caucasus.
t.karmadon gorge@42.9,44.5:
On the evening of 20 September 2002, a hanging glacier high above the Genaldon valley broke away and came down the gorge as a torrent of ice, rock and mud, burying everything in its path for kilometres. Among the dead was the actor and director Sergei Bodrov Jr., who was filming here with his crew, and his loss turned the disaster into a national tragedy. Today the Karmadon Gorge is quiet again, but the scars of the Kolka glacier collapse are still visible in the shape of the valley floor, and there is a memorial by the road.

The gorge cuts deep into the northern flank of the Caucasus south of Vladikavkaz, the capital of North Ossetia, with Mount Kazbek and its glaciers hidden in the clouds above. Steep grass slopes rise to grey rock walls, the river runs milky with glacial silt, and old Ossetian stone towers stand on the spurs. Karmadon was once known for its hot springs, which bubbled up in the valley floor and fed a small resort that the 2002 flow destroyed. Some springs still steam here and there, and locals come to bathe. In the neighbouring valley lies Dargavs, the medieval city of the dead, a hillside of stone crypts that is one of the strangest sights in the Caucasus.

The riding in from Gizel and the Vladikavkaz side is short but scenic, climbing up through the foothills on a road that is paved for much of its length, then narrows and roughens as the gorge closes in. Expect potholes, loose stones and occasional rockfall, as well as livestock wandering across the road. Late spring to early autumn is the window; snow and ice make the upper reaches tricky in winter, and summer thunderstorms can bring mudslides.

There are few services in the gorge itself, apart from small guesthouses and perhaps a roadside stall selling cheese or honey. Gizel, about twenty kilometres away, has a shop and fuel, and Vladikavkaz has everything. Bring food and water. Try the Ossetian pies if you see them, round flatbreads filled with cheese, potato or meat, which are eaten everywhere in the republic and are a perfect riding lunch. Pause by the memorial and look up the valley; the mountains here are beautiful, and they demand respect.
t.kurtat gorge@42.9,44.4:
Stone towers are the signature of the Kurtat Gorge. The valley of the Fiagdon River runs south from the plains of North Ossetia into the high Caucasus, and along its slopes stand the fortified towers, crypts and cliff fortresses of the Ossetian clans who lived here for centuries, guarding their pastures and feuding among themselves. The most dramatic is the Dzivgis cave fortress, a wall of stone built into a shallow cave high in a cliff face, where villagers sheltered in times of danger. Walk up to it if you can; the view down the valley is worth the climb.

Ossetians trace their descent from the Alans, an Iranian-speaking people who once controlled much of the steppe and the northern Caucasus, and who converted to Christianity in the early Middle Ages. In the gorge stands a modern Orthodox monastery dedicated to the Assumption, set dramatically on a slope near the village of Khidikus, along with old shrines and sacred groves that still play a part in local life. In the summer, families come up from the cities to picnic and spend time in their ancestral villages, and the gorge fills with smoke from barbecues and the sound of Ossetian music.

The road up the gorge is paved for most of the way, but narrows as it climbs, with tight bends, rough patches, and sections where rockfall or washouts are common after rain. Traffic is light, apart from weekend visitors and cattle on the road. The Fiagdon river, clear and cold, runs alongside, and the slopes are covered in beech and birch forest giving way to high meadows. In autumn the colours are spectacular, and the light in late afternoon turns the towers golden.

Up the valley there are small guesthouses and cafes in Verkhny Fiagdon, a resort village in the valley, and you may find fuel there, but Alagir, about sixteen kilometres away, is a safer bet for fuel and supplies. Try local honey and the famous Ossetian pies, and if offered, a glass of araka, the local spirit, but only when the riding is done for the day. Then sit and look at the towers, standing as they have for centuries, guarding a valley that still feels a world away from the plains below.
t.digor gorge@42.9,43.6:
The Digor Gorge belongs to the Digor people, a branch of the Ossetians with their own dialect, sometimes considered a separate language, and their own history and pride. The valley of the Urukh River cuts deep into the Caucasus in the west of North Ossetia, and the scenery here is among the most dramatic in the republic. At its lower end the river has carved a narrow canyon through limestone, with sheer walls and the road clinging to a ledge above the water, before the valley opens into a basin of green pastures surrounded by snow-capped peaks.

The upper gorge is dotted with villages, old stone towers and family crypts, some abandoned and some still lived in. In the village of Zadalesk, a tower is linked to a legend about a woman who saved her people's children after an invasion, a story that every Digor child knows. The valley is also rich in wildlife, with chamois and tur on the high slopes, golden eagles above, and wildflowers in the meadows in early summer. The glaciers at the head of the valley feed the river, which runs grey and fast, thundering over rocks.

The road up the Digor Gorge is an adventure. It is paved at first, then narrows, roughens and turns to gravel in places, with tight bends, steep drops and some single-lane sections where you have to pull aside for oncoming vehicles. Rockfalls are common, especially after rain or during the spring thaw, so take it slowly and watch for debris on the road. The canyon section is particularly impressive, and the views open out as you climb into the upper valley. Parts of the valley lie close to the Georgian border and may be in a border zone, so check whether a permit is required.

Supplies are thin on the ground. You will find guesthouses and small shops in some villages, but for fuel and supplies, Chikola, about forty kilometres back down the valley, is the nearest town. Fill up before heading in, carry water and food, and allow plenty of time. The Digor Gorge rewards patience: the deeper you go, the wilder and more beautiful it gets, and the sense of having reached a remote, proud corner of the Caucasus is unforgettable.
t.krasnaya polyana@43.7,40.2:
Krasnaya Polyana means Red Meadow, and before 2014 it was a quiet mountain village in the upper valley of the Mzymta River, settled in the late nineteenth century by Greeks and Estonians after the expulsion of the Circassians who had lived here before. The site has a darker history too: in 1864, Russian forces celebrated the end of the long Caucasian War at a place nearby called Kbaade, and for Circassians it remains a place of mourning. Then came the Winter Olympics, and the village was transformed almost overnight into a sprawling resort.

Today Krasnaya Polyana is the gateway to the mountain cluster of the Sochi Olympics, with ski resorts, hotels, apartment blocks, restaurants and shops spreading along the valley. The surrounding mountains are spectacular, with steep forested slopes, rocky peaks and snowfields lingering well into summer. In the warmer months, gondolas carry hikers and mountain bikers up to high meadows and viewpoints, and the forests around the village are full of waterfalls, walking trails and wild flowers.

The ride from Adler and the coast follows the Mzymta valley, on a modern road built for the Olympics, with tunnels, bridges and long, sweeping bends. The old road, narrower and more winding, still runs alongside in places, and is more fun if you can find it. The surface is generally excellent, but traffic can be heavy, especially at weekends and during holidays. Set off before nine and you will have the valley mostly to yourself. Watch for buses, taxis and impatient drivers.

Krasnaya Polyana has all the services a rider needs: fuel, shops, cafes, restaurants and hotels of every kind. The village has some good places to eat, from simple Caucasian grills to more upscale restaurants. Try khachapuri, the cheese-filled bread popular across the Caucasus, or grilled trout from the mountain rivers. Take a stroll along the river, look up at the peaks, and remember that, behind the shiny resort, there is a much older and more complex story in these mountains.
t.rosa khutor@43.7,40.3:
Rosa Khutor is the end of the road, quite literally. The valley of the Mzymta narrows here, high in the mountains above Krasnaya Polyana, and the resort that hosted the alpine skiing events of the 2014 Winter Olympics fills the floor with hotels, chalets and a riverside promenade designed to look like an Alpine village. Beyond it, the road stops, and the only ways onward are on foot, by mountain bike, or by gondola up to the ridges, where the peaks rise to over two thousand metres and the border with Abkhazia lies just beyond.

The resort itself can feel a little artificial, with its clock tower, neat squares and tidy shopfronts, but the setting is magnificent. The river runs fast and green between the buildings, the mountains rise steeply on all sides, and the forests are thick with beech, fir and chestnut. In summer the high meadows above the resort burst with wildflowers, and the lifts carry walkers up to viewpoints, hiking trails and lakes. In winter the slopes are covered in snow, and the resort is busy with skiers and snowboarders.

As the finish of a ride up from Sochi, Rosa Khutor offers a satisfying conclusion. The road up the valley from Krasnaya Polyana is short but scenic, with bends along the river, bridges and tunnels, and views of the mountains ahead. The surface is excellent, built to Olympic standards, though traffic can be heavy during the holiday season. Parking is available near the resort, and it is easy to walk around once you arrive. Shoulder months, June and late September, give mild weather without the holiday crush.

There are plenty of hotels, cafes and restaurants at Rosa Khutor, catering to every budget, and fuel is available in Krasnaya Polyana, a few kilometres back down the valley. Take a gondola up to the top if you can; the view across the Caucasus, ridge upon ridge, is extraordinary, and the air is cool even in summer. Afterwards, find a terrace by the river, order something warm, and watch the light fade on the peaks above.
t.artvin@41.2,41.8:
Artvin is a mountain city in the far north-east of Turkey, built in steep terraces on the slope above the Çoruh River, and it feels like the end of a long road in the best sense. The valleys here are deep and narrow, the forests are dense and the sky is often full of cloud pushed in from the Black Sea. Roughly twenty-four thousand people live in the city, so fuel, food and a bed are all easy to find, and the road down the valley leads on to Hopa on the coast.

The Çoruh is a powerful river, famed among paddlers, and in recent years it has been dammed in a series of hydroelectric projects that have changed the valley and put some older roads under water. The landscape is a mix of pine and beech forest, high pastures and small villages perched at improbable angles. The region is also the old Georgian borderland, and the valleys around Artvin hold ruined churches and monasteries from the medieval Georgian kingdoms, some of them wonderfully remote.

The riding to get here is dramatic. The roads climb and drop through gorges, often cut into rock walls above the river, with tunnels, tight bends and a surface that ranges from good to rough after landslides or heavy rain. Weather can be wet, and mist in the valley changes visibility quickly, so ride within your sight line and keep your visor clean. Trucks and minibuses use these roads too, and local drivers pass with more confidence than is always wise.

Near the city, in early summer, the Kafkasör festival draws crowds for traditional bull-wrestling on a high meadow, a custom that is more about the contest between the animals than any harm. The area is also known for its honey and for hearty food, with cornmeal dishes, local cheese and fresh trout in the valley restaurants. After a long ride through the Kaçkar valleys, a hot meal, a view across the terraced hillside and a bed with a window facing the river are all you need.
t.near tbilisi@41.7,44.8:
Tbilisi spreads along the Mtkvari river in a bowl of dry hills, and its first impression is of balconies. Old houses lean over narrow streets with carved wooden verandas, sulphur bathhouses sit under domes of brick in the Abanotubani district, and on the ridge above, the ruined Narikala fortress watches the city. The name Tbilisi comes from a Georgian word for warm, and the story says that a hunting king found hot springs here and decided to found a city.

This is where the Georgian Military Highway begins, the old road north to Russia across the central Caucasus. Russia built it in the nineteenth century after taking over Georgia, to move troops and supplies, and it follows an even older caravan route through the Darial gorge. Writers and travellers, from Pushkin to Lermontov to Dumas, have described the journey, and the road still has a romantic reputation. Soon after leaving the city you pass Mtskheta, Georgia's ancient capital, where the sixth-century Jvari monastery stands on a hilltop above the junction of two rivers.

From Tbilisi the road goes north along the Aragvi, past the Zhinvali reservoir and up through Gudauri, a ski resort, to the Jvari Pass at about 2,400 metres, before dropping to Stepantsminda beneath Mount Kazbek. Surfaces are mostly good, though lorry traffic is heavy, and tunnels and avalanche galleries add to the adventure. Snow can close the high section from late autumn to spring. Summer is the best season, with clear air, wildflowers and blue skies.

Tbilisi has everything a rider needs. Fuel stations are everywhere, and there are bike mechanics, shops and plenty of lodging. The city traffic is lively and drivers are creative, so be alert, especially on roundabouts. Food is a delight: khachapuri, the cheese-filled bread, and khinkali, spiced dumplings you eat with your hands, are on every menu, along with the local amber wine made in clay vessels. A day to wander the old town is a good investment before heading north.
t.near gudauri@42.5,44.5:
Gudauri is a ski resort first and a village by accident, strung along the road a little below the Jvari Pass in the High Caucasus, at roughly two thousand metres. In winter it is full of Georgians, Russians and Gulf visitors with skis, and the lifts rise from just behind the hotels. In summer it empties out, the slopes turn into flower meadows, and paragliders drift above the grass. Either way the main road, the old Georgian Military Highway, runs straight through the middle, and everything on it, from lorries to cows, goes by at its own speed.

The highway is the story. For centuries this was the one real road through the central Caucasus, linking Tbilisi with Vladikavkaz and Russia, and the Russians strengthened it after they took over Georgia in 1801. The climb from the south is long and steady, up the valley of the Aragvi, with grassy slopes and then bare mountain, and above Gudauri the road tackles the pass, with hairpins, tunnels and snow galleries. The surface is much better than it used to be, though potholes, rockfall and roadworks are a fact of life. The weather is the real boss: fog, sleet and sudden snow can arrive in any month, and in winter the pass is sometimes closed to heavy traffic.

Just beyond the resort, a big curved concrete viewing platform, decorated with a Soviet-era mosaic, sits on the edge of a vast gorge. It was built in 1983 to mark two hundred years of friendship between Georgia and Russia, and today it is mainly a viewpoint, with a long drop into the green valley below and the road wriggling across the mountainside opposite. Stalls sell wool socks, honey and local sweets, and on a clear day the light on the ridge is fine.

Gudauri has a few stations and shops, but supplies thin out quickly, and prices are those of a resort. The nearest proper town to the south is Pasanauri, about twenty kilometres away, with more services, and it is wise to start the climb with a full tank. Bring warm clothes, even in summer, because the wind at this altitude cuts through a mesh jacket, and keep an eye on the cattle, which have no fear of motorcycles and a firm belief in their right of way.
t.near caykara@40.7,40.1:
Çaykara means tea stream, which is a fair summary of what you see here. The town sits in a deep valley in the eastern Black Sea mountains of Turkey, in Trabzon province, and the slopes around it are covered with tea bushes in neat green terraces, clinging to hillsides that look too steep for any farmer. The air is damp, the clouds sit low, and the whole country smells of wet earth, woodsmoke and the faint bitter-sweet scent of tea leaves.

Tea became the local living in the twentieth century. Before that, the people of these valleys grew hazelnuts, corn and beans, and moved their cattle to the high summer pastures, the yaylas, and some still do. Now the cash crop is tea, and the harvest from spring to autumn shapes the life of the valley: women with baskets work the rows, the factories hum, and every house offers a glass of strong, dark tea in a small tulip-shaped cup. The people speak in a quick, singing accent that other Turks love to imitate, and they are known for their humour and their hospitality.

For riders, Çaykara is the doorway to the high country. The road up the valley leads to Uzungöl, the long lake, and to the yaylas above, and it climbs through forest on a series of bends that grow tighter and wetter as you rise. The tarmac is generally good, but rain is frequent here, so the surface can be slick, and landslides sometimes bring rocks or mud across the road. Fog can turn the mountains into a grey wall. The best time is late spring to early autumn, with mornings usually clearer, and the greenest months are May and June.

As a stop, the town does the job well. It has well over fourteen thousand people, petrol stations, banks, bakeries, small restaurants and shops, and it is the last place to fill the tank properly before the mountains. Local food includes muhlama, a rich dish of melted cheese, butter and cornmeal, along with anchovies from the coast, grilled trout and fresh bread. A tea garden by the river is a pleasant place for a pause.

Buy a packet of local tea if you can. It is cheap and travels well, and it tastes better when you remember the valley.
t.near alaverdi@41.1,44.7:
Alaverdi is squeezed into the bottom of the Debed canyon, in the north of Armenia, so tightly that the houses seem to be stacked on top of each other up both sides. The river runs below, the railway and the road run beside it, and above rise steep green slopes with cliffs and monasteries. The town grew in the Soviet period around a copper smelter, which worked for decades, and the industry has left a distinctive atmosphere: apartment blocks, rusting pipes, and a feeling of a place that has seen better days but has not given up.

The glory of Alaverdi lies above it. On the plateau overlooking the canyon, the monasteries of Sanahin and Haghpat, both founded in the tenth century, are among the finest in Armenia and are recognised by UNESCO. Their dark stone churches, carved crosses called khachkars and old scriptoria create an atmosphere of deep age, and lamps flicker in cool vaults that smell of wax and stone. Sanahin was the birthplace of the Soviet politician Anastas Mikoyan, and a small museum remembers the Mikoyan brothers, one of whom designed the MiG fighter jets.

For riders, the Debed canyon road is the draw. The route from Vanadzor winds through the gorge, with the river at the bottom and forested cliffs overhead, passing small villages and stone bridges, with tight bends and tunnels. A medieval bridge at Sanahin, with a high arch, spans the river. The surface is generally good on the main road but patchy on the side roads that lead up to the monasteries, which are steep and narrow with tight hairpins. Mist often fills the canyon in the morning, and in winter ice is a hazard.

Fuel is easy at Alaverdi, which has several stations, and there are more at Vanadzor, farther south. In a cafe by the road, order khorovats, grilled meat on skewers, with lavash and fresh herbs. The best time to visit is May to October, with autumn colour in the oak and beech forest. Armenian drivers are fast and overtake freely, so keep your wits about you on blind bends.
t.near guayaquil@-2.2,-79.9:
Guayaquil is the biggest city in Ecuador, a hot, noisy and energetic port on the Guayas river, a few degrees south of the equator, and the place where a rider's journey up the coast begins. It is a commercial city, and proud of it. In the nineteenth century, cocoa made fortunes here, and the grand houses and the old customs building along the river recall that boom. The waterfront walk, the Malecón, runs for more than two kilometres along the river with gardens, fountains and a lighthouse, and on a warm evening it is full of families.

The city has a few oddities worth knowing. In a small square near the cathedral, wild iguanas lounge in the trees and on the benches, apparently unbothered by the crowd, and the guides will tell you to look up. The old district of Las Peñas, a steep hillside of painted wooden houses, climbs to a hilltop chapel by four hundred and forty-four steps, and the view from the top over the river and the city is excellent. The food is a pleasure, with ceviche served with popcorn, encebollado, a fish soup that is the traditional hangover cure, and fried plantains.

The ride that starts here is the Ruta del Spondylus, which follows the Pacific coast northwest through fishing villages and beaches. The route is named after the spiny oyster, Spondylus, whose red-orange shell was prized by the peoples of the Andes as a sacred offering and traded for hundreds of kilometres. The road runs through dry scrub on the Santa Elena peninsula, then through greener country toward Manabí, with surf towns, mangroves and long empty beaches. Surfaces are mostly good, with sections of roadworks and occasional potholes.

Leaving Guayaquil is the hardest part, since traffic is heavy, with buses, trucks and motorcycles filling every lane, and the heat and humidity are strong. Set off early, before the roads fill up. Fuel is cheap and plentiful, with stations on every main road, though quality and supply vary in small places, so fill up before leaving the larger towns. Rain is heavy between January and April, and the dry season runs from May to December. The coast gets a morning mist, called garúa, in the cooler months, and the sea is cooler than you might expect.
